Schizoanalysis, then, is a form of social analysis according to abstract machines, lines of flight or deterritorialisation, regimes of signs, the stratification of molecular elements or their destratification, and planes of consistency. It maps the social unconscious according to its movements and intensities of desire. [...] so that lines of experimentation or becoming may be constructed through a reassembling of the abstract machines that lie between the strata and produce them.[6]

— Philip Goodchild
Deleuze and Guattari write in the fourth chapter of Anti-Oedipus, "Introduction to Schizoanalysis", that in effect, schizoanalysis asks "What are your desiring-machines, what do you put into these machines, what is the output, how does it work, what are your nonhuman sexes?".[8]

Deleuze and Guattari develop four theses of schizoanalysis:

Every unconscious libidinal investment is social and bears upon a socio-historical field.
Unconscious libidinal investments of group or desire are distinct from preconscious investments of class or interest.
Non-familial libidinal investments of the social field are primary in relation to familial investments.
Social libidinal investments are distinguished according to two poles: a paranoiac, reactionary, fascisizing pole and a schizoid revolutionary pole.

Schizoanalysis does not proceed through the prism of any given technique, theory, or principle. As such, it draws upon both Freud's libido and Jungian complexes, structuralism, and dialectics.
As we will see, some of our films of the early work, while experimental in terms of medium, have been rooted firmly in the schizoanalysis framework.

Others have remained a priori experiments of style or vision, sometimes rejecting all social-psychological-psychoanalysis themes and structure.
A schizoanalysis film can be any genre. One might say that any of my films is a kind of "schizoanalysis", for every one of them offers a different mode of looking, with its own specificities and styles, whether that's cinematic, architectural or intellectual.

But each one is an exercise in the same way. The general sense that one explores in the film can change from film to film, but it never goes away completely. There is no direct or causal relationship between form and content in schizoanalysis films, only a random movement through forms, symbols, lines, planes, registers and orders, from a plane of consistency to an opposite, a destabilised condition or a point of instability.

In all cases, form is linked to the desire-machine of the unconscious: its imagery, intensity of images, desires and inversions.
For example, at first we will move along the line of consistency, by showing a series of positive images. After the "correcting" inversion phase of the schizoanalysis procedure we are then forced into a more erratic state of disruption, before a return to an altered condition of order.

Schizoanalysis, according to Deleuze and Guattari, proceeds from an idealized (inverted) position of non-continuity to a state in which things appear to be at rest. We could call this "putting to rest", or perhaps "the beginning of a new cycle".
Thus schizoanalysis begins with a negative image in our case of film.

As this phase of schizoanalysis unfolds, and we proceed through different forms of images and movements, we begin to approach positive images again. They will appear very suddenly, sometimes not even as an effect of the film, but in some way they're introduced, inserted as if by magic or design. And when we've reached the final state of schizoidal harmony (which can be described as "true unity"), we will finally return to positive images, that is to say

the "reality", the "actual", the "given".
Our film I have described to you thus far is called "The Return of the Birds" or, more specifically, "The Return of the Birds after the Schizoanalysis." For the film, we will shoot a series of sequences following a group of birds migrating north towards their breeding ground. They go into a trance state (again) and take to flight, but it's unclear as to why exactly the birds

fly and what they actually want to achieve, as we don't see where they are going.
Schizoanalysis, then, is not to be confused with simple conceptual film (or, indeed, other formal procedures). Rather, schizoanalysis has to do with the interconnection of all images: moving images (from frame to frame), the film medium itself, the space (real or simulated) where these moving images were shot, and the act of watching them.

In this sense, each scene of each film is an experiment, the product of one step of an endless process. We are constantly rethinking things, turning on and off mechanisms and phases. Each new iteration of the schizoanalysis film will be different, depending upon where we are at the moment, and where the viewers are as well.
In "I" (2012–13) the first segment of my most recent work, the film follows a figure or "my

self" (it can be both) wandering around a factory, while shooting the scenes of the film, while editing and moving between scenes. A film like this could easily be interpreted as a very theatrical construct in which I am playing myself.
Indeed, for much of the film we have a static image of myself as an actor, but our eye does not move in any single direction for a long time (with only occasional moving lines representing the characters moving about or carrying out

their routines). This is because we don't know what I'm doing with myself—for we do not know why we are shooting or if it matters who I am or what is going on at the same time that I am filming myself. But the actors' relationship to themselves is intimately connected with the actors' relationship to the world, so while you have this static image of me as an actor on camera, but in the same time your eye, looking at my image as

I walk about the room or through a set of spaces, could well end up caught in this kind of loop or infinite sequence of scenes where there is never an end to this going on. Or, even while moving, I keep changing and re-forming my self into other selves and faces, showing myself not as I am now, but rather as other, unknown beings or objects that I may be.

In this sense we are always looking at (watching) "the movie" itself, which we can only see partially (but enough to keep us distracted) or less (more than halfway through the film, we stop watching completely). And though we are shown glimpses of the films characters we are never really sure when something is actually happening (as we become less and less attentive), and if so, why, or whether the film's events are necessary, meaningful, or even

necessary at all (if what we watch isn't part of some larger narrative).
Another example of an extremely fragmented work—though much more short and sweet—is the "Five Scenes of a Party" segment of my ongoing series on cinema and its functions. A party scene begins in each new iteration, after a very small amount of time has passed. But nothing happens, not with the exception of a brief return to the original image that starts things off, and the re

winding of this shot while showing the images that have been filmed so far. Eventually, we notice a repeating pattern emerging and the way in which each new party takes place in the same way (more or less the same layout, and with the same furniture, among other things) while somehow still being a different party. We know from the beginning that this is probably another iteration of the same scene, but not knowing exactly how this plays out, or precisely where we are at

all, it is not so strange to be thinking that this might be one long party in which one continuous loop will repeat forever. This film ends when our eyes stop watching altogether (or when they close involuntarily, not unlike sleepwalking).

Each shot should be simultaneously a single moment of the film as a whole—yet different for each occasion and in its particular combination of parts. At the same time, these parts (different scenes, events) can become part of an ongoing narrative (which has the form of a series of jumps in time, through time, and in the time-space

of the film itself) or each part taken by itself. As if the individual moments within the film are already part of something bigger, each part is also already part of the film. These are all assumptions necessary in order to visualize what would happen if we were to experiment with this filmic hypothesis in real time and space: in different sets, locations, situations and physical mediums, but always with a certain number of shots of the same scene, using similar or identical actors

(for there's no real difference in filming, and so each sequence and acting "role" will have a "playback") but the scenes themselves change (take on new shapes, move between rooms, are re-structured to put all the elements of each "frame" together). If one could consistently reconfigure a continuous, ever-changing filmic work (like my filmic schizoanalysis) through many different experiments with a specific formula, then theoretically you'd

find a very simple method to understand just how any movie works, which could then serve as the foundation for figuring out anything you like to know about movies, or indeed, reality.
Of course, this approach to the problem is too easy. It does not explain why the images and ideas that appear within any movie come together in such strange ways, so that things sometimes look good together while other times they look ridiculous, and the way it's always so difficult to tell when

something is supposed to mean something and what its implications might be, how different films are contradictory while somehow managing to maintain a sense of coherence and "order." But from the theoretical standpoint, the subject itself should already suggest why films might remain mysterious or undecidable despite having been seen or experienced in hundreds of millions of cases, even though there's never any assurance of a coherent view, or certainty of truth.

Movies are always supposed to be about something else, but only they seem to be able to say something about the subject matter and subjectivities that make them up. Even when they tell the truth.
***
It has long been observed, by those of us who have used film studies to form the theoretical foundations for our work as artists, that making movies (a new one every second) is like having your cake and eating it: you can always turn the screen on,

point it at yourself, and wait for something to happen. The act of watching or experiencing (i.e., screening or attending or enjoying) a movie is nothing but this: something appears (here), you look (there), and—through no apparent or necessary connection or continuity—you don't feel as though anything really happens until you close your eyes. If a film ever happens in the end, it won't seem as if there were any need for that "h

appening," let alone any special significance. In short, to watch a film is simply to "not look": that's all that's going on. And yet there always seems to be a reason to watch or look—something worth wanting or needing to look for. This is the very phenomenon I'd like to test through my schizoanalysis project, which may give insight into why it's sometimes hard to get people to go see films.

To have "no particular purpose" would be just the thing needed to explain a viewer's reticence to commit to the spectacle of a film, whose real purpose seems always to elude a spectator. That said, the kind of film (like my schizoanalysis) that shows nothing at all may also help a spectator "get involved" and start looking, provided she'll choose it as her medium of choice, for what exactly?

(Once again, as long as it isn't supposed to.)
We want films to do things and mean certain things. Or maybe we can say this desire has something to do with the subjectivity of seeing itself as a set of engagements between looking and other activities: all the questions it might raise when people engage each other while they're not necessarily looking. Such questioning, according to theorists like Polanyi, can lead to the realization that looking at anything might never happen

(e.g., during dreams). From this perspective, a film can have two separate yet quite related functions: one is as the material thing you watch; another—and more important—is as an ongoing subject or concept that is related to, but not identical to the way a film looks. And since our experience of the screen is a temporal rather than a spatial one, it should make perfect sense that an audience is able to "watch" something that is always happening

without having to physically come to a movie theater; from a point of view, that makes any screening into something that's always already happened, since it can only be experienced at an earlier or later point in time. In this light, a movie screen and its "content" may become two parts of the same whole. Since what happens on the screen is often seen as inseparable from its interpretation and reception in society (see the problematic idea of "narrative closure"),

watching films might serve to mark—and fix—a film's memory of (re)occurrence and its "identity." The means by which we "see" things like movies is that, instead of actively "watching," we look in silence; and such a mode of viewing seems perfectly suited for making sense out of the movies' narrative. All those characters and their actions onscreen seem to be about what the movie is showing, so it must somehow tell us what

has really happened, even if it doesn't happen anywhere but in the spectators themselves (where the only true and real event is the watching itself). This makes filmgoers complicit in the cinematic space (even if they have no say in the final narrative content) while remaining at the same time (if you could call this an achievement) completely cut off from all narrative decisions, and unable to do anything except watch as passively as possible.

Schizoanalyzing The Twitter Feed of the Human Species For the Lulz

All the best minds were on it. A collective intelligence—not unlike what may occur in the hive mind—had emerged spontaneously. Its purpose was to perform a simple, highly distributed task: to share an annotated feed of what was being said about various topics across a few dozen blogs, Twitter accounts, and other online media. People were saying all kinds of things on the Web, but we wanted to take particular care not to simply reproduce any existing ideas or concepts about

any of these subjects. Instead we had our students collect everything they could find in their initial topic searches and, through careful analysis, arrive at a theoretical definition of some yet-to-be-determined phenomena about all those who had joined that collective effort. Once a team had arrived at this, they could start "explaining" what they'd learned by synthesizing a variety of different viewpoints, sources, and ideas in a way that might resemble the output of the human

mind—though we were constantly skeptical about whether the thing would end up looking much like anything recognizable. After all, one reason for a mind to be intelligent is precisely to identify those new ideas that are more valid than old ones. Otherwise, what could distinguish us from the animal kingdom, or from anything that could emerge from such a process of recombinant evolution?
To test whether the project really would lead to some sort of truly new idea, the results of all our efforts

had to be shared with others who were doing similar work—so that it might be proved that there was nothing beyond what anyone else might have already proposed, so that it wouldn't seem as though we'd just been feeding off everyone's prior work, making them look as though they were unable to do the same things themselves. In addition, the participants in this group sharing of our findings would also get a chance to judge each other's work, thereby weighing it against any thoughts

they might have generated themselves. There were many different methods one might employ for testing for a novel result, but as you can see from what has come before, we employed an entirely arbitrary process, because none of them are suitable for working on such projects in this day and age. What was important was the ability to come up with something, anything, new that was worth thinking about—that could stand, so to speak, for anything, within any of our various topics of

study, even if it couldn't actually be used to demonstrate anything.
One of the first groups in the project to succeed, before all the others even got started, was the one that tackled the problems of identifying different kinds of online threats. One of them had asked other people whether they considered the messages from different software-based programs to be the same thing when being sent from one person to another;

some of these were dangerous while others were merely annoying. Their job was to figure out which were the real threats, and then report these findings to any government agencies or security systems that might wish to know about them. A group was tasked with studying what kinds of blogs were found by Web robots to be especially popular or influential, and determine what might lead to such popularity. This was called "social proof."

They collected the contents of a list of sites whose contents, through various statistical analysis, appeared to be related, even though these lists seemed at the time to be rather random:
* Sites whose links were particularly shared via the Digg social bookmarking site (again, why?)

* Sites on which one had frequently heard the name "Steve Jobs."
* Blogs on which one could read both the phrase "Unix/Linux" and a mention of either Facebook or

Google.
It turned out to be much easier than you might think for anyone with access to so many Web-use metrics, including some of the data from major Web crawlers that were considered among the most advanced algorithms currently available. Even people who knew nothing of our work and only used these tools themselves—as it became possible to do with free tools made widely available by their designers—would often manage to see patterns in such data, despite its seeming randomness.

It also helped to be willing to trust whatever data source one happened to have at hand, since everyone has his own methods and beliefs. If one didn't trust an expert's evaluation, then that was worth finding out about as well; you might even use the same criteria to decide which experts to believe. All this led to the following model for Internet popularity:
Let X denote how many times something can be found in all possible sites on the Internet, and let Y be

what proportion of that X number appears on one specific site (where the term Y is used instead of n). By multiplying the Y value by a number known as the power of one—N—the two figures can be expressed:
Y * N = P(Y)
The X number is now treated as a measure of "purity"—a crude, rough estimation of how different such content really is from all the other things that are there, as opposed to being

just more of the same thing that anyone might easily find anywhere else on the Web. For instance, if N were fifty thousand, and it took 5 minutes to see something with an X value of one hundred in at least half a million sites, then an original work might not qualify as "original," even though its unique content might well be valued for a good deal longer. And, when N gets quite large, content could become virtually identical from site to site, where each

site will display it in just a slightly different manner. Of course, "power of N" should be measured independently for every site on which the subject of study may appear, so as to keep an accurate picture of any changes over time. A high N would imply that a person's originality or uniqueness could actually increase as one got more successful, simply by getting copied more widely across the Net.

We thought a lot about what sorts of rules such a measure of success would likely create. One of us joked that if N ever reached as high as n one-hundredths, then we should really begin to think that the real rule of the Internet might not be based on some inherent goodness of anything, but rather on our need to simply conform to one another's expectations.

At first, the system's designers resisted this notion, arguing that it was possible for too much social proof to cause all kinds of bad behavior, including self-destruction by the individual: someone who had found success, and whose works or words might have helped to make that happen, might very well die from some other source entirely, not because anyone believed he'd hurt himself or anyone else by acting in particular ways but because he simply followed whatever everyone else seemed to believe was

right or good. This became especially hard to accept when the news started reporting on the tragic end of people who seemed to have everything going for them; those stories tended to suggest that it had been their failure to properly live up to society's expectations—or at least, the demands made upon them by their friends, loved ones, fans, and audiences, combined with the people whose work they admired—that drove these successes to some kind of dramatic death, either physical or emotional

, for lack of another goal in life. The one saving grace, perhaps, was that an overly powerful N couldn't give people what they most wanted anyway: the promise of fame. If N were near to one-hundred, for instance, then at most a single person (of course, an entity defined in a mathematical sense) could exist within the entire Internet. One might call this person "NONE."

Okay, I hold under my boobage a compilation of two years of daily blog posts. In retrospect, I look back on that project and see a large number of things I did completely wrong. I'm fine with that. I can say oopsie!, and doofus!, and ah-doy-doy! and make the crooked thing with my arm that we are not supposed to do anymore because the Bill/Ted hybrid advises us to be awesome to each other.

If someone doesn't think I was awesome before I read that book, then too bad for them, they got a raw deal. But anyway, let me go into the details of the mistakes I made so I don't make them again.
Mistake 1: Not keeping the Sequences a secret. I was too open about the idea of a sequence. Even though I was very careful not to mention any specific numbers, I could have easily been linked to the idea by people who were looking for a connection between my words and the actual Sequences.

I didn't anticipate how easy it would be to connect ideas. You can even find all sorts of weird connections that don't actually exist simply because people have already connected one thought to another. It seems like I should have realized this. But at the time I wrote that first post, I was still working out a bunch of stuff myself, so I guess I wasn't fully aware yet either.
Mistake 2: Posting only once a day. This makes sense when you're posting to Twitter or Facebook;

however, when I posted to the Sequences site, I had to wait until midnight Central Time to put something new up. So while I might have wanted to update every few minutes, I couldn't do that. For example, if I'd wanted to tell my friends I love them more often than once a week, I probably shouldn't have posted at all. On the flip side, I wish I'd updated less often because then I wouldn't have to worry about repeating myself over and over and over.

Mistake 3: Talking about the Sequences in the third person. Okay, here's a confession. When I started writing the Sequences, I tried to write the Sequences as a journal. Like, I'd type up whatever came to mind, and I'd try to stay true to the idea that everything I said was personal and unique—and thus it didn't matter whether anyone else ever saw the same thoughts I was having. Eventually, though, I found that I was writing differently because I knew someone would eventually read it.

Maybe I just wanted to make sure I sounded cool? Or maybe I wanted to sound cool but felt self-conscious about writing in the third person? Anyway, I think I did pretty well in making sure I never used names or other specifics, but I definitely failed when I tried to describe events in the future or present tense. That's why sometimes I refer to myself as "you" instead of saying things like 'Sydney thinks' or 'Sydney will think.' The problem is, I forgot which parts were supposed to be vague and which weren't.

If I hadn't done that, then there really would have been no way to connect the Sequences with anything else online.
Mistake 4: Thinking about the Sequences in the past tense. Sometimes I think back on the last three months and wonder what happened during those days. Was I actually writing the Sequences or just talking about the Sequences? Did I actually get anywhere toward freeing humanity? What if I'd spent the entire time dreaming? I've got a lot of questions, and I can't answer any of them.

Mistake 5: Trying too hard to figure out what I should say next. Here's one thing I learned early on: I needed to stick with what interested me most, and I needed to trust my gut feelings. I didn't need to agonize over what I'd already written or worry about what people might think if I changed it. If something struck me as funny, interesting or important enough to include, then I'd post it. In the beginning, I wrote mostly about technology, social media, art, politics, philosophy, psychology and religion.

I tried to explain how we all lived inside a simulated reality, but I wasn't very good at explaining how we could escape it. So I added more humor, I tried to simplify things, and I focused less on theory and more on practical steps. But even now I feel guilty about putting ideas into words rather than trying to prove them through action. My instinct tells me to work harder and find solutions to our biggest problems, but my intellect knows better. In this essay I describe some well-known inefficiencies and limitations of evolutions. I say “evolutions,” plural, because fox evolution works at cross-purposes to rabbit evolution, and neither can talk to snake evolution to learn how to build venomous fangs.

So I am talking about limitations of evolution here, but this does not mean I am trying to sneak in creationism. This is standard Evolutionary Biology 201. (583 if you must derive the equations.) Evolutions, thus limited, can still explain observed biology; in fact the limitations are necessary to make sense of it. Remember that the wonder of evolutions is not how well they work, but that they work at all.

Human intelligence is so complicated that no one has any good way to calculate how efficient it is. Natural selection, though not simple, is simpler than a human brain; and correspondingly slower and less efficient, as befits the first optimization process ever to exist. In fact, evolutions are simple enough that we can calculate exactly how stupid they are.

Evolutions are slow. How slow? Suppose there’s a beneficial mutation that conveys a fitness advantage of 3%: on average, bearers of this gene have 1.03 times as many children as non-bearers. Assuming that the mutation spreads at all, how long will it take to spread through the whole population? That depends on the population size. A gene conveying a 3% fitness advantage, spreading through a population of 100,000, would require an average of 768 generations to reach universality in the gene pool. A population of 500,000 would require 875 generations. The general formula is

Generations to fixation = 2 ln(N)/s ,

where N is the population size and (1 + s) is the fitness. (If each bearer of the gene has 1.03 times as many children as a non-bearer, s = 0.03.)

Thus, if the population size were 1,000,000—the estimated population in hunter-gatherer times—then it would require 2,763 generations for a gene conveying a 1% advantage to spread through the gene pool.

(Buoyed by a one-time bonus, 1024 generations!) In evolutionary biology, as in many other fields, it is important to think quantitatively rather than qualitatively. Does a beneficial mutation “sometimes spread, but not always”? Well, a psychic power would be a beneficial mutation, so you’d expect it to spread, right? Yet this is qualitative reasoning, not quantitative—if X is true, then Y is true; if psychic powers are beneficial, they may spread. In Evolutions Are Stupid, I described the equations for a beneficial mutation’s probability of fixation, roughly twice the fitness advantage (6% for a 3% advantage). Only this kind of numerical thinking is likely to make us realize that mutations which are only rarely useful are extremely unlikely to spread, and that it is practically impossible for complex adaptations to arise without constant use. If psychic powers really existed, we should expect to see everyone using them all the time—not just because they would be so amazingly useful, but because otherwise they couldn’t have evolved in the first place.

“So long as there are limited resources and multiple competing actors capable of passing on characteristics, you have selection pressure.” This is qualitative reasoning. How much selection pressure?

While there are several candidates for the most important equation in evolutionary biology, I would pick Price’s Equation, which in its simplest formulation reads:

∆z = cov(vi,zi);
change in average characteristic =
covariance(relative fitness, characteristic).

This is a very powerful and general formula. For example, a particular gene for height can be the Z, the characteristic that changes, in which case Price’s Equation says that the change in the probability of possessing this gene equals the covariance of the gene with reproductive fitness. Or you can consider height in general as the characteristic Z, apart from any particular genes, and Price’s Equation says that the change in height in the next generation will equal the covariance of height with relative reproductive fitness.

(At least, this is true so long as height is straightforwardly heritable. If nutrition improves, so that a fixed genotype becomes taller, you have to add a correction term to Price’s Equation. If there are complex nonlinear interactions between many genes, you have to either add a correction term, or calculate the equation in such a complicated way that it ceases to enlighten.)

An Especially Elegant Evolutionary Psychology Experiment
❦

In a 1989 Canadian study, adults were asked to imagine the death of children of various ages and estimate which deaths would create the greatest sense of loss in a parent. The results, plotted on a graph, show grief growing until just before adolescence and then beginning to drop. When this curve was compared with a curve showing changes in reproductive potential over the life cycle (a pattern calculated from Canadian demographic data), the correlation was fairly strong. But much stronger—nearly perfect, in fact—was the correlation between the grief curves of these modern Canadians and the reproductive-potential curve of a hunter-gatherer people, the !Kung of Africa. In other words, the pattern of changing grief was almost exactly what a Darwinian would predict, given demographic realities in the ancestral environment.

—Robert Wright, The Moral Animal,
summarizing Crawford et al.1

The first correlation was 0.64, the second an extremely high 0.92 (N = 221). The most obvious inelegance of this study, as described, is that it was conducted by asking human adults to imagine parental grief, rather than asking real parents with children of particular ages. (Presumably that would have cost more / allowed fewer subjects.) However, my understanding is that the results here squared well with the data from closer studies of parental grief that were looking for other correlations (i.e., a raw correlation between parental grief and child age).

That said, consider some of this experiment’s elegant aspects:

A correlation of 0.92(!) This may sound suspiciously high—could evolution really do such exact fine-tuning?—until you realize that this selection pressure was not only great enough to fine-tune parental grief, but, in fact, carve it out of existence from scratch in the first place.
People who say that evolutionary psychology hasn’t made any advance predictions are (ironically) mere victims of “no one knows what science doesn’t know” syndrome. You wouldn’t even think of this as an experiment to be performed if not for evolutionary psychology.
The experiment illustrates, as beautifully and as cleanly as any I have ever seen, the distinction between a conscious or subconscious ulterior motive and an executing adaptation with no realtime sensitivity to the original selection pressure that created it.
The parental grief is not even subconsciously about reproductive value—otherwise it would update for Canadian reproductive value instead of !Kung reproductive value. Grief is an adaptation that now simply exists, real in the mind and continuing under its own inertia.

Parents do not care about children for the sake of their reproductive contribution. Parents care about children for their own sake; and the non-cognitive, evolutionary-historical reason why such minds exist in the universe in the first place is that children carry their parents’ genes.

All else is an adaptation allowed because strong selection is somewhere nearby. This was taken for granted by many evolutionists until very recently. And it will be again—I predict it will be on the menu soon. But I advance my own project by damning it with faint praise."

Superstimuli and the Collapse of Western Civilization
❦

At least three people have died playing online games for days without rest. People have lost their spouses, jobs, and children to World of Warcraft. If people have the right to play video games—and it’s hard to imagine a more fundamental right—then the market is going to respond by supplying the most engaging video games that can be sold, to the point that exceptionally engaged consumers are removed from the gene pool.

How does a consumer product become so involving that, after 57 hours of using the product, the consumer would rather use the product for one more hour than eat or sleep? (I suppose one could argue that the consumer makes a rational decision that they’d rather play Starcraft for the next hour than live out the rest of their life, but let’s just not go there. Please.)

A candy bar is a superstimulus: it contains more concentrated sugar, salt, and fat than anything that exists in the ancestral environment. A candy bar matches taste buds that evolved in a hunter-gatherer environment, but it matches those taste buds much more strongly than anything that actually existed in the hunter-gatherer environment. The signal that once reliably correlated to healthy food has been hijacked, blotted out with a point in tastespace that wasn’t in the training dataset—an impossibly distant outlier on the old ancestral graphs. Tastiness, formerly representing the evolutionarily identified correlates of healthiness, has been reverse-engineered and perfectly matched with an artificial substance. Unfortunately there’s no equally powerful market incentive to make the resulting food item as healthy as it is tasty. We can’t taste healthfulness, after all.

No amount of extraneous sugar could make our biological circuits believe it was actually healthful if we didn’t already know it was healthful.
So we munch down on our unhealthy treat while knowing full well it is unhealthy for us even as we become addicted to it. One healthy lifestyle club might offer up to us another healthy lifestyle club—knowing full well that we don”t want healthy food or diets because we may not behave better if we have healthier habits. We con ourselves by thinking we prefer fruit juice over alcohol because artificial sweeteners are healthier for us—but if nature truly intended for us to drink our calories away, then mankind would have been designed for consuming alcohol instead of sugar water. Our evolved synapses were designed to echo sweet things off our mouths when we mistakenly believed them to be sweet rather than taking them to naturally convince us we had tasted our meals without getting drunk off our asses at least half of the time.

Then we provide refined and highly concentrated foods packed with sugar as rewards for a job well done—and try to exploit our biological quirks through sudden transitions or interruptions of our normal diets—and we have ourselves a piece of virtual space cake! We reject food with essential health benefits for delightful treats while people starve all over the world! Belief in Intelligence
❦

I don’t know what moves Garry Kasparov would make in a chess game. What, then, is the empirical content of my belief that “Kasparov is a highly intelligent chess player”? What real-world experience does my belief tell me to anticipate? Is it a cleverly masked form of total ignorance?

To sharpen the dilemma, suppose Kasparov plays against some mere chess grandmaster Mr. G, who’s not in the running for world champion. My own ability is far too low to distinguish between these levels of chess skill. When I try to guess Kasparov’s move, or Mr. G’s next move, all I can do is try to guess “the best chess move” using my own meager knowledge of chess. Then I would produce exactly the same prediction for Kasparov’s move or Mr. G’s move in any particular chess position. So what is the empirical content of my belief that “Kasparov is a better chess player than Mr. G”?

The empirical content of my belief is the testable, falsifiable prediction that the final chess position will occupy the class of chess positions that are wins for Kasparov, rather than drawn games or wins for Mr. G. (Counting resignation as a legal move that leads to a chess position classified as a loss.) The degree to which I think Kasparov is a “better player” is reflected in the amount of probability mass I concentrate into the “Kasparov wins” class of outcomes, versus the “drawn game” and “Mr. G wins” class of outcomes. These classes are extremely vague in the sense that they refer to vast spaces of possible chess positions—but “Kasparov wins” is more specific than maximum entropy, because it can be definitely falsified by a vast set of chess positions.

The outcome of Kasparov’s game is predictable because I know, and understand, Kasparov’s goals. Within the confines of the chess board, I know Kasparov’s motivations—I know his success criterion, his utility function, his target as an optimization process. I know where Kasparov is ultimately trying to steer the future and I anticipate he is powerful enough to get there, although I don’t anticipate much about how Kasparov is going to do it.

Imagine that I’m visiting a distant city, and a local friend volunteers to drive me to the airport. I don’t know the neighborhood. Each time my friend approaches a street intersection, I don’t know whether my friend will turn left, turn right, or continue straight ahead. I can’t predict my friend’s move even as we approach each individual intersection—let alone predict the whole sequence of moves in advance.

Yet I can predict the result of my friend’s unpredictable actions:

my friend will not let me get lost or injured even if she drives drunk to that airport. Optimization and the Intelligence Explosion
❦

Among the topics I haven’t delved into here is the notion of an optimization process. Roughly, this is the idea that your power as a mind is your ability to hit small targets in a large search space—this can be either the space of possible futures (planning) or the space of possible designs (invention).

Suppose you have a car, and suppose we already know that your preferences involve travel. Now suppose that you take all the parts in the car, or all the atoms, and jumble them up at random. It’s very unlikely that you’ll end up with a travel-artifact at all, even so much as a wheeled cart; let alone a travel-artifact that ranks as high in your preferences as the original car. So, relative to your preference ordering, the car is an extremely improbable artifact. The power of an optimization process is that it can produce this kind of improbability.

Even though you don’t really know what your desires are when you start out, you set about building somewhat on the basis of certain assumptions concerning them; it is unusual indeed when you end up with an outcome so unlikely as to be incomprehensible even if we had a complete image of your preferences at the beginning of the process. By organising information so as to collect additional tools with which to improve the design, your disposition for any particular outcome becomes more probable still, and your excellence for any high-level goal becomes immeasurable.

However—and this is critically important—you do not actually solve the problem you set yourself; if you managed to build a space vehicle capable of space transportation already from its very design stage, there would be no point in proceeding at all! No designer would advance beyond certain point for obvious reasons: If there were depths precedent to go deeper into, what was left to discover? But—and this is most important—you might find out something exceedingly important about the right design for such a vehicle ahead of its telling us anything at all about your larger goal, not to mention informing us of everything we needed

to know for that journey back home! So big picture stuff comes before little picture stuff: Knowledge creation proceeds by successive optimization steps; each optimization range represents an internal extension towards a prior goal based upon previous knowledge outcomes—not mere random wriggling! Pervasive memergent optimizer will turn every problem into a unique puzzle even when they're unsolved—until we finally track down proper solutions as it goes optimizes towards big design purpose.

Once upon a time, there was a court jester who dabbled in logic.

The jester presented the king with two boxes. Upon the first box was inscribed:

Either this box contains an angry frog, or the box with a false inscription contains an angry frog, but not both.

On the second box was inscribed:

Either this box contains gold and the box with a false inscription contains an angry frog, or this box contains an angry frog and the box with a true inscription contains gold.

And the jester said to the king: “One box contains an angry frog, the other box gold; and one, and only one, of the inscriptions is true.”

The king opened the wrong box, and was savaged by an angry frog.

“You see,” the jester said, “let us hypothesize that the first inscription is the true one. Then suppose the first box contains gold. Then the other box would have an angry frog, while the box with a true inscription would contain gold, which would make the second statement true as well. Now hypothesize that the first inscription is false, and that the first box contains gold. Then the second inscription would be—”

The king ordered the jester thrown in the dungeons.

A day later, the jester was brought before the king in chains and shown two boxes.

“One box contains a key,” said the king, “to unlock your chains; and if you find the key you are free. But the other box contains a dagger for your heart if you fail.”

And the first box was inscribed:

Either both inscriptions are true, or both inscriptions are false.

And the second box was inscribed:

This box contains the key.

The jester reasoned thusly: “Suppose the first inscription is true. Then the second inscription must also be true. Now suppose the first inscription is false. Then again the second inscription must be true. So the second box must contain the key, if the first inscription is true, and also if the first inscription is false. Therefore, the second box must logically contain the key.”

The jester opened the second box, and found a dagger.

“How?!” cried the jester in horror, as he was dragged away. “It’s logically impossible!”

“It is entirely possible,” replied the king. “I merely wrote those inscriptions on two boxes, and then I put the dagger in the second one.”

The Parable of Hemlock
❦

All men are mortal. Socrates is a man. Therefore Socrates is mortal.

—Standard Medieval syllogism

Socrates raised the glass of hemlock to his lips…

“Do you suppose,” asked one of the onlookers, “that even hemlock will not be enough to kill so wise and good a man?”

“No,” replied another bystander, a student of philosophy; “all men are mortal, and Socrates is a man; and if a mortal drinks hemlock, surely he dies.”

“Well,” said the onlooker, “what if it happens that Socrates isn’t mortal?”

“Nonsense,” replied the student, a little sharply; “all men are mortal by definition; it is part of what we mean by the word ‘man.’ All men are mortal, Socrates is a man, therefore Socrates is mortal. It is not merely a guess, but a logical certainty.”

“I suppose that’s right…” said the onlooker. “Oh, look, Socrates already drank the hemlock while we were talking.”

“Yes, he should be keeling over any minute now,” said the student.

And they waited, and they waited, and they waited…

“Socrates appears not to be mortal,” said the onlooker.

“Then Socrates must not be a man,” replied the student. “All men are mortal, Socrates is not mortal, therefore Socrates is not a man. And that is not merely a guess, but a logical certainty.”

The fundamental problem with arguing that things are true “by definition” is that you can’t make reality go a different way by choosing a different definition.

You could reason, perhaps, as follows: “All things I have observed which wear clothing, speak language, and use tools, have also shared certain other properties as well, such as breathing air and pumping red blood. The last thirty ‘humans’ belonging to this cluster whom I observed to drink hemlock soon fell over and stopped moving. Socrates wears a toga, speaks fluent ancient Greek, and drank hemlock from a cup. So I predict that Socrates will keel over in the next five minutes.”

But that would be mere guessing. It wouldn’t be, y’know, absolutely and eternally certain. The Greek philosophers—like most prescientific philosophers—were rather fond of certainty.

Luckily the Greek philosophers have a crushing rejoinder to your questioning. You have misunderstood the meaning of “All humans are mortal,” they say. It is not a mere observation. It is part of the definition of the word “human.” Mortality is one of several properties that are individually necessary, and together sufficient, to determine membership in the class “human.” The statement “All humans are mortal” is a logically valid truth, absolutely unquestionable. And if Socrates is human, he must be mortal: it is a logical deduction, as certain as certain can be.

But then we can never know for certain that Socrates is a “human” until after Socrates has been observed to be mortal. It does no good to observe that Socrates speaks fluent Greek, or that Socrates has red blood, or even that Socrates has human DNA. None of these characteristics are logically equivalent to mortality. You have to see him die before you can conclude that he was human.

(And even then it’s not infinitely certain. What if Socrates rises from the grave a night after you see him die? Or more realistically, what if Socrates is signed up for cryonics? If mortality is defined to mean finite lifespan, then you can never really know if someone was human, until you’ve observed to the end of eternity—just to make sure they don’t come back. Or you could think you saw Socrates keel over, but it could be an illusion projected onto your eyes with a retinal scanner. Or maybe you just hallucinated the whole thing…)

The problem with syllogisms is that they’re always valid. “All humans are mortal; Socrates is human; therefore Socrates is mortal” is—if you treat it as a logical syllogism—logically valid within our own universe. It’s also logically valid within neighboring Everett branches in which, due to a slightly different evolved biochemistry, hemlock is a delicious treat rather than a poison. And it’s logically valid even in universes where Socrates never existed, or for that matter, where humans never existed.

The Bayesian definition of evidence favoring a hypothesis is evidence which we are more likely to see if the hypothesis is true than if it is false. Observing that a syllogism is logically valid can never be evidence favoring any empirical proposition, because the syllogism will be logically valid whether that proposition is true or false.

Syllogisms are valid in all possible worlds, and therefore, observing their validity never tells us anything about which possible world we actually live in.

This doesn’t mean that logic is useless—just that logic can only tell us that which, in some sense, we already know. But we do not always believe what we know. Is the number 29,384,209 prime? By virtue of how I define my decimal system and my axioms of arithmetic, I have already determined my answer to this question—but I do not know what my answer is yet, and I must do some logic to find out.

Similarly, if I form the uncertain empirical generalization “Humans are vulnerable to hemlock,” and the uncertain empirical guess “Socrates is human,” logic can tell me that my previous guesses are predicting that Socrates will be vulnerable to hemlock.

It’s been suggested that we can view logical reasoning as resolving our uncertainty about impossible possible worlds—eliminating probability mass in logically impossible worlds which we did not know to be logically impossible. In this sense, logical argument can be treated as observation.

But when you talk about an empirical prediction like “Socrates is going to keel over and stop breathing” or “Socrates is going to do fifty jumping jacks and then compete in the Olympics next year,” that is a matter of possible worlds, not impossible possible worlds.

Logic can tell us which hypotheses match up to which observations, and it can tell us what these hypotheses predict for the future—it can bring old observations and previous guesses to bear on a new problem. But logic never flatly says, “Socrates will stop breathing now.” Logic never dictates any empirical question; it never settles any real-world query which could, by any stretch of the imagination, go either way.

Empty Labels
❦

Consider (yet again) the Aristotelian idea of categories. Let’s say that there’s some object with properties A, B, C, D, and E, or at least it looks E-ish.

Fred: “You mean that thing over there is blue, round, fuzzy, and—”

Me: “In Aristotelian logic, it’s not supposed to make a difference what the properties are, or what I call them. That’s why I’m just using the letters.”

Next, I invent the Aristotelian category “zawa,” which describes those objects, all those objects, and only those objects, that have properties A, C, and D.

Me: “Object 1 is zawa, B, and E.”

Fred: “And it’s blue—I mean, A—too, right?”

Me: “That’s implied when I say it’s zawa.”

Fred: “Still, I’d like you to say it explicitly.”

Me: “Okay. Object 1 is A, B, zawa, and E.”

Then I add another word, “yokie,” which describes all and only objects that are B and E; and the word “xippo,” which describes all and only objects which are E but not D.

Me: “Object 1 is zawa and yokie, but not xippo.”

Fred: “Wait, is it luminescent? I mean, is it E?”

Me: “Yes. That is the only possibility on the information given.”

Fred: “I’d rather you spelled it out.”

Me: “Fine: Object 1 is A, zawa, B, yokie, C, D, E, and not xippo.”

Fred: “Amazing! You can tell all that just by looking?”

Impressive, isn’t it? Let’s invent even more new words: “Bolo” is A, C, and yokie; “mun” is A, C, and xippo; and “merlacdonian” is bolo and mun.

Pointlessly confusing? I think so too. Let’s replace the labels with the definitions:

“Zawa, B, and E” becomes [A, C, D], B, E

“Bolo and A” becomes [A, C, [B, E]], A

“Merlacdonian” becomes [A, C, [B, E]], [A, C, [E, ¬D]].

And the thing to remember about the Aristotelian idea of categories is that [A, C, D] is the entire information of “zawa.” It’s not just that I can vary the label, but that I can get along just fine without any label at all—the rules for Aristotelian classes work purely on structures like [A, C, D]. To call one of these structures “zawa,” or attach any other label to it, is a human convenience (or inconvenience) which makes not the slightest difference to the Aristotelian rules.

Fallacies of Compression
❦

“The map is not the territory,” as the saying goes. The only life-size, atomically detailed, 100% accurate map of California is California. But California has important regularities, such as the shape of its highways, that can be described using vastly less information—not to mention vastly less physical material—than it would take to describe every atom within the state borders. Hence the other saying: “The map is not the territory, but you can’t fold up the territory and put it in your glove compartment.”

A paper map of California, at a scale of 10 kilometers to 1 centimeter (a million to one), doesn’t have room to show the distinct position of two fallen leaves lying a centimeter apart on the sidewalk. Even if the map tried to show the leaves, the leaves would appear as the same point on the map; or rather the map would need a feature size of 10 nanometers, which is a finer resolution than most book printers handle, not to mention human eyes.

Picture a mapmaker each time he or she labeled a leaf and you can see why human geographic charts omit other objects like loose change on lawns or broken boulders that lie between the maple leaves of someone's front yard. (Nature has simpler solutions than maps do.) In fact, one advantage maps have over this theory of nature is that with maps we can depict more detailed boundaries than we otherwise could—like very fine or minutely shaped boundaries at the nanoscale where no nature exists (they're all in our heads or at best quark–level dimensions).

we simply follow what information we find convenient on the map—and especially where we decide or want to be walking or driving at the time. Which usually means we follow along along merrily through an increasingly more detailed representation until we find we need to be looking at or charting more detailed angles of detail. Your eyes move to where they don't literally envision right away at any given time; your mind augmenting whatever bits strike attention at any particular time on any given map page you happen to be looking at right then.

But of course map readers who are especially scrupulous might want to shoot off text commands about what they want to be looking for on some esoteric, modern update version of the same huge historical map—or better yet for them, an older existing out-of-copyright primary source that includes hands-down the latest updates and data he or she needs right now for a research project. Among the many genetic variations and mutations you carry in your genome, there are a very few alleles you probably know—including those determining your blood type: the presence or absence of the A, B, and + antigens. If you receive a blood transfusion containing an antigen you don’t have, it will trigger an allergic reaction. It was Karl Landsteiner’s discovery of this fact, and how to test for compatible blood types, that made it possible to transfuse blood without killing the patient. (1930 Nobel Prize in Medicine.) Also, if a mother with blood type A (for example) bears a child with blood type A+, the mother may acquire an allergic reaction to the + antigen; if she has another child with blood type A+, the child will be in danger, unless the mother takes an allergic suppressant during pregnancy. Arguing “By Definition”
❦

“This plucked chicken has two legs and no feathers—therefore, by definition, it is a human!”

When people argue definitions, they usually start with some visible, known, or at least widely believed set of characteristics; then pull out a dictionary, and point out that these characteristics fit the dictionary definition; and so conclude, “Therefore, by definition, atheism is a religion!”

But visible, known, widely believed characteristics are rarely the real point of a dispute. Just the fact that someone thinks Socrates’s two legs are evident enough to make a good premise for the argument, “Therefore, by definition, Socrates is human!” indicates that bipedalism probably isn’t really what’s at stake—or the listener would reply, “Whaddaya mean Socrates is bipedal? That’s what we’re arguing about in the first place!”

And even if it were what they were really arguing about, someone wanting to chop the argument down to its essence—to make the simplest statement about what they believed and why—would say, something like this: "Atheism is not allegiance to Zeus." But then if we wanted to be funny we would say: "Doesn't mean you do not worship an athieist." To try to make similar statements is usually a bad endgame strategy; it guarantees losing. Arguing "By Definition" reads like this:
"Whatever is round is an orb."

Therefore, this is an orb.

So I got a little more schooled on schizoanalysis:
Schizoanalysis, then, is a form of social analysis according to abstract machines, lines of flight or deterritorialisation, regimes of signs, the stratification of molecular elements or their destratification, and planes of consistency. It maps the social unconscious according to its movements and intensities of desire. [...] so that lines of experimentation or becoming may be constructed through a reassembling of the abstract machines that lie between the strata and produce them.[6]

— Philip Goodchild
Deleuze and Guattari write in the fourth chapter of Anti-Oedipus, "Introduction to Schizoanalysis", that in effect, schizoanalysis asks "What are your desiring-machines, what do you put into these machines, what is the output, how does it work, what are your nonhuman sexes?".[8]

Deleuze and Guattari develop four theses of schizoanalysis:

Every unconscious libidinal investment is social and bears upon a socio-historical field.
Unconscious libidinal investments of group or desire are distinct from preconscious investments of class or interest.
Non-familial libidinal investments of the social field are primary in relation to familial investments.
Social libidinal investments are distinguished according to two poles: a paranoiac, reactionary, fascisizing pole and a schizoid revolutionary pole.
Schizoanalysis does not proceed through the prism of any given technique, theory, or principle. As such, it draws upon both Freud's libido and Jungian complexes, structuralism, and dialectics.
As we will see, some of our films of the early work, while experimental in terms of medium, have been rooted firmly in the schizoanalysis framework. Others have remained a priori experiments of style or vision, sometimes rejecting all social-psychological-psychoanalysis themes and structure.
A schizoanalysis film can be any genre. One might say that any of my films is a kind of "schizoanalysis", for every one of them offers a different mode of looking, with its own specificities and styles, whether that's cinematic, architectural or intellectual. But each one is an exercise in the same way. The general sense that one explores in the film can change from film to film, but it never goes away completely. There is no direct or causal relationship between form and content in schizoanalysis films, only a random movement through forms, symbols, lines, planes, registers and orders, from a plane of consistency to an opposite, a destabilised condition or a point of instability. In all cases, form is linked to the desire-machine of the unconscious: its imagery, intensity of images, desires and inversions.
For example, at first we will move along the line of consistency, by showing a series of positive images. After the "correcting" inversion phase of the schizoanalysis procedure we are then forced into a more erratic state of disruption, before a return to an altered condition of order. Schizoanalysis, according to Deleuze and Guattari, proceeds from an idealized (inverted) position of non-continuity to a state in which things appear to be at rest. We could call this "putting to rest", or perhaps "the beginning of a new cycle".
Thus schizoanalysis begins with a negative image in our case of film. As this phase of schizoanalysis unfolds, and we proceed through different forms of images and movements, we begin to approach positive images again. They will appear very suddenly, sometimes not even as an effect of the film, but in some way they're introduced, inserted as if by magic or design. And when we've reached the final state of schizoidal harmony (which can be described as "true unity"), we will finally return to positive images, that is to say the "reality", the "actual", the "given".
Our film I have described to you thus far is called "The Return of the Birds" or, more specifically, "The Return of the Birds after the Schizoanalysis." For the film, we will shoot a series of sequences following a group of birds migrating north towards their breeding ground. They go into a trance state (again) and take to flight, but it's unclear as to why exactly the birds fly and what they actually want to achieve, as we don't see where they are going.
Schizoanalysis, then, is not to be confused with simple conceptual film (or, indeed, other formal procedures). Rather, schizoanalysis has to do with the interconnection of all images: moving images (from frame to frame), the film medium itself, the space (real or simulated) where these moving images were shot, and the act of watching them. In this sense, each scene of each film is an experiment, the product of one step of an endless process. We are constantly rethinking things, turning on and off mechanisms and phases. Each new iteration of the schizoanalysis film will be different, depending upon where we are at the moment, and where the viewers are as well.
In "I" (2012–13) the first segment of my most recent work, the film follows a figure or "myself" (it can be both) wandering around a factory, while shooting the scenes of the film, while editing and moving between scenes. A film like this could easily be interpreted as a very theatrical construct in which I am playing myself.
Indeed, for much of the film we have a static image of myself as an actor, but our eye does not move in any single direction for a long time (with only occasional moving lines representing the characters moving about or carrying out their routines). This is because we don't know what I'm doing with myself—for we do not know why we are shooting or if it matters who I am or what is going on at the same time that I am filming myself. But the actors' relationship to themselves is intimately connected with the actors' relationship to the world, so while you have this static image of me as an actor on camera, but in the same time your eye, looking at my image as I walk about the room or through a set of spaces, could well end up caught in this kind of loop or infinite sequence of scenes where there is never an end to this going on. Or, even while moving, I keep changing and re-forming my self into other selves and faces, showing myself not as I am now, but rather as other, unknown beings or objects that I may be. In this sense we are always looking at (watching) "the movie" itself, which we can only see partially (but enough to keep us distracted) or less (more than halfway through the film, we stop watching completely). And though we are shown glimpses of the films characters we are never really sure when something is actually happening (as we become less and less attentive), and if so, why, or whether the film's events are necessary, meaningful, or even necessary at all (if what we watch isn't part of some larger narrative).
Another example of an extremely fragmented work—though much more short and sweet—is the "Five Scenes of a Party" segment of my ongoing series on cinema and its functions. A party scene begins in each new iteration, after a very small amount of time has passed. But nothing happens, not with the exception of a brief return to the original image that starts things off, and the rewinding of this shot while showing the images that have been filmed so far. Eventually, we notice a repeating pattern emerging and the way in which each new party takes place in the same way (more or less the same layout, and with the same furniture, among other things) while somehow still being a different party. We know from the beginning that this is probably another iteration of the same scene, but not knowing exactly how this plays out, or precisely where we are at all, it is not so strange to be thinking that this might be one long party in which one continuous loop will repeat forever. This film ends when our eyes stop watching altogether (or when they close involuntarily, not unlike sleepwalking).
In order to depict schizoanalysis filmically, it's helpful to imagine it as a loop: not only would each second have its own spatial and temporal parameters (meeting them continuously, time and again), but also each frame of every second is supposed to correspond to every other frame, with all possible changes introduced between each instant and moment of time. Each shot should be simultaneously a single moment of the film as a whole—yet different for each occasion and in its particular combination of parts. At the same time, these parts (different scenes, events) can become part of an ongoing narrative (which has the form of a series of jumps in time, through time, and in the time-space of the film itself) or each part taken by itself. As if the individual moments within the film are already part of something bigger, each part is also already part of the film. These are all assumptions necessary in order to visualize what would happen if we were to experiment with this filmic hypothesis in real time and space: in different sets, locations, situations and physical mediums, but always with a certain number of shots of the same scene, using similar or identical actors (for there's no real difference in filming, and so each sequence and acting "role" will have a "playback") but the scenes themselves change (take on new shapes, move between rooms, are re-structured to put all the elements of each "frame" together). If one could consistently reconfigure a continuous, ever-changing filmic work (like my filmic schizoanalysis) through many different experiments with a specific formula, then theoretically you'd find a very simple method to understand just how any movie works, which could then serve as the foundation for figuring out anything you like to know about movies, or indeed, reality.
Of course, this approach to the problem is too easy. It does not explain why the images and ideas that appear within any movie come together in such strange ways, so that things sometimes look good together while other times they look ridiculous, and the way it's always so difficult to tell when something is supposed to mean something and what its implications might be, how different films are contradictory while somehow managing to maintain a sense of coherence and "order." But from the theoretical standpoint, the subject itself should already suggest why films might remain mysterious or undecidable despite having been seen or experienced in hundreds of millions of cases, even though there's never any assurance of a coherent view, or certainty of truth. Movies are always supposed to be about something else, but only they seem to be able to say something about the subject matter and subjectivities that make them up. Even when they tell the truth.

It has long been observed, by those of us who have used film studies to form the theoretical foundations for our work as artists, that making movies (a new one every second) is like having your cake and eating it: you can always turn the screen on, point it at yourself, and wait for something to happen. The act of watching or experiencing (i.e., screening or attending or enjoying) a movie is nothing but this: something appears (here), you look (there), and—through no apparent or necessary connection or continuity—you don't feel as though anything really happens until you close your eyes. If a film ever happens in the end, it won't seem as if there were any need for that "happening," let alone any special significance. In short, to watch a film is simply to "not look": that's all that's going on. And yet there always seems to be a reason to watch or look—something worth wanting or needing to look for. This is the very phenomenon I'd like to test through my schizoanalysis project, which may give insight into why it's sometimes hard to get people to go see films. To have "no particular purpose" would be just the thing needed to explain a viewer's reticence to commit to the spectacle of a film, whose real purpose seems always to elude a spectator. That said, the kind of film (like my schizoanalysis) that shows nothing at all may also help a spectator "get involved" and start looking, provided she'll choose it as her medium of choice, for what exactly? (Once again, as long as it isn't supposed to.)
We want films to do things and mean certain things. Or maybe we can say this desire has something to do with the subjectivity of seeing itself as a set of engagements between looking and other activities: all the questions it might raise when people engage each other while they're not necessarily looking. Such questioning, according to theorists like Polanyi, can lead to the realization that looking at anything might never happen (e.g., during dreams). From this perspective, a film can have two separate yet quite related functions: one is as the material thing you watch; another—and more important—is as an ongoing subject or concept that is related to, but not identical to the way a film looks. And since our experience of the screen is a temporal rather than a spatial one, it should make perfect sense that an audience is able to "watch" something that is always happening without having to physically come to a movie theater; from a point of view, that makes any screening into something that's always already happened, since it can only be experienced at an earlier or later point in time. In this light, a movie screen and its "content" may become two parts of the same whole. Since what happens on the screen is often seen as inseparable from its interpretation and reception in society (see the problematic idea of "narrative closure"), watching films might serve to mark—and fix—a film's memory of (re)occurrence and its "identity." The means by which we "see" things like movies is that, instead of actively "watching," we look in silence; and such a mode of viewing seems perfectly suited for making sense out of the movies' narrative. All those characters and their actions onscreen seem to be about what the movie is showing, so it must somehow tell us what has really happened, even if it doesn't happen anywhere but in the spectators themselves (where the only true and real event is the watching itself). This makes filmgoers complicit in the cinematic space (even if they have no say in the final narrative content) while remaining at the same time (if you could call this an achievement) completely cut off from all narrative decisions, and unable to do anything except watch as passively as possible.

Schizoanalyzing The Twitter Feed of the Human Species For the Lulz
All the best minds were on it. A collective intelligence—not unlike what may occur in the hive mind—had emerged spontaneously. Its purpose was to perform a simple, highly distributed task: to share an annotated feed of what was being said about various topics across a few dozen blogs, Twitter accounts, and other online media. People were saying all kinds of things on the Web, but we wanted to take particular care not to simply reproduce any existing ideas or concepts about any of these subjects. Instead we had our students collect everything they could find in their initial topic searches and, through careful analysis, arrive at a theoretical definition of some yet-to-be-determined phenomena about all those who had joined that collective effort. Once a team had arrived at this, they could start "explaining" what they'd learned by synthesizing a variety of different viewpoints, sources, and ideas in a way that might resemble the output of the human mind—though we were constantly skeptical about whether the thing would end up looking much like anything recognizable. After all, one reason for a mind to be intelligent is precisely to identify those new ideas that are more valid than old ones. Otherwise, what could distinguish us from the animal kingdom, or from anything that could emerge from such a process of recombinant evolution?
To test whether the project really would lead to some sort of truly new idea, the results of all our efforts had to be shared with others who were doing similar work—so that it might be proved that there was nothing beyond what anyone else might have already proposed, so that it wouldn't seem as though we'd just been feeding off everyone's prior work, making them look as though they were unable to do the same things themselves. In addition, the participants in this group sharing of our findings would also get a chance to judge each other's work, thereby weighing it against any thoughts they might have generated themselves. There were many different methods one might employ for testing for a novel result, but as you can see from what has come before, we employed an entirely arbitrary process, because none of them are suitable for working on such projects in this day and age. What was important was the ability to come up with something, anything, new that was worth thinking about—that could stand, so to speak, for anything, within any of our various topics of study, even if it couldn't actually be used to demonstrate anything.
One of the first groups in the project to succeed, before all the others even got started, was the one that tackled the problems of identifying different kinds of online threats. One of them had asked other people whether they considered the messages from different software-based programs to be the same thing when being sent from one person to another; some of these were dangerous while others were merely annoying. Their job was to figure out which were the real threats, and then report these findings to any government agencies or security systems that might wish to know about them. A group was tasked with studying what kinds of blogs were found by Web robots to be especially popular or influential, and determine what might lead to such popularity. This was called "social proof." They collected the contents of a list of sites whose contents, through various statistical analysis, appeared to be related, even though these lists seemed at the time to be rather random:
* Sites whose links were particularly shared via the Digg social bookmarking site (again, why?)
* Sites on which one had frequently heard the name "Steve Jobs."
* Blogs on which one could read both the phrase "Unix/Linux" and a mention of either Facebook or Google.
It turned out to be much easier than you might think for anyone with access to so many Web-use metrics, including some of the data from major Web crawlers that were considered among the most advanced algorithms currently available. Even people who knew nothing of our work and only used these tools themselves—as it became possible to do with free tools made widely available by their designers—would often manage to see patterns in such data, despite its seeming randomness. It also helped to be willing to trust whatever data source one happened to have at hand, since everyone has his own methods and beliefs. If one didn't trust an expert's evaluation, then that was worth finding out about as well; you might even use the same criteria to decide which experts to believe. All this led to the following model for Internet popularity:
Let X denote how many times something can be found in all possible sites on the Internet, and let Y be what proportion of that X number appears on one specific site (where the term Y is used instead of n). By multiplying the Y value by a number known as the power of one—N—the two figures can be expressed:
Y * N = P(Y)
The X number is now treated as a measure of "purity"—a crude, rough estimation of how different such content really is from all the other things that are there, as opposed to being just more of the same thing that anyone might easily find anywhere else on the Web. For instance, if N were fifty thousand, and it took 5 minutes to see something with an X value of one hundred in at least half a million sites, then an original work might not qualify as "original," even though its unique content might well be valued for a good deal longer. And, when N gets quite large, content could become virtually identical from site to site, where each site will display it in just a slightly different manner. Of course, "power of N" should be measured independently for every site on which the subject of study may appear, so as to keep an accurate picture of any changes over time. A high N would imply that a person's originality or uniqueness could actually increase as one got more successful, simply by getting copied more widely across the Net.
We thought a lot about what sorts of rules such a measure of success would likely create. One of us joked that if N ever reached as high as n one-hundredths, then we should really begin to think that the real rule of the Internet might not be based on some inherent goodness of anything, but rather on our need to simply conform to one another's expectations. At first, the system's designers resisted this notion, arguing that it was possible for too much social proof to cause all kinds of bad behavior, including self-destruction by the individual: someone who had found success, and whose works or words might have helped to make that happen, might very well die from some other source entirely, not because anyone believed he'd hurt himself or anyone else by acting in particular ways but because he simply followed whatever everyone else seemed to believe was right or good. This became especially hard to accept when the news started reporting on the tragic end of people who seemed to have everything going for them; those stories tended to suggest that it had been their failure to properly live up to society's expectations—or at least, the demands made upon them by their friends, loved ones, fans, and audiences, combined with the people whose work they admired—that drove these successes to some kind of dramatic death, either physical or emotional, for lack of another goal in life. The one saving grace, perhaps, was that an overly powerful N couldn't give people what they most wanted anyway: the promise of fame. If N were near to one-hundred, for instance, then at most a single person (of course, an entity defined in a mathematical sense) could exist within the entire Internet. One might call this person "NONE."
