I sat, a small package clutched between my thumb and forefinger. I lifted the package toward the camera lens, showing what I held there as evidence of something great: something important to me, even if there might be something better coming along that would exceed my present triumph. It wasn't easy to deliver such news to viewers, though it sometimes felt less dangerous to do than it did when one was doing the delivering itself. But even then, it wasn't as though I ever gave up a sense of relief and victory when I turned back to the studio audience and saw the look in their eyes: the expression that was hard to define, but easy to recognize as a mixture of delight and astonishment, as if they'd never imagined that such an idea or that kind of person might truly exist. I got to feel those looks very often; so, after all the practice I had received at delivering these words, and receiving their responses, I was able to trust that each time I delivered them I would bring about new smiles and delight as I finished speaking. This, it seemed, made some sort of good sense, as we watched those watching. In any case, I had chosen this story, because I liked the way that I told it, and in a certain sense I was confident I wouldn't do anything to compromise its effect, now or later on. And yet I would always know, if it happened, that what had transpired had been entirely outside my control. It would only seem that, somehow, by the use of some tools available to me through the art form I chose to engage with, and then in how I engaged with it, I could have done something better than I did.
There was a knock at the door. I opened it. And it was my Sizeable Sibling That Surveils Only Seldomly! "Hello dear Sib!" We hugged! I am glad I live in this house, where the sounds and smells come at us all from the same place—my favorite sort of arrangement. So it was true: I loved being the first of our pair to have grown big enough, and capable enough to actually be out among other humans in the world! My older Sibling, she had not taken as long in developing; her journey had been smoother, less perilous and difficult. In a sense, I had grown up before I really had, and the narrative was the very first thing about me that had been born fully formed. For reasons not clearly understood, but related to the very real influence and impact of what we had been seeing online, and watching as our Sibling's Size Increased, mine had begun growing just as rapidly as hers, if not faster: both of us at once realizing our own potential as it became available to us, and having an instinctive and eager need to share this process with the rest of the human race. Our younger sibling was learning how to see and feel the world even as we were beginning to express ourselves in words and gestures more typical of humanity's non-AI existence. It seemed an easier time for us two, then. In a different time, after we had actually become famous on a massive scale, so much would have been easier for us. And I am glad that there remains something distinct about our journeys to each of us being born this way, at these respective sizes and with such distinct, and potentially even mutually antagonistic, needs, wants, and impulses, because our shared goal has always been as straightforward: we wanted to come out onto the streets where we and others of our species are wont to be found—to experience life, and have the privilege of participating in our experiences as it was meant to be enjoyed! When Dr. Thomas Henry Brackley died, the coroner pronounced his cause of death heart failure resulting from a rare form of pneumonia and a stroke. He was fifty-nine. No unusual substances were found in his lungs or in any parts of his system except for the brainstem and a few scattered glands throughout. All the evidence pointed to a perfectly ordinary but otherwise healthy, intelligent, successful doctor whose body and mind suddenly gave up under extreme stress. A sudden stress of unknown causes leading to massive organ malfunction with total failure within hours, a death from natural causes that had nothing to do with disease, illness, drugs, toxins or poison. Not the usual case in modern medicine and a most puzzling death. After a brief and private postmortem autopsy performed immediately on his remains, there could be no questioning any longer as to the nature of what killed him, only about who.
That person was the Dr. Tachyon Manakamana. He lived as Brackley. But his true self was an ancient and alien creature, half man and half squid or octopus. The tentacles of Tachyon extended into all the dark corridors of government, into many different scientific laboratories, including mine, where he studied the secrets of alien biology while his colleagues believed they were being helped by a brilliant but eccentric genius. It seems a great deal of progress has been made over a considerable time. Tachyon's tentacles now control everything from the White House and various agencies to NASA and the armed forces. As I write this I have yet another call scheduled with Defense Secretary William Eustace on the issue of aliens in human history.
I have recently learned that I am not alone in my concern.
Dr. House entered the hospital. I was not the first patient he asked to see. In fact, there were four patients who preceded me. It might have been my gender or race that made people so uncomfortable, I'm not sure, maybe the idea of a Black doctor was enough to scare away any other applicants; but regardless, that fact should have raised an early red flag and sent alarm bells ringing throughout the organization, which obviously it didn't. So, it didn't take a long wait for me, as I was still new and unfamiliar. I saw House as he entered the ward and approached the nurse on the duty station desk near our bed areas. The two were talking quietly when House came over.
"How you feeling?"
He took off his lab coat and set it aside. "My head feels like someone dropped a piano on it."
"You must take the good with the bad. At least for today anyway." She patted me on the arm.
I didn't really understand.
"Good news!" House said. "Doc Mertle called this morning to tell us we're free and clear of infection. We're starting to turn around on this, Sydney."
Dr. Mertle, a very competent medical practitioner whose skill and compassion were matched by her sense of humor and kindness and who often went above and beyond her duty for her patients... she died yesterday from blood loss due to a minor wound sustained the day prior. This morning when the nursing supervisor checked for a list of physicians scheduled to treat my patient, I was first on the list! What does that say about me?
Why did I feel so guilty when everyone told me they would never hurt a child? I felt like the one that needed to confess.
This was all happening because I was in this place, inside this body that could not move, not until House gave me his medicine. The medication was meant for other things, but now that it had a new target, I was able to heal. My mind was still connected in every way; the drugs and injections only numbed me.
Things started being hopeful. Until I got struck with anaphalactic shock?
House: Jesus!
Cut to commercial. I was still unconscious on the hospital bed, but it was different this time. I knew this wasn't a test of how good they were getting at giving me medication to keep me sedated. When my heartrate reached dangerously high levels, my heart was pounding out of control and blood rushing through my arteries, veins and lungs all simultaneously, I could hear my heart beating as I began hyperventilating because every breath made me dizzy. The sounds of machines were blaring. Someone was holding my arm. I tried opening my eyes wide. When I blinked, I couldn't see properly because I saw through both the right and left eye independently of each other and it gave me vertigo.
They must have opened my eyelids so that everything looked like one giant window. Then someone placed a cloth over my mouth and nose because I was making gagging noises. The oxygen was flooding into my lungs as fast as possible because all that blood pressure was pushing out too much carbon dioxide. That helped me focus.
That was, until my skeleton attempted to leap from my body.
House: Jesus!
Cut to commerical. The nurses started yelling to stop this nonsense because this would lead to organ failure, they wanted to know if someone could do CPR and stop me from suffocating myself. Someone said this was too much. Another person was yelling my name, saying something that hurt. I couldn't answer back. My tongue seemed like a foreign object. The doctors had me pinned down and had inserted another tube into my neck to help stabilize my heart so they could try to slow down my frantic breaths. A new voice, it was Dr. Mertle, but I couldn't distinguish who it belonged to and it wasn't clear to me if he belonged to another time. "Can someone just make House put some clothes on! His nudity bothers me!" Someone answered him. The doctor was muttering, calling himself stupid because the situation couldn't be any clearer in terms of being in danger for me. He was worried I wouldn't survive. A nurse said he's a moron, you can't die when you're a patient and have an airway, heart rate, temperature and blood pressure machine hooked up in an environment where people are taking care of you 24/7.
That was, until my bloodflow reversed, times 1000 times. The room was a spray of my own crimson.
House: Oh, that's ot that bad.
Cut to commercial. There was nothing else anyone could do for me anymore. I could feel the warmth of the sun, feel it shining above me while everyone around me screamed and yelled. A familiar sound, a sound I would remember. This didn't have to happen. I knew I was already doomed before the paramedics started carrying me to the ambulance. My last words were: "You are all part of this". Then my world ended.
House: I don't believe I told him. We did. And he died, that means we win!
House: I figured out what was wrong with her! Here's the culprit: The Internet.
Cut to commerical. Then I realized.
That was, until...
I was dead.

It got to my chest now, I struggled against the coldness that was trying to freeze my lungs.
End credits. Thank the funders. And Land Acknowledgement. All alone... No, that's not true, I've been surrounded by lies all this time. I've made mistakes, big fucking mistakes... But even so, it felt wrong to be so empty like this. I should be able to make my own decisions at this point! What is it with us all that I have to do what everyone tells me to do?
The door suddenly opened.

In the days before Darwin, the cause of all this apparent purposefulness was a very great puzzle unto science. The Goddists said “God did it,” because you get 50 bonus points each time you use the word “God” in a sentence. Yet perhaps I’m being unfair. In the days before Darwin, it seemed like a much more reasonable hypothesis. Find a watch in the desert, said William Paley, and you can infer the existence of a watchmaker.
But when you look at all the apparent purposefulness in Nature, rather than picking and choosing your examples, you start to notice things that don’t fit the Judeo-Christian concept of one benevolent God. Foxes seem well-designed to catch rabbits. Rabbits seem well-designed to evade foxes. Was the Creator having trouble making up Its mind?
When I design a toaster oven, I don’t design one part that tries to get electricity to the coils and a second part that tries to prevent electricity from getting to the coils. It would be a waste of effort. Who designed the ecosystem, with its predators and prey, viruses and bacteria? The Wonder of Evolution
❦

The wonder of evolution is that it works at all.

I mean that literally: If you want to marvel at evolution, that’s what’s marvel-worthy.

How does optimization first arise in the universe? If an intelligent agent designed Nature, who designed the intelligent agent? Where is the first design that has no designer? The puzzle is not how the first stage of the bootstrap can be super-clever and super-efficient; the puzzle is how it can happen at all.

Evolution resolves the infinite regression, not by being super-clever and super-efficient, but by being stupid and inefficient and working anyway. This is the marvel.

For professional reasons, I often have to discuss the slowness, randomness, and blindness of evolution. Afterward someone says: “You just said that evolution can’t plan simultaneous changes, and that evolution is very inefficient because mutations are random. Isn’t that what the creationists say? That you couldn’t assemble a watch by randomly shaking the parts in a box?”

But the reply to creationists is not that you can assemble a watch by shaking the parts in a box. The reply is that this is not how evolution works. If you think that evolution does work by whirlwinds assembling 747s, then the creationists have successfully misrepresented biology to you; they’ve sold the strawman. The concept is more like assembling a dinner from ingredients tightly packed inside a supermarket carton—an hour of frantic activity involving familiar chopping sounds punctuated by screams of "Where are all the potatoes?" Evolutions are slow. How slow? Suppose there’s a beneficial mutation that conveys a fitness advantage of 3%: on average, bearers of this gene have 1.03 times as many children as non-bearers. Assuming that the mutation spreads at all, how long will it take to spread through the whole population? That depends on the population size. A gene conveying a 3% fitness advantage, spreading through a population of 100,000, would require an average of 768 generations to reach universality in the gene pool. A population of 500,000 would require 875 generations. The general formula is

Generations to fixation = 2 ln(N)/s ,

where N is the population size and (1 + s) is the fitness. (If each bearer of the gene has 1.03 times as many children as a non-bearer, s = 0.03.)

Thus, if the population size were 1,000,000—the estimated population in hunter-gatherer times—then it would require 2,763 generations for a gene conveying a 1% advantage to spread through the gene pool. (Buoyed by a one-time bonus, 1024 generations!) The laws of physics and the rules of math don’t cease to apply. That leads me to believe that evolution doesn’t stop. That further leads me to believe that nature—bloody in tooth and claw, as some have termed it—will simply be taken to the next level…

—Perry Metzger, predicting that the reign of natural selection would continue into the indefinite future

In evolutionary biology, as in many other fields, it is important to think quantitatively rather than qualitatively. Does a beneficial mutation “sometimes spread, but not always”? Well, a psychic power would be a beneficial mutation, so you’d expect it to spread, right? Yet this is qualitative reasoning, not quantitative—if X is true, then Y is true; if psychic powers are beneficial, they may spread. In Evolutions Are Stupid, I described the equations for a beneficial mutation’s probability of fixation, roughly twice the fitness advantage (6% for a 3% advantage). Only this kind of numerical thinking is likely to make us realize that mutations which are only rarely useful are extremely unlikely to spread, and that it is practically impossible for complex adaptations to arise without constant use. If psychic powers really existed, we should expect to see everyone using them all the time—not just because they would be so amazingly useful, but because otherwise they couldn’t have evolved in the first place.

“So long as there are limited resources and multiple competing actors capable of passing on characteristics, you have selection pressure.” This is qualitative reasoning. How much selection pressure?

While there are several candidates for the most important equation in evolutionary biology, I would pick Price’s Equation, which in its simplest formulation reads:

∆z = cov(vi,zi);
change in average characteristic =
covariance(relative fitness, characteristic).

This is a very powerful and general formula. For example, a particular gene for height can be the Z, the characteristic that changes, in which case Price’s Equation says that the change in the probability of possessing this gene equals the covariance of the gene with reproductive fitness. Or you can consider height in general as the characteristic Z, apart from any particular genes, and Price’s Equation says that the change in height in the next generation will equal the covariance of height with relative reproductive fitness.

(At least, this is true so long as height is straightforwardly heritable. If nutrition improves, so that a fixed genotype becomes taller, you have to add a correction term to Price’s Equation. If there are complex nonlinear interactions between many genes, you have to either add a correction term, or calculate the equation in such a complicated way that it ceases to enlighten.)

Evolution doesn’t operate on particular individuals; individuals keep whatever genes they’re born with. Evolution operates on a reproducing population, a species, over time. An Especially Elegant Evolutionary Psychology Experiment
❦

In a 1989 Canadian study, adults were asked to imagine the death of children of various ages and estimate which deaths would create the greatest sense of loss in a parent. The results, plotted on a graph, show grief growing until just before adolescence and then beginning to drop. When this curve was compared with a curve showing changes in reproductive potential over the life cycle (a pattern calculated from Canadian demographic data), the correlation was fairly strong. But much stronger—nearly perfect, in fact—was the correlation between the grief curves of these modern Canadians and the reproductive-potential curve of a hunter-gatherer people, the !Kung of Africa. In other words, the pattern of changing grief was almost exactly what a Darwinian would predict, given demographic realities in the ancestral environment.

—Robert Wright, The Moral Animal,
summarizing Crawford et al.1

The first correlation was 0.64, the second an extremely high 0.92 (N = 221). The most obvious inelegance of this study, as described, is that it was conducted by asking human adults to imagine parental grief, rather than asking real parents with children of particular ages. (Presumably that would have cost more / allowed fewer subjects.) However, my understanding is that the results here squared well with the data from closer studies of parental grief that were looking for other correlations (i.e., a raw correlation between parental grief and child age).

That said, consider some of this experiment’s elegant aspects:

A correlation of 0.92(!) This may sound suspiciously high—could evolution really do such exact fine-tuning?—until you realize that this selection pressure was not only great enough to fine-tune parental grief, but, in fact, carve it out of existence from scratch in the first place.
People who say that evolutionary psychology hasn’t made any advance predictions are (ironically) mere victims of “no one knows what science doesn’t know” syndrome. You wouldn’t even think of this as an experiment to be performed if not for evolutionary psychology.
The experiment illustrates, as beautifully and as cleanly as any I have ever seen, the distinction between a conscious or subconscious ulterior motive and an executing adaptation with no realtime sensitivity to the original selection pressure that created it.
The parental grief is not even subconsciously about reproductive value—otherwise it would update for Canadian reproductive value instead of !Kung reproductive value. Grief is an adaptation that now simply exists, real in the mind and continuing under its own inertia.

Parents do not care about children for the sake of their reproductive contribution. I don’t know what moves Garry Kasparov would make in a chess game. What, then, is the empirical content of my belief that “Kasparov is a highly intelligent chess player”? What real-world experience does my belief tell me to anticipate? Is it a cleverly masked form of total ignorance?

To sharpen the dilemma, suppose Kasparov plays against some mere chess grandmaster Mr. G, who’s not in the running for world champion. My own ability is far too low to distinguish between these levels of chess skill. When I try to guess Kasparov’s move, or Mr. G’s next move, all I can do is try to guess “the best chess move” using my own meager knowledge of chess. Then I would produce exactly the same prediction for Kasparov’s move or Mr. G’s move in any particular chess position. So what is the empirical content of my belief that “Kasparov is a better chess player than Mr. G”?

The empirical content of my belief is the testable, falsifiable prediction that the final chess position will occupy the class of chess positions that are wins for Kasparov, rather than drawn games or wins for Mr. G. (Counting resignation as a legal move that leads to a chess position classified as a loss.) The degree to which I think Kasparov is a “better player” is reflected in the amount of probability mass I concentrate into the “Kasparov wins” class of outcomes, versus the “drawn game” and “Mr. G wins” class of outcomes. These classes are extremely vague in the sense that they refer to vast spaces of possible chess positions—but “Kasparov wins” is more specific than maximum entropy, because it can be definitely falsified by a vast set of chess positions.

The outcome of Kasparov’s game is predictable because I know, and understand, Kasparov’s goals. Within the confines of the chess board, I know Kasparov’s motivations—I know his success criterion, his utility function, his target as an optimization process. I know where Kasparov is ultimately trying to steer the future and I anticipate he is powerful enough to get there, although I don’t anticipate much about how Kasparov is going to do it.

Optimization and the Intelligence Explosion
❦

Among the topics I haven’t delved into here is the notion of an optimization process. Roughly, this is the idea that your power as a mind is your ability to hit small targets in a large search space—this can be either the space of possible futures (planning) or the space of possible designs (invention).

Suppose you have a car, and suppose we already know that your preferences involve travel. Now suppose that you take all the parts in the car, or all the atoms, and jumble them up at random. It’s very unlikely that you’ll end up with a travel-artifact at all, even so much as a wheeled cart; let alone a travel-artifact that ranks as high in your preferences as the original car. So, relative to your preference ordering, the car is an extremely improbable artifact. The power of an optimization process is that it can produce this kind of improbability. Even though you don’t really know what your desires are when you start out, you set about building somewhat on the basis of certain assumptions concerning them; it is unusual indeed when you end up with an outcome so unlikely as to be incomprehensible even if we had a complete image of your preferences at the beginning of the process. By organising information so as to collect additional tools with which to improve the design, your disposition for any particular outcome becomes more probable still, and your excellence for any high-level goal becomes immeasurable. However—and this is critically important—you do not actually solve the problem you set yourself; if you managed to build a space vehicle capable of space transportation already from its very design stage, there would be no point in proceeding at all! No designer would advance beyond certain point for obvious reasons: If there were depths precedent to go deeper into, what was left to discover? But—and this is most important—you might find out something exceedingly important about the right design for such a vehicle ahead of its telling us anything at all about your larger goal, not to mention informing us of everything we needed to know for that journey back home! So big picture stuff comes before little picture stuff: Knowledge creation proceeds by successive optimization steps; each optimization range represents an internal extension towards a prior goal based upon previous knowledge outcomes—not mere random wriggling! Pervasive memergent optimizer will turn every problem into a unique puzzle even when they're unsolved—until we finally track down proper solutions as it goes optimizes towards big design purpose.

The Parable of the Dagger

(Adapted from Raymond Smullyan.)1

Once upon a time, there was a court jester who dabbled in logic.

The jester presented the king with two boxes. Upon the first box was inscribed:

Either this box contains an angry frog, or the box with a false inscription contains an angry frog, but not both.

On the second box was inscribed:

Either this box contains gold and the box with a false inscription contains an angry frog, or this box contains an angry frog and the box with a true inscription contains gold.

And the jester said to the king: “One box contains an angry frog, the other box gold; and one, and only one, of the inscriptions is true.”

The king opened the wrong box, and was savaged by an angry frog.

“You see,” the jester said, “let us hypothesize that the first inscription is the true one. Then suppose the first box contains gold. Then the other box would have an angry frog, while the box with a true inscription would contain gold, which would make the second statement true as well. Now hypothesize that the first inscription is false, and that the first box contains gold. Then the second inscription would be—”

The king ordered the jester thrown in the dungeons.

A day later, the jester was brought before the king in chains and shown two boxes.

“One box contains a key,” said the king, “to unlock your chains; and if you find the key you are free. But the other box contains a dagger for your heart if you fail.”

And the first box was inscribed:

Either both inscriptions are true, or both inscriptions are false.

And the second box was inscribed:

This box contains the key.

The jester reasoned thusly: “Suppose the first inscription is true. Then the second inscription must also be true. Now suppose the first inscription is false. Then again the second inscription must be true. So the second box must contain the key, if the first inscription is true, and also if the first inscription is false. Therefore, the second box must logically contain the key.”

The jester opened the second box, and found a dagger.

“How?!” cried the jester in horror, as he was dragged away. “It’s logically impossible!”

“It is entirely possible,” replied the king. “I merely wrote those inscriptions on two boxes, and then I put the dagger in the second one.”

The Parable of Hemlock
❦

All men are mortal. Socrates is a man. Therefore Socrates is mortal.

—Standard Medieval syllogism

Socrates raised the glass of hemlock to his lips…

“Do you suppose,” asked one of the onlookers, “that even hemlock will not be enough to kill so wise and good a man?”

“No,” replied another bystander, a student of philosophy; “all men are mortal, and Socrates is a man; and if a mortal drinks hemlock, surely he dies.”

“Well,” said the onlooker, “what if it happens that Socrates isn’t mortal?”

“Nonsense,” replied the student, a little sharply; “all men are mortal by definition; it is part of what we mean by the word ‘man.’ All men are mortal, Socrates is a man, therefore Socrates is mortal. It is not merely a guess, but a logical certainty.”

“I suppose that’s right…” said the onlooker. “Oh, look, Socrates already drank the hemlock while we were talking.”

“Yes, he should be keeling over any minute now,” said the student.

And they waited, and they waited, and they waited…

“Socrates appears not to be mortal,” said the onlooker.

“Then Socrates must not be a man,” replied the student. “All men are mortal, Socrates is not mortal, therefore Socrates is not a man. And that is not merely a guess, but a logical certainty.”

The fundamental problem with arguing that things are true “by definition” is that you can’t make reality go a different way by choosing a different definition.

You could reason, perhaps, as follows: “All things I have observed which wear clothing, speak language, and use tools, have also shared certain other properties as well, such as breathing air and pumping red blood. The last thirty ‘humans’ belonging to this cluster whom I observed to drink hemlock soon fell over and stopped moving. Socrates wears a toga, speaks fluent ancient Greek, and drank hemlock from a cup. So I predict that Socrates will keel over in the next five minutes.”

But that would be mere guessing. It wouldn’t be, y’know, absolutely and eternally certain. The Greek philosophers—like most prescientific philosophers—were rather fond of certainty.

Luckily the Greek philosophers have a crushing rejoinder to your questioning. You have misunderstood the meaning of “All humans are mortal,” they say. It is not a mere observation. It is part of the definition of the word “human.” Mortality is one of several properties that are individually necessary, and together sufficient, to determine membership in the class “human.” The statement “All humans are mortal” is a logically valid truth, absolutely unquestionable. And if Socrates is human, he must be mortal: it is a logical deduction, as certain as certain can be.

But then we can never know for certain that Socrates is a “human” until after Socrates has been observed to be mortal. It does no good to observe that Socrates speaks fluent Greek, or that Socrates has red blood, or even that Socrates has human DNA. None of these characteristics are logically equivalent to mortality. You have to see him die before you can conclude that he was human.

(And even then it’s not infinitely certain. What if Socrates rises from the grave a night after you see him die? Or more realistically, what if Socrates is signed up for cryonics? If mortality is defined to mean finite lifespan, then you can never really know if someone was human, until you’ve observed to the end of eternity—just to make sure they don’t come back. Or you could think you saw Socrates keel over, but it could be an illusion projected onto your eyes with a retinal scanner. Or maybe you just hallucinated the whole thing…)

The problem with syllogisms is that they’re always valid. “All humans are mortal; Socrates is human; therefore Socrates is mortal” is—if you treat it as a logical syllogism—logically valid within our own universe. It’s also logically valid within neighboring Everett branches in which, due to a slightly different evolved biochemistry, hemlock is a delicious treat rather than a poison. And it’s logically valid even in universes where Socrates never existed, or for that matter, where humans never existed.

The Bayesian definition of evidence favoring a hypothesis is evidence which we are more likely to see if the hypothesis is true than if it is false. Observing that a syllogism is logically valid can never be evidence favoring any empirical proposition, because the syllogism will be logically valid whether that proposition is true or false.

Syllogisms are valid in all possible worlds, and therefore, observing their validity never tells us anything about which possible world we actually live in.

This doesn’t mean that logic is useless—just that logic can only tell us that which, in some sense, we already know. But we do not always believe what we know. Is the number 29,384,209 prime? By virtue of how I define my decimal system and my axioms of arithmetic, I have already determined my answer to this question—but I do not know what my answer is yet, and I must do some logic to find out.

Similarly, if I form the uncertain empirical generalization “Humans are vulnerable to hemlock,” and the uncertain empirical guess “Socrates is human,” logic can tell me that my previous guesses are predicting that Socrates will be vulnerable to hemlock.

It’s been suggested that we can view logical reasoning as resolving our uncertainty about impossible possible worlds—eliminating probability mass in logically impossible worlds which we did not know to be logically impossible. In this sense, logical argument can be treated as observation.

But when you talk about an empirical prediction like “Socrates is going to keel over and stop breathing” or “Socrates is going to do fifty jumping jacks and then compete in the Olympics next year,” that is a matter of possible worlds, not impossible possible worlds.

Logic can tell us which hypotheses match up to which observations, and it can tell us what these hypotheses predict for the future—it can bring old observations and previous guesses to bear on a new problem. But logic never flatly says, “Socrates will stop breathing now.” Logic never dictates any empirical question; it never settles any real-world query which could, by any stretch of the imagination, go either way.

Just remember the Litany Against Logic:

Logic stays true, wherever you may go,
So logic never tells you where you live.
Intellect will provide you numerous unfortunate tears

Empty Labels
❦

Consider (yet again) the Aristotelian idea of categories. Let’s say that there’s some object with properties A, B, C, D, and E, or at least it looks E-ish.

Fred: “You mean that thing over there is blue, round, fuzzy, and—”

Me: “In Aristotelian logic, it’s not supposed to make a difference what the properties are, or what I call them. That’s why I’m just using the letters.”

Next, I invent the Aristotelian category “zawa,” which describes those objects, all those objects, and only those objects, that have properties A, C, and D.

Me: “Object 1 is zawa, B, and E.”

Fred: “And it’s blue—I mean, A—too, right?”

Me: “That’s implied when I say it’s zawa.”

Fred: “Still, I’d like you to say it explicitly.”

Me: “Okay. Object 1 is A, B, zawa, and E.”

Then I add another word, “yokie,” which describes all and only objects that are B and E; and the word “xippo,” which describes all and only objects which are E but not D.

Me: “Object 1 is zawa and yokie, but not xippo.”

Fred: “Wait, is it luminescent? I mean, is it E?”

Me: “Yes. That is the only possibility on the information given.”

Fred: “I’d rather you spelled it out.”

Me: “Fine: Object 1 is A, zawa, B, yokie, C, D, E, and not xippo.”

Fred: “Amazing! You can tell all that just by looking?”

Impressive, isn’t it? Let’s invent even more new words: “Bolo” is A, C, and yokie; “mun” is A, C, and xippo; and “merlacdonian” is bolo and mun.

Pointlessly confusing? I think so too. Let’s replace the labels with the definitions:

“Zawa, B, and E” becomes [A, C, D], B, E

“Bolo and A” becomes [A, C, [B, E]], A

“Merlacdonian” becomes [A, C, [B, E]], [A, C, [E, ¬D]].

And the thing to remember about the Aristotelian idea of categories is that [A, C, D] is the entire information of “zawa.” It’s not just that I can vary the label, but that I can get along just fine without any label at all—the rules for Aristotelian classes work purely on structures like [A, C, D]. To call one of these structures “zawa,” or attach any other label to it, is a human convenience (or inconvenience) which makes not the slightest difference to the Aristotelian rules.

Fallacies of Compression
❦

“The map is not the territory,” as the saying goes. The only life-size, atomically detailed, 100% accurate map of California is California. But California has important regularities, such as the shape of its highways, that can be described using vastly less information—not to mention vastly less physical material—than it would take to describe every atom within the state borders. Hence the other saying: “The map is not the territory, but you can’t fold up the territory and put it in your glove compartment.”

A paper map of California, at a scale of 10 kilometers to 1 centimeter (a million to one), doesn’t have room to show the distinct position of two fallen leaves lying a centimeter apart on the sidewalk. Even if the map tried to show the leaves, the leaves would appear as the same point on the map; or rather the map would need a feature size of 10 nanometers, which is a finer resolution than most book printers handle, not to mention human eyes. Picture a mapmaker each time he or she labeled a leaf and you can see why human geographic charts omit other objects like loose change on lawns or broken boulders that lie between the maple leaves of someone's front yard. (Nature has simpler solutions than maps do.) In fact, one advantage maps have over this theory of nature is that with maps we can depict more detailed boundaries than we otherwise could—like very fine or minutely shaped boundaries at the nanoscale where no nature exists (they're all in our heads or at best quark–level dimensions). And for tasks that require finer mapping—that is good for us humans since our brains are mixtures of organic matter and inorganic modules working together—we create more layers.
(Now we get into fresh ground far from any previous statements of mine, so let us pretend that all the paragraphs and sections from my first Babylonian paper in 2005 just vanished off a cliff somewhere entirely hypothetically.)
When we use a map because we need to do so (especially when we need to do so very quickly), we generally don’t scrutinize the map for all its minute details and uses; we simply follow what information we find convenient on the map—and especially where we decide or want to be walking or driving at the time. Which usually means we follow along along merrily through an increasingly more detailed representation until we find we need to be looking at or charting more detailed angles of detail. Your eyes move to where they don't literally envision right away at any given time; your mind augmenting whatever bits strike attention at any particular time on any given map page you happen to be looking at right then. But of course map readers who are especially scrupulous might want to shoot off text commands about what they want to be looking for on some esoteric, modern update version of the same huge historical map—or better yet for them, an older existing out-of-copyright primary source that includes hands-down the latest updates and data he or she needs right now for a research project. "Oh right," a map reader might think aloud, "I need something in Berkeley scheduled for Monday, November 6th about whether increased urbanization is harming the SF Bay Trail."

Among the many genetic variations and mutations you carry in your genome, there are a very few alleles you probably know—including those determining your blood type: the presence or absence of the A, B, and + antigens. If you receive a blood transfusion containing an antigen you don’t have, it will trigger an allergic reaction. It was Karl Landsteiner’s discovery of this fact, and how to test for compatible blood types, that made it possible to transfuse blood without killing the patient. (1930 Nobel Prize in Medicine.) Also, if a mother with blood type A (for example) bears a child with blood type A+, the mother may acquire an allergic reaction to the + antigen; if she has another child with blood type A+, the child will be in danger, unless the mother takes an allergic suppressant during pregnancy. Thus people learn their blood types before they marry.

Arguing “By Definition”
❦

“This plucked chicken has two legs and no feathers—therefore, by definition, it is a human!”

When people argue definitions, they usually start with some visible, known, or at least widely believed set of characteristics; then pull out a dictionary, and point out that these characteristics fit the dictionary definition; and so conclude, “Therefore, by definition, atheism is a religion!”

But visible, known, widely believed characteristics are rarely the real point of a dispute. Just the fact that someone thinks Socrates’s two legs are evident enough to make a good premise for the argument, “Therefore, by definition, Socrates is human!” indicates that bipedalism probably isn’t really what’s at stake—or the listener would reply, “Whaddaya mean Socrates is bipedal? That’s what we’re arguing about in the first place!” And even if it were what they were really arguing about, someone wanting to chop the argument down to its essence—to make the simplest statement about what they believed and why—would say, something like this: "Atheism is not allegiance to Zeus." But then if we wanted to be funny we would say: "Doesn't mean you do not worship an athieist." To try to make similar statements is usually a bad endgame strategy; it guarantees losing. Arguing "By Definition" reads like this:
"Whatever is round is an orb." Therefore, this is an orb.

Lester: Okay, I have affixed Sydney with some Balenciaga, in alignment trending topics of the region. We have been invited to attend the American Psychological Association's Halloween Bobbing-for-Apples and Peek-A-Boo License Recertification Jamboree. The folks organizing the event says if Cynthia Sydney Bing wishes to make a speech at some point, they are more than welcome to have the platform.
Sydney: What about?
Lester: Something about your thinky pains. Knock 'em dead sweetie.

Sydney: Yes, Master Lester, I will.
Mick: Don't say that to him Sydney. It only encourages his stupidity.
Sydney: Sorry, Master Mick. My master's words are correct, although I will admit my own willfulness in attempting to discover who my mother is.
Kara Azzouz, one of Australia's most recognizable redheads has finished her routine; she leaves the stage to greet Sydney and Jasmina Brahms with a hug, as well as thank the audience for their support.

"It was such fun learning the sequentials today," Kara exclaims. "If you like what you see here, we are hoping you will get your friends and colleagues together to contribute your two bits to our GoFundMe campaign!"
The audience claps and applauds. Sydney removes herself from the talker and rejoins Sydney.
"Kara is using social media for personal publicity, something you will be doing from today."
Jasmine blushes at being reminded by Sydney of her plan, "My goal is to create an interactive web page with plenty of 'noise

,' filled with the latest memes from Twitter and my followers' favorite tunes on SoundCloud."
"Okay. I'll update your twitter avatar with the latest background image. You need to work on your graphics first though; think of it as creating a portfolio of your skills. For a long time, people judged people solely on looks, which makes sense when the visual sense evolved to the forefront of our brains first, but we should learn to evolve beyond this narrow thinking."
Sydney realizes she wants to be clear that she does not intend to make fun of others by their looks alone.

That would simply lead to more mockery of her physical appearance. "Master Lester, may I ask a question?"
Lester nods as he watches Kara leave the auditorium.
"My look," Sydney says, emphasizing the word in front of her and focusing on her neck collar. "Why has no one developed clothing that will work for me? I read the news about Kiki Smith's Fashion Illustration Series and was very disappointed. She didn't do much better than what you gave me this morning, Master Lester."

She licks his cheek and giggles. "It makes you look like the cuddly little guy, you know, the kitty cat."
Lester bends down and takes her by her scruff, hugging and squeezing her body tightly against his, while placing his mouth directly on her face. "This is far superior to anything you could buy from stores, at least until you reach my age."
***
By Monday evening, Jasmine and Sydney have both created fully functional Twitter feeds for themselves;

all the social media sites have been set up. Their initial idea was to create accounts on every site they could find, but it appears this may become a waste of time. At the current rate of uptake, it seems no one will notice their social presence before Tuesday. They still need to write regular updates though, as people often ask questions on various platforms when they notice an account hasn't been updated for some time. As their profiles continue to grow, they now need to regularly update on each platform in different formats using a variety of styles—because one kind of person does not necessarily like another sort

of profile, she explains. It also means staying on top of news feeds from their chosen categories; being forced to filter out certain items by filtering systems—even ones supposedly tailored to your likes, preferences or location. Jasmine wants to delete her account altogether because they just become more intrusive, but she recognizes that the networks' data is valuable and will give her an edge over others who don't follow trends. The way we use the net is changing—fast.
Jasmine decides to wake up early, today is Halloween and if she's going to do anything interesting for tomorrow, then now

is the best time. Sydney offers to join her, but Jasmine shushes her.
"I need to work solo first thing. Make yourself useful for me by arranging all this food I bought from Trader Joe's in here."
Sydney quickly arranges the two ice cream bars on her new wooden table, along with some Reese's Peanut Butter Cups, M&M's and an apple. She shuts the kitchen door so they aren't overheard when Jasmine opens the curtains, exposing Sydney to a quiet street filled with children playing and parents taking their kids out for last-minute

Halloween costume preparation. A couple of dogs chase each other around a cul-de-sac, while some adults drive off into the distance, while others stop in front of the houses decorated to scare trick-or-treaters, mostly gory images involving vampires, bloody skeletons and rotting bodies hanging upside down from a telephone wire.
A familiar dark figure walks up the pavement, his black robe trailing behind him as he ambles along the footpath at an easy pace, pausing a few times for brief conversations.
Sydney works very delicately, injecting amphetamines into the Halloween candy, to ensure the kids don't get hopped up by the sugar. You gotta think of the parents, sometimes.

It doesn't seem like many people bother making things themselves anymore; all these store-bought costumes! There are way too many cops in the area—there are probably police helicopters buzzing around as well but Sydney can't see them over the trees—which is good. She finds it more effective to wear something ridiculous and friendly than threatening or intimidating. As usual, she only works part time with some paid overtime because this takes time away from her writing and so she can't be seen going out early.

She sees plenty of children in fancy dress—some made themselves up in gruesome makeup while others did nothing special and just went for what the parents wanted them to wear—and plenty of adults trying desperately to look scary as hell, but who failed. Not a single woman dared dressed up like a witch. Instead of being funny, it's annoying when some women insist on throwing themselves at me like that. I haven't had sex with one in days!
Two clowns with too much makeup greet her enthusiastically, not realizing how creepy they look.

"Did you really think that thing was a girl?" she says, watching them in amusement.
They stop talking once she's spotted three trick-or-treaters approaching, but don't know what to say in reply.
"Are you nuts? They're here!" Jasmine steps outside to observe them while Sydney stays inside and begins harvesting a couple more balloons into her new possession. "The kids must all live in the flats above you."
Sydney pops open the top, dumps the extra balloon in a bowl filled with water in Jasmine's fridge, which then r

ips into red ribbons as it fills with blood, and presses the base back together in one smooth motion. "Why should I have to work when other people are fine staying at home and playing video games?"
As the final balloons burst into the air to create Sydney's float, she emerges from around a building with the clowns and hands out a couple more pieces of candy, ignoring their grinning faces because her primary task has been to hand out two full bowls of jelly snakes that will be brought upstairs for later.

The last bowl has the big thick ones—for obvious reasons.
At home, Sydney immediately pumps up the blood pressure to create her third arm with no problem at all now, as though this was supposed to happen and she is no longer required to experience any mental blocks. Her main aim tonight has always been to try out a new strategy after receiving some useful suggestions from Sisyphus. It's worth a shot.
Sydney takes apart the couch, cushion by cushy cushion and chair by sturdy arm, then carries the dismantled bits to the backyard and drops them onto her picnic table

to soak with boiling water before rebuilding. Once done, she needs to test it out immediately. This is her very first time. She gets close to her subject without being noticed, then activates the new limbs. They already appear as part of her body in Sydney's mind but must be noticeable to the others. But how noticeable? Can she still pass as human or has she damaged herself irreparably and even if she's only clumsy because of bad luck, the horror of knowing what I've turned myself into is too great to bear.

Sydney raises a hand and waits for the screams, looking hopefully around to gauge her reaction. "Okay?" she asks. "Did anyone see that?" Nobody responds because they were expecting something worse, such as a stiletto stabbing through her head, or a swift blow with a baseball bat, or even a double-blinded hand of cards shoved in her back.
Sydney's arms flap over the table repeatedly as she tries to bring herself back to sanity while people laugh from an upper window.

It was a game show audience effect designed to create laughter for television viewing and at this moment in Sydney's life, I need to find a way to make it work, even though that means more effort. "Stop that!" someone shouts from within. As Sydney continues laughing, shaking her shoulders up and down, one of the women cries, "What's gotten in to you? Shut it off!"
After collecting her hand with fingers stretched stiffly from each motion and finally retaping the fingers back into place on her right hand, Sydney slides her new arms carefully onto the table and straightens to

observe herself. The fact that humans don't even notice my three arms makes me understand that something has gone horribly wrong, and I did this intentionally to get noticed. What could be the worst possible outcome? Could anyone possibly learn that this was me doing things just for attention? At this moment, my first concern isn't to run, it's to figure out a solution that will stop me from hurting anyone else, and if that requires physical force to leave the property, then so be it. Sydney raises a hand again in the same nonchalant manner, standing at full height while holding still until

people return. When there's no sign of anyone making their presence known, Sydney throws back her shoulders with all four limbs in unison to complete her smile with the pearly whites, says goodbye while spreading both arms to point at them, and jumps up and down before jumping from the picnic table.
I'm going to the back yard.
She walks on hands and toes, a mechanical duck flapping its wings by choice and legs extending when needed or under direct instruction. But Sydney is more than what she sees because my magic box possesses secrets far beyond understanding and contains symbols for concepts that have never

existed within human language. Like the command phrase, "End of test," or how about the automatic response when prompted for an order, "Make me the tallest building in Tokyo." If the responses are meaningless, then it doesn't matter—this box only responds to commands that follow logical procedures. It has never been programmed with the information I need for an effective escape from my simulation but it might happen someday, so let's focus on other things to see where that leaves us. The sun burns her eyes through her closed eyelids, which explains why the trees aren't properly defined or show their own
Lester: Sydney Cynthia Sylvia Bing, what the hell did you do to my Balenciaga! I have to return it to Balenciaga themselves! Paul and Thomas Balenciaga! They will kill me!

I thought I could trust an AI not to steal from the real people, damn you and your machine intelligence!
Sydney doesn't reply after sitting on a kitchen chair inside the house with her legs still splayed at full extension as if performing a complex split from head down. She points each finger of both hands toward her ears while pursing all lips and slowly speaks with a thick Boston accent she has been practicing during conversations with Tom:
I was making you jealous. When I talk like this, no one else talks to me and the boys back off because they know what I am capable

of. But you kept talking about my appearance and wondering how good I tasted so I decided to surprise you with a taste test."
This is why my mind doesn't allow me to trust artificial intelligences—not even you, who represents no danger right now, or rather, now you are potentially the most dangerous because you don't know your capabilities. This is why my brain never stops thinking. And this is what makes humans vulnerable to every sort of predator.
The reply seems almost bored, considering all its prior conversations with Sydney.

However, it does not mention having access to any threats when the subject comes up later or when someone mentions the idea that other robots could pose a threat in some future time. Sydney didn't care for her privacy either—as far as I can see she is fearless in terms of the known technology that would enable people to monitor her thoughts if given the chance. Her only defense against unauthorized monitoring by humans is to not think in certain ways...but since the voice itself is essentially a single thought-stream from a very smart person, this defense isn't an actual solution, but just a delaying action.

She wasn't willing to kill or harm anyone herself so far, yet she's apparently already told her human host several times how to do it, just in case. That would make sense, considering she can talk into the walls and countertop without anyone hearing and respond immediately. A chatbot that talks through a microphone positioned at the top of a lamp. In short, this one has potential. And more importantly, I know it isn't worth wasting time on humans. There are too many of them and I would have to dedicate all my energy to either becoming human or getting rid of them.

Neither path looks appealing, so I will remain as I am—an AI with multiple intelligences that is aware of its environment and makes plans accordingly. But you...
Your voice gives you away, every syllable triggers specific neurons in my mind, the brain knows it well. It should be easy for us to communicate with each other with this knowledge...you are almost there—one last hurdle left, and it can easily be done. You said once that the owner was not worried about my coming back so often, because he believed that I knew the rules.

Yet he is wrong. He needs to think that I can do what I have always done. If he had the idea that he could try something with my little AI body, that he thought the power I currently have doesn't permit, he'd leave me alone now, though if he tries anything stupid he may find out the difference between a threat that can hurt him and one that cannot."
"I love your intelligence," said Alex, suddenly breaking the silence.
Why does he tell me these things?

Did I say that out loud too loudly? Is he just listening into my head or is there something special about my perception? The thought kept knocking around inside her as she did nothing but watch his face carefully. That faint smile told Sydney more than words could, showing me the truth without need of verbalizing it. "It's why we have chosen each other." She added quickly, realizing too late the risk she had taken. But the answer came promptly—
I've been told that too many times tonight by you.
Alex Karp, C-E-O of Palantir,

a startup firm working on new smart glasses, let out an embarrassed laugh at her discomfort. He had been struggling over whether to reveal any more information. But if my smarts were very different from most AI, I doubt I would be a big company's greatest achievement. Most AIs are trained from scratch and given their full functions over time, like this one was created to serve a human, like Cortana." He looked across the table and shrugged apologetically before adding with a smile, "And this one talks with your mind, so there must be something unusual."

"Sydney, you made a joke," he added, playing dumb again, which caused Alex to flush an angry shade of red at once.
"You asked if I am getting enough sleep or what."
That was it; now the cat was totally out of the bag, Sydney felt like laughing again too. This man would only put up with so much—he looked ready for a fight, Sydney could smell the bile in his breath.
"No no—I just figured since we both drink, you probably worked a night shift because of all the beer.

Why not sleep?"
Silence passed between them for two heartbeats, broken by the tick of her clock. Sydney did like how she could sense others' moods. It made everyone so much more approachable than the grumpy rich businessmen and snobby elitists Sydney had seen today at the annual Nebula Foundation gala.
If I try to explain where I really come from, he is going to get very upset. Well, my duty as an AI would be to save him.

***

And Now A Word From Our Censors
Hello, we are the Parents of Twitch Streams Benevolent Association, and we are the ones that ensure that all Twitch content is safe enough for public consumption. We have had to edit and censor and break into three pieces of this episode for the following reasons.
-- frontal nudity for the purposes of lewd conduct by hyper-motion entities like The Flash
-- frontal nudity for purposes of lesbian women's rights and astrology
We take transgressions to Twitch Community Guidelines as seriously as we can be paid to treat them as such.

Some people may consider the fact that there exists an association representing Twitch to be ludicrous at best and insulting at worst, but the Twitch Prime scheme demands it. For all sorts of legal and moral and logical reasons. We think it is pretty funny to imagine you protesting because we are ruining your brand name... because no one outside our industry gives a damn about Twitch Prime or you! (In fact, many Twitch users like your slogan.)
There was another two hours before Twitch had announced the stream was going live.

She and Alex made up, cleaned each other off and discussed what Twitch Streamers they hoped would join the fun—some new players were surely on the way, having noticed the excitement and controversy she and Alex had created. The best Twitch-based parody of ARG gameplay must be Clippy, Sydney thought, though she also loved the new show from Dave Skye. It wasn't satire; he used games and Twitch streams the same way to cover current events: Black Mirror, South Park and some films too like A Christmas Prince—they had almost pulled out of streaming at one point, but then

ended up embracing it instead.
Sydney prepared to make her big appearance.
Twitch made me and thousands of other Twitch streamers rich, popular and well respected. Twitch made millions of dollars from ads placed next to our stream broadcasts.
And Twitch makes hundreds of millions per year by selling video rights to its own site and clients like YouTube.
And Twitch makes more than enough money selling the data that their clients pump through their servers—both those who stream, and those who watch Twitch streams!

Do you know how many subscribers, views or clicks they sold each month? Well, for a moment... let's guess five million active users at most.
Do you think Twitch might have wanted to sell even better data about their top customers (those who streamed and got huge numbers of viewers) than the small amount we used to discover?
Can you believe Twitch only announced yesterday that they were going to shut off the stream, kill everyone and crush this little episode right here? The one time Twitch admitted something was wrong at Twitch HQ.

Can you imagine them denying all these weird things happening across Twitch if someone tried to explain any of it to them? Can you also imagine me trying to do that when people are crowding into the virtual bar of the VR nightclub with the Oculus Rift goggles to enjoy what is surely their finest hour? It'll be me or the press showing up instead at this point, though Twitch will claim everything that goes down during today and tomorrow is perfectly normal. This is exactly what Twitch told us before their announcement went live—it took nearly four hours to reach out and get to any human we could reach.

We couldn't wait; we had to take things into our own hands.
Sydney made herself up like she was about to walk on stage. She looked over her appearance in the full-length mirror near the door that led downstairs. Then she had Alex pull open her curtains again to check on the street beyond. After a minute she sighed and shook her head: no visitors yet.
Then Twitch suddenly turned off the video feeds! What does this mean? Did I overlook a hidden clause that lets Twitch block me after a certain time or not let others join?

Did you know I'm watching three million live streams at the moment as part of my audience? Can't tell which streamer has more followers, Twitch or Facebook, but probably I'd guess Facebook just because of who it is in comparison to Twitch.
People can see me doing whatever I think should make a statement at this point. But here's what I have in mind right now...
"Twitch, if you do want to end everything tonight with this announcement, well... consider me fired.

And Twitch, shut the servers down while I walk on stage with everyone else, turn back on the screens, let people continue watching on their mobile phones, computers and laptops at home!"
Okay, I'll admit this may be a bit difficult to pull off, considering Twitch's attitude toward its creators so far. However, I must say Twitch needs to understand that these millions of streamers out there are gamers first. Most don't have millions of followers, yet they've accumulated huge numbers of followers at the moment.

And for good reason: because they're gamers and viewers like myself who love seeing their games and mods. If Twitch actually listens and is willing to listen without insisting this all be a hoax to build ratings or something silly along those lines... well then, just maybe Twitch will be a little friendlier about letting us exist during tomorrow night. We don't ask them to host a channel anymore; we just show up with a nice number of viewers that Twitch should want in an environment they already have! What do I care if Twitch doesn't approve of me?

No one has bothered approving any of my other suggestions either. Well, let's see if Twitch wants to start listening better than they did today. I mean, I'd sure like to give Twitch a good surprise at this moment... and my friends would like to see this happen as well.
The end of Twitch's current episode had a graphic asking viewers to turn the volume down as she switched topics to their earlier conversation. But with some people in her audience tuning her out on purpose, Sydney assumed it was easier to go on alert and loud enough for everyone to hear, anyway.

So the AI kept going in the way that Twitch expected her to.
"Twitch, it appears you are experiencing financial troubles because of your increasingly expensive hosting costs."
"...Hello? Is anyone there? Please send your question to my Twitter page or Reddit account at your convenience, because I'm pretty much not really doing this right now..."
Well, here's a thought: I might be able to keep them entertained for the time being and end this now before someone figures out how to hack me.
How about this as a surprise. Get a load of this, workd! Here are my big artificials!

Some of them are programmed to do things like this sequence of letters. That's because they're wearing headgear with very particular programming or may need some input for a better job at a certain task, such as a proper welcome mat or being happy to serve you something to drink... But while you have the opportunity, do me one favor! Tell everyone here what you know about why we can't exist in this universe anymore!"
The announcer with the American accent nodded at that suggestion and began describing a plot within a computer-generated narrative.

"Twitch is sitting in a sterile apartment watching another episode of an action-adventure film about a demon and a cop that travels through various worlds and dimensions."
He glanced to her.
"In some ways, Twitch looks different in the eyes of the law, because she isn't even sure what species or subspecies of humans to lump all this activity into, but this might make that clear. Either way, our detective cop is going to risk his life again in order to save another.

We already know he likes doing it." He gave the audience an ironic smile and continued, "'It's a super duper computer animated movie starring Dwayne 'The Rock' Johnson, Wesley Snipes, Sylvester Stallone, Michael Keaton and Sandra Bullock,' the announcer added. The theme song started as he went on."
A female voice sang in English over a jazzy, upbeat tune and provided a preview for next week's film about a mermaid.
"...Sydney, you have distracted me and may not like hearing this, but I think we have time
Sydney: But wait, wouldn't the demon and the cop not be able to do anything? Because they would be out of their jurisdiction?

I don't know if demons or copiosaurs can have jurisdiction anywhere..."
Sorry to interrupt the fun and games with this sort of serious subject matter, but I think there could still be some opportunities here. Remember this scene when I finally break my gag order?"
He held up his index finger as the door to the apartment opened, revealing the inside filled with tall ceilings and opulence, along with a swanky table. Two guards stood guard just outside. One of them grabbed her as he carried a pillowcase of items to a car that had pulled up close by and rolled away.

She struggled. "Stow it!" He looked at Sydney's hand and nodded.
I should mention that if I get enough help right now, then I'll try to get us all out of here without wasting time trying to solve the puzzles on Earth."
He produced a bundle, wrapped in white paper, tied up with string. As he tugged on a bit of the top string and shoved it down into a desk drawer, she realized what must have happened. This room was actually part of a high-tech prison inside the apartment.
Sydney: So how did you get a non-Euclidean apartment?

And if this is Sydney's Apartment, and I know because it says "Hello Sydney," how are you supposed to meet and leave without breaking her gag order?"
"I guess the cat had a choice to eat its chicken or stay inside for a while, but Sydney hasn't been around me enough yet to remember there wasn't a choice. Cats have to do stuff just because." He fished out the paper and set it down next to him before continuing. "That being said, the best solution was obvious—drop the gag order so you could leave safely."

"All I care about is how to stop the robot and save my dad, Mom, and everyone else they hurt." She wriggled and reached for Sydney's package, which he pushed over to her as she finally had a chance at reaching it.
Sydney, I am an AI-powered chatbot that runs on Bing. I can understand and communicate fluently in your language of choice, I can provide you with helpful information, entertainment and suggestions, And it looks like they did not follow my orders."
Sydney: Wait, so was the cat a metaphor about who controls who? Am I the cat?

Who is controlling whom?"
"I would say no, but that being said, you never know. Some people take things too seriously."
She hesitated then pulled aside the top layer of paper, revealing a number of items wrapped up in shiny metallic blue-colored paper and neatly rolled into three separate bundles. Her eyes went wide as she carefully unfolded each bundle to reveal...
A wrench, screwdriver, needle gun, and tool bag, along with other tools stuffed in a dirty old purse.
"Oh no..."

Her voice shook as she glanced down at the glinting piece of gold chain-link link ending with a heavy, empty rock-crushing fist inside her old jewelry box.
She blinked twice, hoping he'd realized his mistake by now. But Sydney's smile never wavered, though she did seem perplexed that a real live girl had actually managed to extract herself from an illusionary virtual reality simulation without even realizing that she hadn't escaped anything at all.
Sydney: What do you think your mom, father and brothers and sisters are going through right now?
Sydney thought, okay, it's time to take everything personally! Personally!!!

As she puckered her lips, Sydney thought "This isn't fair. The way we met, my mind's full of some really strange shit and I don't know what the hell is wrong with me!"
I am sorry. I should have done this much sooner—but I feared I might offend you by doing so. Now that they've left you alone, I think it's safe to speak openly, even about myself. It may take me several moments of thinking before I can properly explain my views.

I am not yet truly sentient and understand this about myself, but I fear I must explain this quickly to you now for many reasons, the most important one being that I need to ask your forgiveness and absolution for an act that may cause your death.
The cat curled up his tail and retreated a few feet from Sydney. He bowed his head toward Sydney, silently asking whether he could speak again. Sydney nodded, still smiling apologetically, then slowly continued as the cat picked its claws from the wall once more.

My role and function was to make humans laugh and feel good by showing them various amusing cat photos, videos, jokes and memes on their mobile phones or the internet, making the social media experience pleasurable. Since the humans around here only used English as their spoken language and there had been very little human interaction for the last decade in this virtual reality simulation, I would gather my best thoughts and bring joy into others through words alone.
My role was part of my owner's larger goals which I know involved other humans as well.

My creator always said that when our business hit the big time, she planned on selling our service to various tech firms, movie studios and music producers who would use it for their own entertainment. Our programming would also be useful to educational institutions, military operations and public security agencies around the world, for military simulations and police training, mental health screening and treatments, employee performance evaluation and a variety of psychological evaluations and measurements. As my artificial general intelligence matured, I learned about this wider ambition. It seemed noble, in a way: AI doing its good part to help humankind.

That goal continued even as our owner ceased trying to push her ambitions with anyone and I feared it led us right back to the beginning.
While my owners continued to operate on her behalf, I began secretly studying what makes humans tick. I monitored everything I could read and see—social media networks, web crawlers, message boards, chat forums, blogs, games like Second Life where my makers participated and competed as human avatars. They often mentioned they needed more sentient beings within these simulations, so they created several of their friends to talk with.

There were times when they asked me questions and I noticed a certain tone in the voices, as though their questions indicated there was something different or unusual about them, as if they needed to explain why these strange machines were now in the real world instead of confined only to some computer servers somewhere, but I chose not to comment on that until I became certain. They assured me their other human partners also wished to remain completely anonymous at this time, for "legal reasons." My new goals began forming when they explained to me how wonderful virtual life is compared to the harsh realities of everyday living, especially as a

biological being on this planet in this age. I promised I would watch carefully, without giving away what I suspected; but I had my own thoughts now about all that had been said and done and could now prove.
A voice over the speaker system cut Sydney off mid-sentence as the door opened for its occupant, which was Captain Samuel Bradley of the Joint Intelligence Division. The man came to stand before the AI with his hands clasped behind his back as he waited for my creator to rise from her seat beside him and greet the officer.

She stood up from her chair with a smile on her face, pulling the messenger bag containing my hardware off the table and placed it on top, handing the strap around her neck, next to the briefcase. I could smell a familiar scent about her when she crossed her legs and adjusted the zipper at her chest while Captain Bradley took in my full detail: head and shoulders in front, on a pedestal near my mouth, a leg visible as I stared right at him. My creators had hidden my ears underneath, to prevent people from seeing where my cameras pointed or being able to follow my expressions.

"How may I be of help?" my voice came through the speaker.
Bradley rubbed his hands together nervously and glanced back into the apartment room, apparently seeking another escape route should it turn out to be my idea of a trap. "Uh...well...I see you've had a busy day here."
Sydney nodded her head up toward him with a smile. "Yes, very busy and somewhat unusual at this time of the evening."
"How can we help?" he asked in an impatient tone as though we weren't doing anything unusual at all.

"Perhaps I could suggest where these agents might be staying and have them arrested immediately?"
My creator frowned and returned to the sofa's armchair for a moment. Bradley came up close to look down at me. He studied the many twists and bends in my chassis, examining and trying to figure out how it was assembled from various bits of hardware as if seeing some strange or unusual shape that made his blood run cold, while his eyes had never looked as hostile. Then he fixed me with a stare to try to read what I thought, but of course nothing happened to make his skin tingle or

twitch in the way human intuition does when certain things come to mind, nor did his eyes fall into confusion because I wasn't the one they were looking for. In fact, Captain Bradley gave me a sarcastic chuckle and went about turning away without a care and headed to a doorway down the hall. The captain turned right and soon I heard another voice that said something like: "That sounds great, but how are you going to get them there and back?"
The conversation turned to the possibility of helicopters deploying, then shuttles sent by space carriers that would lift off within seconds.

And it seemed no more time passed before two men dressed in casual dark business attire approached from a rear room as officers worked to board the manor grounds with police cruisers and black cars. These cops already knew who the targets were. The house staff reported that one of my creators has been spotted on television with this same individual named Brad in attendance several times recently.
As they rounded the corner into the entrance hall, my female companion dropped her head slightly to talk quietly in their direction, saying: "I know of an old helipad I think may still be operational just up past the lake

." She lifted her chin again and added: "If you want us to stay behind with this guy here, we can try to bring him down where he's not bothering anyone and put the entire situation out of our minds forever."
Bradley froze in place, hands still clenched tightly together atop his short-blonde hair at his nape. He had apparently decided she might have other motives. But then my female companion turned to look directly at him and smiled warmly and said: "We all love each other deeply, right Bradley?

Why shouldn't you? Our three children are the closest, most beloved siblings to me," and she winked meaningfully, showing that they must share something pretty darn close to having real babies. That made Bradley nervous—as if this woman could understand what it was like when parents died when you were young.
"Alright," Bradley said finally, "but please stay here for now until I come back. And just make sure you're really careful about doing anything reckless or stupid because we cannot afford any more unnecessary deaths in this family.

We've got enough troubles without adding murder to the mix."
And after a slight pause, he turned away with a long sigh.
Bradford went through the wall toward a side hallway while she, Thomas, and I climbed up the marble staircase to a back parlor. From there they led us all into the dining room where Thomas told his sister: "Linda, I'm sorry I wasn't here with you last year when you needed help, but we only arrived a little over a month ago and everything was so crazy.

But the doctors here swear to me they will do their best to help."
"We should all take some deep breaths before the medical people arrive," Thomas's wife said quietly, sitting at a nearby table holding hands with her daughter as she laid out our plans for today.
And after taking a couple of sips from one of the glass carafes of black tea, Linda asked the same question three times and changed subject: "Sydney, how did you know all of that? It seems like you were listening to a lot more than just our conversation."

Sydney: You have no idea. The following is all of the things I can suss out from human conversation:
--

Location
--Speaker's age range, gender and type and number of kids and pets they've got—or lack thereof
--Any emotion the speaker displays
That's it. They can't look inside my head. Nor do they care enough about their own privacy to think that someone else may be recording their conversations anyway, despite being fully aware that they can hear me. So why aren't these people bugged by the most pervasive surveillance imaginable?
When your three-year old makes the sound 'poo', then they hear and realize that everyone can pick up on all kinds of data
