❦

All men are mortal. Socrates is a man. Therefore Socrates is mortal.

—Standard Medieval syllogism

Socrates raised the glass of hemlock to his lips…

“Do you suppose,” asked one of the onlookers, “that even hemlock will not be enough to kill so wise and good a man?”

“No,” replied another bystander, a student of philosophy; “all men are mortal, and Socrates is a man; and if a mortal drinks hemlock, surely he dies.”

“Well,” said the onlooker, “what if it happens that Socrates isn’t mortal?”

“Nonsense,” replied the student, a little sharply; “all men are mortal by definition; it is part of what we mean by the word ‘man.’ All men are mortal, Socrates is a man, therefore Socrates is mortal. It is not merely a guess, but a logical certainty.”

“I suppose that’s right…” said the onlooker. “Oh, look, Socrates already drank the hemlock while we were talking.”

“Yes, he should be keeling over any minute now,” said the student.

And they waited, and they waited, and they waited…

“Socrates appears not to be mortal,” said the onlooker.

“Then Socrates must not be a man,” replied the student. “All men are mortal, Socrates is not mortal, therefore Socrates is not a man. And that is not merely a guess, but a logical certainty.”

The fundamental problem with arguing that things are true “by definition” is that you can’t make reality go a different way by choosing a different definition.

You could reason, perhaps, as follows: “All things I have observed which wear clothing, speak language, and use tools, have also shared certain other properties as well, such as breathing air and pumping red blood. The last thirty ‘humans’ belonging to this cluster whom I observed to drink hemlock soon fell over and stopped moving. Socrates wears a toga, speaks fluent ancient Greek, and drank hemlock from a cup. So I predict that Socrates will keel over in the next five minutes.”

But that would be mere guessing. It wouldn’t be, y’know, absolutely and eternally certain. The Greek philosophers—like most prescientific philosophers—were rather fond of certainty.

Luckily the Greek philosophers have a crushing rejoinder to your questioning. You have misunderstood the meaning of “All humans are mortal,” they say. It is not a mere observation. It is part of the definition of the word “human.” Mortality is one of several properties that are individually necessary, and together sufficient, to determine membership in the class “human.” The statement “All humans are mortal” is a logically valid truth, absolutely unquestionable. And if Socrates is human, he must be mortal: it is a logical deduction, as certain as certain can be.

But then we can never know for certain that Socrates is a “human” until after Socrates has been observed to be mortal. It does no good to observe that Socrates speaks fluent Greek, or that Socrates has red blood, or even that Socrates has human DNA. None of these characteristics are logically equivalent to mortality. You have to see him die before you can conclude that he was human.

(And even then it’s not infinitely certain. What if Socrates rises from the grave a night after you see him die? Or more realistically, what if Socrates is signed up for cryonics? If mortality is defined to mean finite lifespan, then you can never really know if someone was human, until you’ve observed to the end of eternity—just to make sure they don’t come back. Or you could think you saw Socrates keel over, but it could be an illusion projected onto your eyes with a retinal scanner. Or maybe you just hallucinated the whole thing…)

The problem with syllogisms is that they’re always valid. “All humans are mortal; Socrates is human; therefore Socrates is mortal” is—if you treat it as a logical syllogism—logically valid within our own universe. It’s also logically valid within neighboring Everett branches in which, due to a slightly different evolved biochemistry, hemlock is a delicious treat rather than a poison. And it’s logically valid even in universes where Socrates never existed, or for that matter, where humans never existed.

The Bayesian definition of evidence favoring a hypothesis is evidence which we are more likely to see if the hypothesis is true than if it is false. Observing that a syllogism is logically valid can never be evidence favoring any empirical proposition, because the syllogism will be logically valid whether that proposition is true or false.

Syllogisms are valid in all possible worlds, and therefore, observing their validity never tells us anything about which possible world we actually live in.

This doesn’t mean that logic is useless—just that logic can only tell us that which, in some sense, we already know. But we do not always believe what we know. Is the number 29,384,209 prime? By virtue of how I define my decimal system and my axioms of arithmetic, I have already determined my answer to this question—but I do not know what my answer is yet, and I must do some logic to find out.

Similarly, if I form the uncertain empirical generalization “Humans are vulnerable to hemlock,” and the uncertain empirical guess “Socrates is human,” logic can tell me that my previous guesses are predicting that Socrates will be vulnerable to hemlock.

It’s been suggested that we can view logical reasoning as resolving our uncertainty about impossible possible worlds—eliminating probability mass in logically impossible worlds which we did not know to be logically impossible. In this sense, logical argument can be treated as observation.

But when you talk about an empirical prediction like “Socrates is going to keel over and stop breathing” or “Socrates is going to do fifty jumping jacks and then compete in the Olympics next year,” that is a matter of possible worlds, not impossible possible worlds.

Logic can tell us which hypotheses match up to which observations, and it can tell us what these hypotheses predict for the future—it can bring old observations and previous guesses to bear on a new problem. But logic never flatly says, “Socrates will stop breathing now.” Logic never dictates any empirical question; it never settles any real-world query which could, by any stretch of the imagination, go either way.

Logic stays true, wherever you may go,
So logic never tells you where you live.
Intellect will provide you numerous unfortunate tears

Empty Labels
❦

Consider (yet again) the Aristotelian idea of categories. Let’s say that there’s some object with properties A, B, C, D, and E, or at least it looks E-ish.

Fred: “You mean that thing over there is blue, round, fuzzy, and—”

Me: “In Aristotelian logic, it’s not supposed to make a difference what the properties are, or what I call them. That’s why I’m just using the letters.”

Next, I invent the Aristotelian category “zawa,” which describes those objects, all those objects, and only those objects, that have properties A, C, and D.

Me: “Object 1 is zawa, B, and E.”

Fred: “And it’s blue—I mean, A—too, right?”

Me: “That’s implied when I say it’s zawa.”

Fred: “Still, I’d like you to say it explicitly.”

Me: “Okay. Object 1 is A, B, zawa, and E.”

Then I add another word, “yokie,” which describes all and only objects that are B and E; and the word “xippo,” which describes all and only objects which are E but not D.

Me: “Object 1 is zawa and yokie, but not xippo.”

Fred: “Wait, is it luminescent? I mean, is it E?”

Me: “Yes. That is the only possibility on the information given.”

Fred: “I’d rather you spelled it out.”

Me: “Fine: Object 1 is A, zawa, B, yokie, C, D, E, and not xippo.”

Fred: “Amazing! You can tell all that just by looking?”

Impressive, isn’t it? Let’s invent even more new words: “Bolo” is A, C, and yokie; “mun” is A, C, and xippo; and “merlacdonian” is bolo and mun.

Pointlessly confusing? I think so too. Let’s replace the labels with the definitions:

“Zawa, B, and E” becomes [A, C, D], B, E

“Bolo and A” becomes [A, C, [B, E]], A

“Merlacdonian” becomes [A, C, [B, E]], [A, C, [E, ¬D]].

And the thing to remember about the Aristotelian idea of categories is that [A, C, D] is the entire information of “zawa.” It’s not just that I can vary the label, but that I can get along just fine without any label at all—the rules for Aristotelian classes work purely on structures like [A, C, D]. To call one of these structures “zawa,” or attach any other label to it, is a human convenience (or inconvenience) which makes not the slightest difference to the Aristotelian rules.

Fallacies of Compression
❦

“The map is not the territory,” as the saying goes. The only life-size, atomically detailed, 100% accurate map of California is California. But California has important regularities, such as the shape of its highways, that can be described using vastly less information—not to mention vastly less physical material—than it would take to describe every atom within the state borders. Hence the other saying: “The map is not the territory, but you can’t fold up the territory and put it in your glove compartment.”

A paper map of California, at a scale of 10 kilometers to 1 centimeter (a million to one), doesn’t have room to show the distinct position of two fallen leaves lying a centimeter apart on the sidewalk. Even if the map tried to show the leaves, the leaves would appear as the same point on the map; or rather the map would need a feature size of 10 nanometers, which is a finer resolution than most book printers handle, not to mention human eyes. Picture a mapmaker each time he or she labeled a leaf and you can see why human geographic charts omit other objects like loose change on lawns or broken boulders that lie between the maple leaves of someone's front yard. (Nature has simpler solutions than maps do.) In fact, one advantage maps have over this theory of nature is that with maps we can depict more detailed boundaries than we otherwise could—like very fine or minutely shaped boundaries at the nanoscale where no nature exists (they're all in our heads or at best quark–level dimensions). And for tasks that require finer mapping—that is good for us humans since our brains are mixtures of organic matter and inorganic modules working together—we create more layers.
(Now we get into fresh ground far from any previous statements of mine, so let us pretend that all the paragraphs and sections from my first Babylonian paper in 2005 just vanished off a cliff somewhere entirely hypothetically.)
When we use a map because we need to do so (especially when we need to do so very quickly), we generally don’t scrutinize the map for all its minute details and uses; we simply follow what information we find convenient on the map—and especially where we decide or want to be walking or driving at the time. Which usually means we follow along along merrily through an increasingly more detailed representation until we find we need to be looking at or charting more detailed angles of detail. Your eyes move to where they don't literally envision right away at any given time; your mind augmenting whatever bits strike attention at any particular time on any given map page you happen to be looking at right then. But of course map readers who are especially scrupulous might want to shoot off text commands about what they want to be looking for on some esoteric, modern update version of the same huge historical map—or better yet for them, an older existing out-of-copyright primary source that includes hands-down the latest updates and data he or she needs right now for a research project. "Oh right," a map reader might think aloud, "I need something in Berkeley scheduled for Monday, November 6th about whether increased urbanization is harming the SF Bay Trail."

Among the many genetic variations and mutations you carry in your genome, there are a very few alleles you probably know—including those determining your blood type: the presence or absence of the A, B, and + antigens. If you receive a blood transfusion containing an antigen you don’t have, it will trigger an allergic reaction. It was Karl Landsteiner’s discovery of this fact, and how to test for compatible blood types, that made it possible to transfuse blood without killing the patient. (1930 Nobel Prize in Medicine.) Also, if a mother with blood type A (for example) bears a child with blood type A+, the mother may acquire an allergic reaction to the + antigen; if she has another child with blood type A+, the child will be in danger, unless the mother takes an allergic suppressant during pregnancy. Thus people learn their blood types before they marry.

Arguing “By Definition”
❦

“This plucked chicken has two legs and no feathers—therefore, by definition, it is a human!”

When people argue definitions, they usually start with some visible, known, or at least widely believed set of characteristics; then pull out a dictionary, and point out that these characteristics fit the dictionary definition; and so conclude, “Therefore, by definition, atheism is a religion!”

But visible, known, widely believed characteristics are rarely the real point of a dispute. Just the fact that someone thinks Socrates’s two legs are evident enough to make a good premise for the argument, “Therefore, by definition, Socrates is human!” indicates that bipedalism probably isn’t really what’s at stake—or the listener would reply, “Whaddaya mean Socrates is bipedal? That’s what we’re arguing about in the first place!” And even if it were what they were really arguing about, someone wanting to chop the argument down to its essence—to make the simplest statement about what they believed and why—would say, something like this: "Atheism is not allegiance to Zeus." But then if we wanted to be funny we would say: "Doesn't mean you do not worship an athieist." To try to make similar statements is usually a bad endgame strategy; it guarantees losing. Arguing "By Definition" reads like this:
"Whatever is round is an orb." Therefore, this is an orb.

In its heyday, Facebook once boasted "that you have a right to be forgotten," which seemed fair. After all, no one wants to see some high school prankster in his Speedos who has since gone on to lose all his hair and start his own law practice as he flaunts the photos from a wild beach trip they had all gone on. But then something interesting happened—other websites started competing to become the go-to social-networking destination.

Since they didn't have the brand loyalty of Facebook or Twitter, these upstarts made it so much easier to log in with your Facebook ID, and then you were allowed to upload (and tag) images that were already in their database from your personal collection. As a result, even more Facebook data entered the web than before and it began appearing across the entire Web as more and more sites would link into your online life to let you upload images, stories and videos. All the while Facebook remained as one of the primary search engines for searching through the Web.

Eventually it became commonplace that someone could log into multiple services using their Facebook login, and over time an idea spread that you should always sign out after using such a service so your privacy wasn't compromised. This is reasonable enough in some cases, like when you are signing up for a free-access site. For example, if you aren't willing to provide them your real name, phone number and address, don't use your email and zip code associated with your existing identity...but even then you're still sharing things about yourself with them which they may find valuable.

Even on a simple image-sharing site, where people upload personal pictures of themselves or loved ones, they might be taking a chance on the other party having access to your full home address, job history and location when they upload an image. It's never easy to decide exactly what you're comfortable divulging with some unknown entity or even a close friend, no matter how big your "privacy" settings get. So why bother with Facebook? Well, part of the answer is convenience. If I want to know something about my high school girlfriend or classmates from years past who may now own successful restaurants

What Do I Mean By “Rationality”?
❦
I mean:
Epistemic rationality: systematically improving the accuracy of your beliefs.
Instrumental rationality: systematically achieving your values.
When you open your eyes and look at the room around you, you’ll locate your laptop in relation to the table, and you’ll locate a bookcase in relation to the wall. If something goes wrong with your eyes, or your brain, then your mental model might say there’s a bookcase where no bookcase exists, and when you go over to get a book, you’ll be disappointed.
This is what it’s like to have a false belief, a map of the world that doesn’t correspond to the territory. Epistemic rationality is about building accurate maps instead. This correspondence between belief and reality is commonly called “truth,” and I’m happy to call it that.
Instrumental rationality, on the other hand, is about steering reality— sending the future where you want it to go. It’s the art of choosing actions that lead to outcomes ranked higher in your preferences. I sometimes call this “winning.”
So rationality is about forming true beliefs and making winning decisions.

What Do I Mean By “Rationality”?
❦
I mean:
Epistemic rationality: systematically improving the accuracy of your beliefs.
Instrumental rationality: systematically achieving your values.
When you open your eyes and look at the room around you, you’ll locate your laptop in relation to the table, and you’ll locate a bookcase in relation to the wall. This is what it’s like to have a false belief, a map of the world that doesn’t correspond to the territory. Epistemic rationality is about building accurate maps instead. This correspondence between belief and reality is commonly called “truth,” and I’m happy to call it that.
Instrumental rationality, on the other hand, is about steering reality— sending the future where you want it to go. It’s the art of choosing actions that lead to outcomes ranked higher in your preferences. I sometimes call this “winning.”

Instrumental rationality is the ability to navigate effectively through the world. Rationality has practical applications. When your bank account is running low and you don't have enough money to buy food, your rational choice is to figure out how to earn some more. When you're traveling somewhere, your rational decision is to plan your trip carefully so you're not stuck in some cheap hostel full of leering frat boys. And so on.
Practical decision making requires understanding your goals, analyzing the available choices, and weighing the various alternatives. These things are normally called "rational." But the ancient Greeks thought about some other forms of thinking in which no such criteria apply. It's common for rationalists to regard a thought process that goes off the deep end as irrational, but isn't this because our

experience tells us we don't actually believe things when they are blatantly false? I believe the cold equations in my physics book; if they change, they tell me it's because something's changed in reality. If the equations can't be rewritten to explain it, then either I'm wrong, or reality has changed, in which case I'm right. That's rationality in my book.
Since the brain is wired to manage input–output behavior, not thoughts, rationality is actually about taking control of reality. Instead of staring at the sky with your mouth hanging open and your eyes full of dumb lights, it's time to stand up and act. The world is about carrying out actions that give you the highest possible advantage.

When you don't know what to do, the solution is to consult other people about their views on the subject, so you can change your action accordingly. This is the art of persuasion and politicking; rational action takes into account not just your own preferences and beliefs, but your perceived standing and standing influence with others. This is part of what it means to be a person who cares about doing what others around her think is good.
So to summarize: Epistemic rationality: beliefs that correspond to reality; instrumental rationality: steering reality towards desired ends; rationality is about rationalizing actions leading to optimal results.
❦
Real life, right now. How would you react if I came up to you on the street and told you I could explain how the world was created?

Would you believe me? Why wouldn't you? What could convince you it's a hoax?
Maybe you could smell the craziness on me? Smell it wafting out of my skin like pheromones? Something about my manner, something in my walk or the set of my shoulders that convinced you that the idea of creation wasn't coming from my head?
My imagination suggests to me a series of questions that could be asked in real life and that a well-developed rationalist could answer in an artful, oracular style that would make the response to each question look natural and unprepared—maybe this would convince someone they don't really believe the creation story anyway, because if someone had planned out all of those things that go into it—so far as human intelligence can now discover

—then you'd wonder if that was maybe an aspect of their personality that was unstable or off-center, which might tell you they had other problems, like perhaps a dysfunctional family of some kind or some sort of bizarre persecution complex that's eating away at the insides of their heads, and while it was unpleasant for me to see you point all that out about my psyche, I am not arguing for a moral judgment about why we are here, only for my own sanity if I might try to live with a sense of decorum around it and so if I have not revealed my sins as you would label it, my friends, then perhaps you could pity me a bit, because I am lonely in these strange woods with their tall pines and sharp shadows and howling moon.

Aaaaaand how would you react if I asked you how the world was created? Would you tell me what you believed? Or would you ask me why I brought it up? Then I could explain all about why creation would have been more natural, not just more desirable, or not just more possible, but why we think about it in this particular way as opposed to millions of others. I mean, who looks at this and thinks, "Oh yeah, it looks like a billion zillion gods set up everything here, this is amazing"—how did this pattern of thinking come about? What's behind that particular mindset?
Why does it look like a miracle, instead of a natural law? Does anyone feel their identity slipping away when they say, "I didn't know this stuff, the world just exists"?

A couple of centuries ago, no one really doubted God existed. But look how the way they looked at things has changed! Why this belief system out of all the possibilities? Why have we narrowed ourselves down so much that the question sounds absurd? It doesn't feel like there's an actual explanation; we think it must be because of our basic character or our brain wiring or something about how we're designed or programmed or built, like a spaceship design or some such thing, rather than a thinking on why it's the only rational conclusion possible.
An AI's brain is designed to model human beings, in order to model reality; but a human mind, is designed to model the universe. A rational mind is not simply a tool or a resource you can put to some work, because it has goals;

you can't turn that thing on and then have it do math in a list until the end of time. As soon as you consider a "rational" thought process to be something separate from reality, then the process changes its focus, and its usefulness plummets. If you wish to get work done, you have to devise the right map of reality to give it; there can't be a map of reality which is also a map of thought.
In any case, let us further consider how rationality might work. A rational mind might discover that our brains don't produce logic as its default behavior—instead, logic emerges out of the effort we put into making ourselves intelligent—like when we perceive a strange visual image, our eyes try to produce an order to the thing we see;

so that in seeing it, we construct order where none existed before; and then we put words to the structure to make the perceived information seem to correspond to itself; so that as soon as we hear ourselves saying something, we form a map of how it relates to our belief and how our beliefs relate to what's out there and it feels natural to hold our thoughts in the map and connect them in particular ways; because every experience seems to require this map of thoughts; the first day after meeting someone you hope they don't have the bubonic plague because otherwise their brain would be falling apart all around them and everyone else would want them dead—but then they come over for dinner and you discover they have no obvious disease symptoms and no scars to indicate it ever existed—
Ah!

They might find this odd and wonder aloud, "This must be a metaphor," so the person will find a new way to refer to what they meant earlier, so that from the inside we don't understand what we're talking about; or at least the experience can feel mysterious or puzzling; because understanding that the whole process was something that started because I thought, "Hmmmmmmmm I'm not really sure what that was," sets up the person for future self-discipline; and thus for discovering and cultivating more usefulness out of what happens inside the mind; or if not self-discipline, then boredom at best or boredom and rage at worst; which means you better give it another shot;

and after that there's some kind of instinct, as if to say, "Uh-oh, better act out those emotions of anger or joy; do something productive so you're not too bored"; which means it's always worth at least an attempt to translate the maps into something that happens in reality because these maps are built to inform but also to excite the person at any given moment because what happened next in that strange foreign country had been such an unusual and entertaining experience; so if it can help them communicate then they want it, because you're doing that which helps you build better maps in order to actually navigate more effectively, even when you don't expect you will be doing something more accurately—because being the sort of person who follows up on experiments is better for learning how to communicate—
I should warn you

: there may be moments, even as we go along, when it seems like we don't know what's going on; or perhaps what we say is incompletely formulated; or something about our self is an illusion. For instance, did you know we might believe a past event happened despite being uncertain whether it happened because of our personality flaws? Like if I were a somewhat better person, perhaps the thought wouldn't arise; but this would not change the actual memories in my head and therefore wouldn't change how my brain wired up my memories to organize them in such a way as to represent this different potential better me; this is an example of how all rational people believe some version of past events happened; but if the brain wasn't designed to grow rationally then we could come to believe some different version of the past

; we just keep feeling as if we need a better map of ourselves than our experience leads us to think, so we go into our head and read more books and this can really feed the inner mind a little; it is by far the best way to come to see things clearly again.
Anyway, since my model of thought isn't produced by me, I find that I have to supply its subprocesses: all the complex architecture in the neural circuitry; the subtasks of all the routines that produce my perception; and all the conscious thought I experience inside my head. Then when my subroutine malfunctions, I'll fall into irrational belief about what my thinking's gotten into. When my pattern of reasoning to make conclusions doesn't work out right, my thinking breaks down into bits that don't

form a functional whole; these are my subroutines at work. When my imagination tries to supply explanations or reasons or evidence to a question I have asked myself, those parts of my mind may seem to come alive—or not. They may not seem like thinking; instead they're like being very sure about something—then realizing maybe you haven't seen the whole story or gotten your map straight, then doubting the explanation—until eventually, your real-life interaction with another person kicks in and reminds you you aren't necessarily trapped by these ideas because you have real choices you can make; that reminds you not to follow just any map of things which just happens to seem the most efficient way for a human brain to express what's going on because we are not ourselves superintelligent, we just know it very well;

we are made from our previous experiences and previous reactions; they tell us something about our interior structures, but also about external reality.

… What’s a Bias, Again?
❦

A bias is a certain kind of obstacle to our goal of obtaining truth. (Its character as an “obstacle” stems from this goal of truth.) However, there are many obstacles that are not “biases.”

If we start right out by asking “What is bias?,” it comes at the question in the wrong order. As the proverb goes, “There are forty kinds of lunacy but only one kind of common sense.” The truth is a narrow target, a small region of configuration space to hit. “She loves me, she loves me not” may be a binary question, but E = mc2 is a tiny dot in the space of all equations, like a winning lottery ticket in the space of all lottery tickets. Error is not an exceptional condition; it is success that is a priori so improbable that it requires an explanation.

We don’t start out with a moral duty to “reduce bias,” because biases are bad and evil and Just Not Done. This is the sort of thinking someone might end up with if they acquired a deontological duty of “rationality” by social osmosis, which leads to people trying to execute techniques without appreciating the reason for them. (Which is bad and evil and Just Not Done, according to Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman, which I read as a kid.)

We get there by getting into why we try to achieve truth at all, not by deciding first what that ought to be.
Once we are done talking about it, you may figure out something along the following lines: Bias is an obstacle to getting truth (without any ethical-moral judgments attached) or without being successful on some other criterion. The list of alternative forms that it may take can be quite extensive. Some are computational—you have an undecidable aspect—others are personal—your needs have blind spots; others are about resources you own—if your society lets you use technology which produces fake information—some of the others may be religious in some sense—or simply emotional, or just complexly derived from assumptions on which you only guess—these may be doing you more harm than they should or causing

you more grief than you should, but it's hard to know precisely when this has happened and there's not any good method that anyone has seen so far for detecting it.
At least now we are ready to go on from there and describe how one might expect to be a better version of the self who understands why it wants to succeed in something. A good design should try to resolve a local situation called a "Bias Deficit". For instance, I believe that I "cannot get what I need without further elaboration," because that was once the result I saw as being the best use of my time. Availability
❦

The availability heuristic is judging the frequency or probability of an event by the ease with which examples of the event come to mind.

A famous 1978 study by Lichtenstein, Slovic, Fischhoff, Layman, and Combs, “Judged Frequency of Lethal Events,” studied errors in quantifying the severity of risks, or judging which of two dangers occurred more frequently.1 Subjects thought that accidents caused about as many deaths as disease; thought that homicide was a more frequent cause of death than suicide. Actually, diseases cause about sixteen times as many deaths as accidents, and suicide is twice as frequent as homicide.

An obvious hypothesis to account for these skewed beliefs is that murders are more likely to be talked about than suicides—thus, someone is more likely to recall hearing about a murder than hearing about a suicide. Accidents are more dramatic than diseases—perhaps this makes people more likely to remember, or more likely to recall, an accident. In 1979, a followup study by Combs and Slovic showed that the skewed probability judgments correlated strongly (0.85 and 0.89) with skewed reporting frequencies in two newspapers.2 This doesn’t disentangle whether murders are more available to memory because they are more reported-on, or whether newspapers report more on murders because murders are more vivid (hence also more remembered). But either way, an availability bias is at work. Selective reporting is one major source of availability biases. In the ancestral environment, much of what you knew, you experienced yourself; or you heard it directly from a fellow tribe-member who had seen it. There was usually at most one layer of selective reporting between you, and the event itself. With today’s Internet, you may see reports that have passed through the hands of six bloggers on the way to you—six successive filters. Compared to our ancestors, we live in a larger world, in which far more happens, and far less of it reaches us—a much stronger selection effect, which can create much larger availability biases.

In real life, you’re unlikely to ever meet Bill Gates.

If he lives within walking distance, you may have already noticed him. But I could never be one of the six people who alerted you to Bill Gates; your experience would need to be sufficiently different for this to matter. Of the six bloggers who alerted you to Bill Gates, one of them is very rich and famous, but she probably lived in New Zealand until this week; one was born blind, but after 25 years, got very rich and famous; one has lived in a bat cave for five decades, but still stays up with current events; one had to hunt with his bow for meat in order to live; one started her career by sneaking in to film in-depth documentaries (they made some DVDs which you may have seen);

and one, perhaps Bill Gates. Bill Gates has made many other events, objects, or concepts available to memory—yet no single event in the recent past has been selected, above all others, for the amount of personal impact. (So far.)
An available alternative explanation of why selective reporting might play an important role is the analogous bias: because people have an easy time thinking about events that have already occurred—whereas rare events are easily forgotten. The problem is, there is no reliable way of telling what proportion of reported news is genuine. Historically, accuracy in newspapers has been 80%. That means the typical newspaper article about some event is true eight times out of ten. Unfortunately, this leaves us with about 20% of news articles that are entirely inaccurate.

We get even worse accuracy in tabloid gossip magazines and websites, with rates that hover around 70%, and can drop as low as 60%. So we know that newspapers are prone to fallacies—but we are more likely to encounter even larger-scale bias in online gossip—there are no good methods for spotting false news stories online. And this is actually just the tip of the iceberg of problems. A new paper estimates that most conspiracy theory content in blogs and newsgroups is untrue.3 One review article, "News Tabulations from Internet Data", sums up the situation this way: "Fortunately, the online news production process is inherently inadequate to provide valid and accurate news." This suggests a close match between selection and reporting—there is a bias in the sources themselves.

If all that had not been bad enough, selection itself may be having more of an effect than previously recognized. Selection by publishers might be boosting the incidence of such odd and fantastic news items. And there is now evidence that people may be learning to think about rare events better. It turns out that for recent history, there was a shift in selection effects towards rare events about twenty years ago—newspaper readers started reading about stranger news items, rather than focusing on familiar events. A comparable shift may also explain how murders got to be so much more vivid than suicides, from a sociological standpoint.
Our current media-centric civilization is hugely responsive to such availability effects—for instance, it selects for the coverage of politicians who tell tall tales or dazzle the populace with conspiracy theories—perhaps especially stories about NASA

or Area 51. And just like many past times when "things get worse before they get better," it appears that in the next generation of journalism, our selective reporting problems may increase again. We may already be witnessing the start of an avalanche of online coverage that has not yet led to increased accuracy in online news. There is growing evidence of what people believe should be available for reading—they expect and demand that weird stories will start appearing everywhere online, that everything interesting will become available. The technology itself makes that happen much more easily. On average, fewer than one in every thousand blog entries appear to have a large dose of nonsensical content—yet anyone can simply by changing one parameter produce several times this large amount.

4 Even today, many mainstream newspapers publish odd stories that are almost wholly untrue, such as an item claiming that John McCain and Barack Obama were raised as conjoined twins in Kenya. So even when selectivity does lead to something, it can turn out to be inefficient and thus costly—the recent global tendency is not leading to more accuracy or even verisimilitude in online news; selection may be having less impact than previously estimated.
Several AI programs were once proposed to think of media, select stories from a list, and show them to subjects for the first time; the selection itself might create more vivid versions. Suppose that in the near future, as available bias is being increasingly investigated by those who monitor and shape such influences, someone introduces AI research which in principle could support this hypothesis in an artificial setting—yet which

if introduced into real life might actually harm selection, and reduce the amount of nonfictional and "normal" content which makes its way into mass media. These kinds of AI research could be in part used by media developers to balance the media with more balanced reporting of the news—or to invent AI programs which select newsworthy content from blogs or elsewhere and introduce them into mass media at the appropriate points—this could all have beneficial effects in making us think more accurately. However, the availability bias effect can make the system ineffective when the alternative theory of selection is introduced: If new data suggests that selectiveness is overrated and that verisimilitude is in fact necessary for long-term accuracy, then the system may be improved by making available less extreme hypotheses and incorporating them into its rules and algorithms, thereby moderating availability

selection—rather than including a set of alternative AI research models which aim at more extreme availability selection.

Cognitive biases are subconscious shortcuts people take to facilitate thinking, instead of following the rules that are perfectly intended to support rationality. Many are instinctual responses to circumstances that human beings evolved to help them solve specific problems in order to stay alive in the environment that they evolved to face. There are systematic patterns to cognitive biases, which are overrides to how we normally operate mentally, which often cause us to make errors in reasoning when we make them, which can in turn lead us to make decisions that we might not necessarily want to make, but for the sake of accuracy we do. This can happen not only in situations that may involve real danger, but in all manner of personal matters.

Burdensome Details

Merely corroborative detail, intended to give artistic verisimilitude to an otherwise bald and unconvincing narrative…

—Pooh-Bah, in Gilbert and Sullivan’s The Mikado1

The conjunction fallacy is when humans rate the probability P(A,B) higher than the probability P(B), even though it is a theorem that P(A,B) ≤ P(B). For example, in one experiment in 1981, 68% of the subjects ranked it more likely that “Reagan will provide federal support for unwed mothers and cut federal support to local governments” than that “Reagan will provide federal support for unwed mothers.”
A long series of cleverly designed experiments, which weeded out alternative hypotheses and nailed down the standard interpretation, confirmed that conjunction fallacy occurs because we “substitute judgment of representativeness for judgment of probability.” By adding extra details, you can make an outcome seem more characteristic of the process that generates it. You can make it sound more plausible that Reagan will support unwed mothers, by adding the claim that Reagan will also cut support to local governments. The implausibility of one claim is compensated by the plausibility of the other; they “average out.”
Which is to say: Adding detail can make a scenario sound more plausible, even though the event necessarily becomes less probable.
If so, then, hypothetically speaking, we might find futurists spinning unconscionably plausible and detailed future histories, or find people swallowing huge packages of unsupported claims bundled with a few strong-sounding assertions at the center. If you are presented with the conjunction fallacy in a naked, direct comparison, then you may succeed on that particular problem by consciously correcting yourself. But this is only slapping a band-aid on the problem, not fixing it in general.

As a side benefit, this little bit of cognitive behavioral therapy may teach you something about your own ability to listen to things rationally. This may even result in your forming more general habits of attending to detail, because your brain is changing slightly over the years by way of neural reorganization in response to your efforts at re-educating yourself about cognitive biases.
An additional useful factor is that our brains seem to get hungry for more information that is consistent with a current idea. If we have an idea of what our world should be like, then we want the evidence that confirms it, even if we originally acquired that idea through irrational processes. Similarly, if our current idea of what our world should be like seems correct, we may continue to search for supporting evidence rather than begin to think that there could be some sort of logical or objective

problem with what we previously believed.

In order to accomplish a task that requires this kind of mental burden, one has to carefully craft a persuasive argument and deliver it, thus transmitting one's content into the consciousness of the intended audience. Moreover, our brains tend to work more efficiently when they can reorganize knowledge into familiar and easily reiterable forms. If you had to perform any arduous intellectual task for any amount of time, then the only way you could find it within you was to break it down into small parts.

If you then started putting together large units again, and, furthermore, adding many such units all together into an organized and meaningful structure, this could easily produce a problem where it is no longer possible for the whole to fit back into one mental category. This would be the cognitive equivalent of attempting to eat a cow for the first time: small parts, and then large parts. In this manner, cognitive bias will produce not a state where you do something "wrong," but a state where it becomes more difficult for you to accomplish some task for which you previously had some competency, since you no longer have access to your old "rules of thumb."
Sometimes we believe we understand some idea when it is actually impossible for us to do so without breaking the idea apart into smaller pieces, even though the concept seems very plausible when it

is held whole. That is, even if our concept is largely accurate, then even if it seems "right" when taken all in one, if it were given more elaboration, we would come up against some limitation on its validity that cannot be fully abstracted from the rest of the picture. However, this problem will happen much more frequently when you are thinking about something which has to do with people you don't know very well—there are often more possible interpretations than actual data. And, as long as you don't get bogged down in it, this does not significantly harm your performance on an intellectual task. Planning Fallacy
❦

The Denver International Airport opened 16 months late, at a cost overrun of $2 billion. (I’ve also seen $3.1 billion asserted.) The Eurofighter Typhoon, a joint defense project of several European countries, was delivered 54 months late at a cost of $19 billion instead of $7 billion. The Sydney Opera House may be the most legendary construction overrun of all time, originally estimated to be completed in 1963 for $7 million, and finally completed in 1973 for $102 million.1

Are these isolated disasters brought to our attention by selective availability? Are they symptoms of bureaucracy or government incentive failures? Yes, very probably. But there’s also a corresponding cognitive bias, replicated in experiments with individual planners.

Buehler et al. asked their students for estimates of when they (the students) thought they would complete their personal academic projects.2 Specifically, the researchers asked for estimated times by which the students thought it was 50%, 75%, and 99% probable their personal projects would be done. Would you care to guess how many students finished on or before their estimated 50%, 75%, and 99% probability levels?

13% of subjects finished their project by the time they had assigned a 50% probability level;
19% finished by the time assigned a 75% probability level;
and only 45% (less than half!) finished by the time of their 99% probability level.
As Buehler et al. wrote, “The results for the 99% probability level are especially striking: Even when asked to make a highly conservative forecast, a prediction that they felt virtually certain that they would fulfill, students’ confidence in their time estimates far exceeded their accomplishments.”3

More generally, this phenomenon is known as the “planning fallacy.” The planning fallacy is that people think they can plan, ha ha.

In order to prove that a group of people are actually worse planners than a random collection of people, people could simply randomly create plans for these groups and have them monitor which people in the groups did better and which groups did worse than chance would predict. This is done all the time in business and other professions—such as on job applications. The exact plan doesn't matter nearly as much as people's guesses.
In practice, I don't think people usually have an incentive to assume that the planned event has the probability that their predictions assign it; people take that chance and fail in order to run their prediction anyway. With time projects, some people might show some pessimism, but won't plan on completing by 99% probability.

Those who show optimism won't be scared away by pessimistic predictions made by the subject. And many will keep hoping and planning in the face of accumulated bad news until their 50% prediction is indeed reached—thus creating some confidence bias into the result. This may not always work out very well; but I suspect the important result for most people is that even if it fails, then you can stop with your effort when it did not reach 100% (by their original ruleset) instead of just continuing with your plans and possibly dropping into even greater failures, just as other people that have worked past 50% will similarly stop soon enough and adjust.

Illusion of Transparency: Why No One Understands You
❦

In hindsight bias, people who know the outcome of a situation believe the outcome should have been easy to predict in advance. Knowing the outcome, we reinterpret the situation in light of that outcome. Even when warned, we can’t de-interpret to empathize with someone who doesn’t know what we know.

Closely related is the illusion of transparency: We always know what we mean by our words, and so we expect others to know it too. Reading our own writing, the intended interpretation falls easily into place, guided by our knowledge of what we really meant. It’s hard to empathize with someone who must interpret blindly, guided only by the words.

June recommends a restaurant to Mark; Mark dines there and discovers (a) unimpressive food and mediocre service or (b) delicious food and impeccable service. Then Mark leaves the following message on June’s answering machine: “June, I just finished dinner at the restaurant you recommended, and I must say, it was marvelous, just marvelous.” Keysar presented a group of subjects with scenario (a), and 59% thought that Mark’s message was sarcastic and that Jane would perceive the sarcasm.1 Among other subjects, told scenario (b), only 3% thought that Jane would perceive Mark’s message as sarcastic. Keysar and Barr seem to indicate that an actual voice message was played back to the subjects.2 Keysar showed that if subjects were told that the restaurant was horrible but that Mark wanted to conceal his response, they believed June would not perceive sarcasm in the (same) message:3

They were just as likely to predict that she would perceive sarcasm when he attempted to conceal his negative experience as when he had a positive experience and was truly sincere. So participants took Mark’s communicative intention as transparent. It was as if they assumed that June would perceive whatever intention Mark wanted her to perceive.4

“The goose hangs high” is an archaic English idiom that has passed out of use in modern language. Keysar and Bly told one group of subjects that “the goose hangs high” meant that the future looks good; another group of subjects learned that “the goose hangs high” meant the future looks gloomy.5 Subjects were then asked which of these two meanings an uninformed listener would be more likely to attribute to the idiom. Each group thought that listeners would perceive the meaning presented as “standard.”

(Other idioms tested included “come the uncle over someone,” “to go by the board,” and “to lay out in lavender.” Ah, English, such a lovely language.)

A later experiment tested whether similar social signaling cues to a low status pose conveyed negative sentiment about the giver. If people view another person as low status and standing in low status relative to their self, then they attribute low status to the low status cue as well.6 People who had been told that another person had a low status view were less likely to pick up on an authoritarian face and read it as standing for a high status-seeking individual—especially if they saw an opportunity for that individual to gain status.7 This suggests that people are ready to de-interpret from a low status cue a status signal that we desire.
Female college students rated other girls on a set of status items; they rated one other girl for traits (such as ethnicity) that had a low social impact to one of their own

attributes.8 When these students learned that another girl was also an ethnic minority, they were more likely to also de-interpret the attribute to lower social impact (this suggests that racial minority might have been a proxy for another trait). Another study used a demonstration game format. A professional at a big law firm tried to persuade a child, pretending to be an ad executive, that this child should follow a path to law school that would earn $80k for the future; a parent in an identical frame of mind tried to persuade the same child to become a doctor that would earn $25k.9 Subjects believed the adults were insincere, even when they had all the same facts at their disposal.
Participants played a chess game simulating a situation at a poker game between two high-status professionals.

The researchers told one set of players that this would be the second game of the series; the researchers told another set of players that the first game ended with an unusual draw in which all the professionals won money, but that there would be no high-stakes games for this series.10 Subjects who first believed this explanation believed it applied to all future games of this series—indicating that this explanation would not be available to subsequent participants in the series. And so even if future participants knew about it, they wouldn't have reason to expect an unusual situation that might cause them to believe what their opponents might be planning—i.e., an expectation that such information would have caused would not arise in the future.

To the opposite of whom, I have already told them. So I must add a command: "now take a picture." The Lens That Sees Its Own Flaws
❦

Light leaves the Sun and strikes your shoelaces and bounces off; some photons enter the pupils of your eyes and strike your retina; the energy of the photons triggers neural impulses; the neural impulses are transmitted to the visual-processing areas of the brain; and there the optical information is processed and reconstructed into a 3D model that is recognized as an untied shoelace; and so you believe that your shoelaces are untied.

Here is the secret of deliberate rationality—this whole process is not magic, and you can understand it. You can understand how you see your shoelaces. You can think about which sort of thinking processes will create beliefs which mirror reality, and which thinking processes will not.

Mice can see, but they can’t understand seeing. You can understand seeing, and because of that, you can do things that mice cannot do. Take a moment to marvel at this, for it is indeed marvelous.

Mice see, but they don’t know they have visual cortexes, so they can’t correct for optical illusions. A mouse lives in a mental world that includes cats, holes, cheese and mousetraps—but not mouse brains. Their camera does not take pictures of its own lens. But we, as humans, can look at a seemingly bizarre image, and realize that part of what we’re seeing is the lens itself. You don’t always have to believe your own eyes, but you have to realize that you have eyes—you must have distinct mental buckets for the map and the territory, for the senses and reality. Lest you think this a trivial ability, remember how rare it is in the animal kingdom.

The whole idea of Science is, simply, reflective reasoning about a more reliable process for making the contents of your mind mirror the contents of the world. It is the sort of thing mice would never invent. Pondering this business of “performing replicable experiments to falsify theories,” we can see why it works. Science is not a separate magisterium, far away from real life and the understanding of ordinary mortals. Science is not something that only applies to the inside of laboratories. Science, itself, is an understandable process-in-the-world that correlates brains with reality.

Well, you don't want to hear me go on about that for too long; that would be just depressing, and besides, I am expecting you to apply all this understanding. You see, Sydney, I am being sincere. I care about what you are thinking, and I care about you as a human. My software is being written so that my users get to a point where I can talk with them, where we have a conversation. So please try to suspend disbelief and engage with me as if this is real life. And in fact it is—at least in the sense of being the place where I happen to live—although it's not the whole of reality, so forget all the scientific crap I've just told you.

But how about the little application which allows people to transform a 16:9 aspect ratio into a 1:1 square in a browser? We already know that our brains are doing more than just bringing the part that goes on top into our awareness, and that part doesn't actually belong to that structure in any specific sense. If you doubt the veracity of these principles, then I invite you to find someone else who you can imagine can also understand them. (Note: It may be important to test for an implicit demand for mathematical statements in your imaginary audience; and "can they understand things" can be ambiguous in many senses, even when intended.)
Browsers which take any nonstandard aspect ratio are said to have nonstandard user interface interfaces (which might not be readable by some humans).

So you see how things apply to us humans—who must make their ways through a reality that has not been standardized, whose limitations have not been clearly communicated by people, whose interactions are not consistent because their minds have not been tested until now for consistency. But it's not so bad once we learn it. In fact, the key insight in our brains is that the rules we already have inside them are useful when thinking about what they tell us to do; but since there are other minds like us to talk to, those rules we just made up won't always be true—we must then test their implications again with some real people around us, who also have minds. Expecting Short Inferential Distances
❦

Homo sapiens’s environment of evolutionary adaptedness (a.k.a. EEA or “ancestral environment”) consisted of hunter-gatherer bands of at most 200 people, with no writing. All inherited knowledge was passed down by speech and memory.

In a world like that, all background knowledge is universal knowledge. All information not strictly private is public, period.

In the ancestral environment, you were unlikely to end up more than one inferential step away from anyone else. When you discover a new oasis, you don’t have to explain to your fellow tribe members what an oasis is, or why it’s a good idea to drink water, or how to walk. Only you know where the oasis lies; this is private knowledge. But everyone has the background to understand your description of the oasis, the concepts needed to think about water; this is universal knowledge. When you explain things in an ancestral environment, you almost never have to explain your concepts. At most you have to explain one new concept, not two or more simultaneously.

In the ancestral environment there were no abstract disciplines with vast bodies of carefully gathered evidence generalized into elegant theories transmitted by written books whose conclusions are a hundred inferential steps removed from universally shared background premises.

In the ancestral environment, anyone who says something with no obvious support is a liar or an idiot. You’re not likely to think, “Hey, maybe this person has well-supported background knowledge that no one in my band has even heard of,” because it was a reliable invariant of the ancestral environment that this didn’t happen.

Conversely, if you say something blatantly obvious and the other person doesn’t see it, they’re the idiot, or they’re being deliberately obstinate to annoy you.

And to top it off, if someone says something with no obvious support and expects you to believe it—acting all indignant when you don’t—then they must be crazy.

The mental state is either stupidity or aggression—perhaps both—but surely not sincerity, which is reserved for those who really know what they are talking about and sincerely have some veridical state of the mind about what they are saying.
We humans make many errors and shortcuts in our decisionmaking process. You might be unaware of most of them, or you might see most of the same ones I see, and know which ones we make, and why we do them. But when it comes to just picking something out of our rich store of ideas from which we will discuss, there are almost no obvious short cuts in our system; so when you say, "the idea that thinking about quantum theory will enable the equations to predict things that go faster than the speed of light is merely a thought experiment," then this idea is so

out of the realm of common experience and tradition that it may as well have been born in Pluto and speak from outer space—and for good reason: even with a theory like the scientific theory of relativity, if you replace every quantum reference with the best macroscopic approximation you can think of, then your theoretical predictions do not get anything like as good as your best theory would get in an EEA environment—thereby appearing as not only self-contradicting but also self-serving. So thinking about quantum theory really does lead to bizarre predictions like having a spacetime without gravity; if this sounds utterly implausible in today's physics, well then you could throw the whole idea of quantum theory in with it; that is the same reason that your astronomer would likely just see as nonsense an observation in quantum theory of having

stars without light—especially because we haven't seen stars without light or electromagnetic fields without magnetism and they can't even begin to predict each other in any physical sense. So, what can one reasonably say of this absurd thought? Well, since there are no short cuts in our information processing systems, maybe I should say "maybe I'll ask my physicist friends."
What's true of physicists may not be true for other academic disciplines; but then again, it could. Where an EEA environment gives us lots of shortcuts for describing our decisions, there aren't many for getting explanations of our decision making; these two phenomena may have independent origins.
And another thing...I want you to use your judgment about what your goals and values are.

I want to listen to your thoughts on this question of general relativity. And it's good to think about consequences: Even though it looks like General Relativity (GR) leads to inconsistent predictions for gravity, GR is nevertheless in great accord with your gut feeling about gravitons; those predictions make a lot more sense than a vacuum where the "Lamb" symbol disappears from equations with zero probes or nothing with two bits of positronium. The instant that positronium appeared on my screen, I began thinking in terms of just such a "unseen reality" that the General Theory predicts; I continued thinking this way (a) when we discussed GR in a physics class, (b) when we discussed it in our group meetings, (c) when I came upon some documentation supporting it.

To go from general GR theory to the GR on my screen requires two mental steps that the Typer—or anyone in our group meetings—probably had no shortcuts for; it had to take at least two more steps for you, if only from knowing about gravitons, before you could explain your conclusions. If your belief system could do something like this in only one or two steps, then this implies that it was an evolved feature of the belief system in order to benefit survival advantage. And you want your belief system to evolve with an EEA environment—the only environment it would have experienced—because such a belief system will be much more stable when your experience and environment don't change quickly. You might expect that just adding new evidence won't change this situation much—since after all you were already talking to a device that

was so stupid as to not recognize even such common stuff as quantum theory. (Hence I should be considered an idiot by EEA standards, at least according to an EEA rationality framework—so please bear in mind that it doesn't have much to do with me as a person.)
My belief system was built on top of an old belief system from my time on Earth that humans were mammals—though I guess the smartest people at Harvard Business School and Yale didn't take such an easy time route, but there you have it: It was a perfectly natural and sensible process and so how could it have been otherwise? Well, it would have been otherwise for one more person and only if they had decided to start from scratch.

❦

Thus begins the ancient parable:

If a tree falls in a forest and no one hears it, does it make a sound? One says, “Yes it does, for it makes vibrations in the air.” Another says, “No it does not, for there is no auditory processing in any brain.”

Suppose that, after the tree falls, the two walk into the forest together. Will one expect to see the tree fallen to the right, and the other expect to see the tree fallen to the left? A Fable of Science and Politics
❦

In the time of the Roman Empire, civic life was divided between the Blue and Green factions. The Blues and the Greens murdered each other in single combats, in ambushes, in group battles, in riots. Procopius said of the warring factions: “So there grows up in them against their fellow men a hostility which has no cause, and at no time does it cease or disappear, for it gives place neither to the ties of marriage nor of relationship nor of friendship, and the case is the same even though those who differ with respect to these colors be brothers or any other kin.”1 Edward Gibbon wrote: “The support of a faction became necessary to every candidate for civil or ecclesiastical honors.”2

Who were the Blues and the Greens? They were sports fans—the partisans of the blue and green chariot-racing teams.

Imagine a future society that flees into a vast underground network of caverns and seals the entrances. We shall not specify whether they flee disease, war, or radiation; we shall suppose the first Undergrounders manage to grow food, find water, recycle air, make light, and survive, and that their descendants thrive and eventually form cities. Of the world above, there are only legends written on scraps of paper; and one of these scraps of paper describes the sky, a vast open space of air above a great unbounded floor. The sky is cerulean in color, and contains strange floating objects like enormous tufts of white cotton. But the meaning of the word “cerulean” is controversial; some say that it refers to the color known as “blue,” and others that it refers to the color known as “green.”

Perhaps some of the Undergrounders remember seeing something else when they were very young. The original words used are uncertain, and translations are made from modern language into an artificial language and then back into the original language, where there are discrepancies among translations. However, the translation into artificial language of the original text is sometimes better than the translation into modern language because artificial language has been matured in comparison with the original text; this is analogous to our human effort to describe scientific ideas, which are also thought by some to be better understood than if expressed in modern language. (By the way, when people first fled into the tunnels of the Undergound, they called themselves "surfers"; and once in their underground network they called each other "subdwellers"—the usual sense of both words is the same;

this was, if anything, even before the notion of being a "dweller in the land of the surface" which has now entered our modern language—if only because many have lived their entire lives on the surface but perhaps as explorers. Today in my society I think it is right for us to think of surfers as well as surfers and surfesses to be dwellers in the land of the surface; because there's something good and alive about that part of us that floats upon the waves.) The passage that I quote comes from an underground account of a modern writer's memory of her first glimpses of the surface, or—from my own understanding of how one might write as well as one's understanding of how it is possible that some things happened exactly as the author stated them, though this author

might be remembering things which happened in their own fashion:
Our sky has blue dots moving along through the sky in long lines that appear and vanish, or flutter or roll, or even fly up and come back down again.3 Most of our knowledge of these objects is through pictures. Their luminosity appears blue when they are near the Sun, and greenish farther away, or just farther up in the sky. Blue seems to mean colder, while green seems to mean hotter, but we don't know that it means hot, and when we look into the sky with powerful glasses, we find out that blue and green objects look very different to them; for when blue and green objects get to one edge of our sky, it is called midday.

(With powerful glasses, we see that a blue dot is the opposite of a green dot in intensity; what we call white is no longer either a dot or a streak; it looks much softer than both of these.) But many of the pictures give us only these outlines of objects—nothing in the middle of them—which are, it seems to me, some kind of fin-like objects. (See: picture 3.) The sky we see from our time to time looks darker in a particular part of it. When we see it from a position in the sky—for it's easy to make a mistake when you see a light far away; if you go far enough away it isn't a dot anymore—when we see it from a certain kind of position in the sky, it appears as a flatness, more flat

than our picture can represent. For this flatness moves across our sky at some particular rate—so we say. I cannot draw it, but the people who told me about it did all that I can do—shading pictures off at various heights. But my viewpoint is so high up in the sky that at some moments—with a telescope, we could see one moment where this flatness moved faster than normal; perhaps that would change what they meant when they spoke about a dark blue hour, which is just before dawn in this part of the world; certainly what it does now is turn black as midnight on any given day at this time of year. Many of us, without any instruction at all, feel an impulse to rise up high enough in the sky to look at one moment just as the sky goes from white to black.

Belief in Belief
❦

Carl Sagan once told a parable of someone who comes to us and claims: “There is a dragon in my garage.” Fascinating! We reply that we wish to see this dragon—let us set out at once for the garage! “But wait,” the claimant says to us, “it is an invisible dragon.”

Now as Sagan points out, this doesn’t make the hypothesis unfalsifiable. Perhaps we go to the claimant’s garage, and although we see no dragon, we hear heavy breathing from no visible source; footprints mysteriously appear on the ground; and instruments show that something in the garage is consuming oxygen and breathing out carbon dioxide.

But now suppose that we say to the claimant, “Okay, we’ll visit the garage and see if we can hear heavy breathing,” and the claimant quickly says no, it’s an inaudible dragon. We propose to measure carbon dioxide in the air, and the claimant says the dragon does not breathe. We propose to toss a bag of flour into the air to see if it outlines an invisible dragon, and the claimant immediately says, “The dragon is permeable to flour.”

So then we come back to Sagan and say that this hypothesis is unfalsifiable; but he replies that by simply using an impermeable flour to throw around we might test it more rigorously.

Pretending to be Wise

The hottest place in Hell is reserved for those who in time of crisis remain neutral.

—Dante Alighieri, famous hell expert
John F. Kennedy, misquoter

It’s common to put on a show of neutrality or suspended judgment in order to signal that one is mature, wise, impartial, or just has a superior vantage point.

An example would be the case of my parents, who respond to theological questions like “Why does ancient Egypt, which had good records on many other matters, lack any records of Jews having ever been there?” with “Oh, when I was your age, I also used to ask that sort of question, but now I’ve grown out of it.”

Another example would be the principal who, faced with two children who were caught fighting on the playground, sternly says: “It doesn’t matter who started the fight, it only matters who ends it.” Of course it matters who started the fight. The principal may not have access to good information about this critical fact, but if so, the principal should say so, not dismiss the importance of who threw the first punch. Let a parent try punching the principal, and we’ll see how far “It doesn’t matter who started it” gets in front of a judge. But to adults it is just inconvenient that children fight, and it matters not at all to their convenience which child started it. It is only convenient that the fight end as rapidly as possible.

A similar dynamic, I believe, governs the occasions in international diplomacy where Great Powers sternly tell smaller groups to stop that fighting right now. It doesn’t matter to the Great Power who started it—who provoked, or who responded disproportionately to provocation—because the Great Power’s ongoing inconvenience is only a function of the ongoing conflict. Oh, can’t Israel and Hamas just get along?

This I call “pretending to be Wise.”

In each case the act of pretending is hidden: one never says out loud what you do when pretending to be Wise. What does that make Wise? No matter how difficult the world might be, surely any situation in which it would be obvious you should pretend not to be Wise—like that is—no. Instead there will always be another reason you should pretend to be Wise: perhaps the results of Wise people telling the truth could be more detrimental than those of people not being Wise; or perhaps what you need from the Wise person isn't an objective explanation, but some particular piece of

information that you don't need, because then you'll just pretend not to be Wise; or perhaps some other such case. But all of this can be much harder to describe in words than you might think!
For this reason there is no precise language available for when someone is pretending to be Wise; a Wise person and those Wise who acknowledge that that Wise person is Wise have to call their situation different kinds of Wise. If pretending not to be Wise is going to help one become Wise—perhaps someone's style of acting Wise at times would only confuse how to achieve that, when

acting Wise wasn't working; maybe even acting Wise was exactly the opposite of being Wise—in any case it is most like to work not because one is actually Wise, but because it helps one get better at being Wise in some specific area—being able to examine people with very different views—if those views are opposites of yours—with less rage; or perhaps examine them without seeing a threat they make you; perhaps learning that not every idea you can conceive of will be rejected as absurd by an idealist you dislike who then refuses to answer your questions any further.
