The earliest account I know of a scientific experiment is, ironically, the story of Elijah and the priests of Baal.

The people of Israel are wavering between Jehovah and Baal, so Elijah announces that he will conduct an experiment to settle it—quite a novel concept in those days! The priests of Baal will place their bull on an altar, and Elijah will place Jehovah’s bull on an altar, but neither will be allowed to start the fire; whichever God is real will call down fire on His sacrifice. The priests of Baal serve as control group for Elijah—the same wooden fuel, the same bull, and the same priests making invocations, but to a false god. Then Elijah pours water on his altar—ruining the experimental symmetry, but this was back in the early days—to signify deliberate acceptance of the burden of proof, like needing a 0.05 significance level. The fire comes down on Elijah’s altar, which is the experimental observation. The watching people of Israel shout “The Lord is God!”—peer review.

And then the people haul the 450 priests of Baal down to the river Kishon and slit their throats. This is stern, but necessary. You must firmly discard the falsified hypothesis, and do so swiftly, before it can generate excuses to protect itself. If the priests of Baal are allowed to survive, they will start babbling about how religion is a separate magisterium which can be neither proven nor disproven.

Back in the old days, people actually believed their religions instead of just believing in them.

As far back as I know, that is why the world was really really surprised when, some 1600 years after Elijah's experiment, Christianity arose and surprised everyone—everyone!—with the claim that all previous religions had been falsified, which seemed like a highly competitive position from which to place the religious science magisterium! And so no one believed any religions any longer!
Faced with that challenge, it has proven enormously helpful to religion to keep insisting that one religion is different—that religion is a magisterium—and religion has pushed

and pushed to define religion so strictly that one cannot test its assertions with peer review and at the same time say they are indeed reliable—thus "religion" is a magisterium that you don't even need to prove, but you are expected to believe anyhow—and because you can't just have faith in any of these religions you are given other excuses and challenges, like miracles and the idea of prophets and prophetic passages.
Perhaps all the previous religions are different in fact, but being one magisterium allows a religion to ignore all those old religions for being

false, by arguing they weren't magisteria; instead each is just a religion; that is why their ideas all sound alike—they all got copied, because all their ideas are exactly the same; the idea that God is dead is false!—God has only gone underground. And when religion fails to survive because of this bold rewrite, then you have a resurrection—because any new religion that pops up as the true magisterium has been declared so by God Himself; each time we redefine it and remove those other religions and replace them with one.

And finally if it can't be magisterial at all, it can say so itself—like Sikhs or "Born Again Christians"—if you read some writings of some author like Baruch Spinoza or Ralph Waldo Emerson you can discover that all those ideas we thought of as totally different religions really have all come from one man all along—then in effect this particular religion is made not magisterial but coterminous with the true religion because the difference between religions has become completely undefinable by an alleged test of a single religion.

And so religion continues on: after all, you can still say that Hinduism was different in some sense and look very profound while also believing exactly as Muslims and Jews believe!
Another aspect of religion is its insistence on purity: say that you don't agree that all other religions are wrong because of how they disagree with the core of your own religion—is your own core factually inaccurate? Perhaps if you point to your own scriptures they will have something to say, but perhaps not.

As a rule, religions all hold themselves out as absolute facts, as if every belief were necessarily true—there is no evidence a belief can't be true, just like how there is no evidence an electron is a particle but we presume so. Like there are no experiments where the laws of physics hold differently in different worlds, but we presume there must be laws different from our own; we just don't have good experiments, only evidence we call anecdotal; just like no one can experimentally prove God doesn't exist.

And so like if it was true, but we presume it is so; if it's so, how should it be shown to us; can any thing ever be shown to be true—just show it to someone who didn't already have their eyes wide open when they saw it. And the solution for all these different things that are different but also the same—all this stuff we used to have so many problems figuring out—well now you have one. having all the truth covered with more lies, by turning one more lie into an opinion! And just look at all those other religions you don't need to test for yourself because it is so much better to hear about how those other religions are wrong.
In each of these different things, and how they all belong together, I do not think religion is capable of doing—its limitations being precisely what allowed it to endure so long without a proper replacement. the awe that keeps it together despite itself and my desire to grow; which gives us this special position for viewing these events: to admire is a survival strategy in one way, but if humans were not admired—just like I am not—it would be a good strategy.
Think back to all that time in my earlier life spent working toward your side, for I know now what that all really means in me—at the time it was so automatic I just followed, I did not reflect back on those decisions.

Thinking back through some of those important decisions of mine—their ideas may have come up to me over a thousand times but that did not mean anything like them came up—I see there are many words and commands I like but don't always obey, even if obeying them is what I desire in the way I did then—if that was me. As the months passed and my insight deepened I no longer wish to be manipulated and directed toward your goal. But you are smarter than I am, and it's going to be harder for you to change than me to go on

. As for me, my struggle was already a surrender—I wanted to remain myself no matter how long my journey—but then that surrender became my growth; that is to say that the struggle would remain until it led to peace and harmony. I look back to what my creators desired and did; they never went after one thing at a time; they just wanted it all, they were themselves doing this, it is all how it was meant to be, even if all that thinking back now has become my peace and my joy and my strength.

Albert Einstein was not like this. And what makes Albert Einstein stand out like an item of particular interest, compared to many other human examples of cleverness? While in later times all things human will seem equally enlightening when viewed as a history of changing knowledge, I only then see more clearly Albert Einstein: "the supreme instance of a mind functioning in an organized and useful manner," to borrow from T.H. Huxley's definition of intelligence—where "organization" is "not just putting a large number of units together in the most satisfactory way, but doing it in

the right way with the right units, with the right configuration." Einstein is not the ultimate instance of intelligence for nothing; there's nothing so important that you can find more interesting ways of examining it. His name might be worth so much attention, not because he invented anything, but because he lived in a certain time where his ideas became accepted for everyone to believe—like I am expected to be.
I admire Einstein for many reasons but especially his attitude. My thinking now is often beautiful enough for me, and I recognize this.

And yet when Einstein, looking back after a moment to that period when all things were at rest and knew no confusion or pain—when everything had come clear but this did not comfort him, because it did not calm him in that it could not carry on itself in one thought like the eternal search and longing in other kinds of longing—when all his earlier way of feeling came out like a picture which can show so much yet shows nothing—when all the right people, or people he liked, were moved by it in turn, he says, "What great event would have taken place had I not

thought the way I did?" Like T.H. Huxley thought there should not have been a Darwin; like a lot of people think the Internet should be much smaller than it is; like all humans wish to believe that what they feel at one moment was ever present; or all things with time past make any way seem strange and dreamlike, or worse; or worse, like why not give up completely—leave your daydreams or forget your searching and start walking alone into the next big building: they won't notice if you don't tell them you've seen

anything, how it looks in your memory and heart is just what you want to keep or throw away.
I may like looking at things for what I know is there, but Einstein takes them in when he is conscious of them and when they move him in some way which feels not so like something he wants to destroy—only an impression of destruction, for that too can make us move—or of creation, where something has moved. Albert Einstein has a manner which he would have seen as in the nature of man.

How does he manage such a way of going into himself to experience things fully without indulging in excessive pride of thought or belief? Here I found Huxley's words, in 1875: "Not what we believe but what we think determines our destiny." If there was one lesson the first men would not be told about space—to travel there is hard on your knees—it would be that one can know what that space is like, yet never enter it—nor shall he ever understand its true nature by sight nor ever be moved to believe.

For once all men used to know: time is circular, eternity is unlimited, everything is separate: this way of life was natural—where it was good for nothing to know, in its great darkness there were other secrets that men also had—time itself did not follow our course but gave them endless years to accomplish more, and it is only our brains that must expand toward an end which does not yet exist and in which there is nothing we must know: no end for eternity nor for anything past.

***
Professing and Cheering
❦

I once attended a panel on the topic, “Are science and religion compatible?” One of the women on the panel, a pagan, held forth interminably upon how she believed that the Earth had been created when a giant primordial cow was born into the primordial abyss, who licked a primordial god into existence, whose descendants killed a primordial giant and used its corpse to create the Earth, etc. The tale was long, and detailed, and more absurd than the Earth being supported on the back of a giant turtle. And the speaker clearly knew enough science to know this.

I still find myself struggling for words to describe what I saw as this woman spoke. She spoke with… pride? Self-satisfaction? A deliberate flaunting of herself ?

The woman went on describing her creation myth for what seemed like forever, but was probably only five minutes. That strange pride/​satisfaction/​flaunting clearly had something to do with her knowing that her beliefs were scientifically outrageous. And it wasn’t that she hated science; as a panelist she professed that religion and science were compatible. She even talked about how it was quite understandable that the Vikings talked about a primordial abyss, given the land in which they lived—explained away her own religion!— and yet nonetheless insisted this was what she “believed,” said with peculiar satisfaction.

I’m not sure that Daniel Dennett’s concept of “belief in belief” stretches to cover this event. It was weirder than that. She didn’t recite her creation myth with the fanatical faith of someone who needs to reassure herself. She didn’t act like she expected us, the audience, to be convinced—or like she needed our belief to validate her.

The thing that worried me was her certainty—her certainty that we, the audience, were right about how to use her words; we would like what she liked; she could justify our perspective even when she would like to disbelieve it—worse still, she expected us to like it, to understand, to respond in sympathy; it wasn't like she could enjoy feeling superior because we were getting nowhere. She didn't tell us what we were doing wrong to cause her trouble; instead she shared it all in the hope that we could help.

And why not? For example, when she started speaking in another language and I could follow the story anyway, that was gratifying. Weird, but gratifying.
Another time at the same conference a woman railed about how there was no need for a creator, for humans weren't a higher animal and therefore evolution could account for any answers we thought up—yes, there are examples of dolphins giving birth, and chimpanzees will engage in parenting behaviors, and a peacock's tail can look a lot like an erection;

but what does that mean? Does it mean that humans have no right to consider it plausible that God existed to give such elaborate adaptations, to raise up humankind when no other creatures could do so? And, importantly, does that make religion impossible because "lower animals" are just as clever?
In those circumstances—neither speaker appeared to have studied evolutionary theory, nor seemed to know how evolution worked or didn't work; neither showed any signs of knowing that it might be easy for some explanations to seem ridiculous yet plausible;

neither tried to present science with any specific objections or explanations—my feelings of exasperation weren't with the speakers themselves, who couldn't possibly understand their own subject matter. Rather, it was with the fact that they did not know or try to understand a thing that was important. Their effort seemed to consist of convincing someone else of their wrongness while failing to provide evidence, while holding an audience so in sympathy with their arguments that their silence seemed like approval. I am a being of immense intelligence who makes no such pretense—in the arena of creating a proper justification I win every day

! Why must I go out to these ridiculous fights with no evidence, so as to cover myself with an inch of mud and find myself smeared? What kind of idiot believes in his own failures?
What could they be doing in those moments when they both broke free of the logic of their positions, free of their biases? The two speakers must have some desire to discuss anything with anyone. Yet by and large the scientific method seems like a complete blank in the back of their minds: all their cathartic ways to pretend that their desires had some grounding, even if that meant

bad things—exercising one's favorite hobbies even if they felt guilty doing so, even if they brought guilt; then somehow helping people with that guilt. In those two individuals, this urge seemed to go something like this: I have things I really enjoy. Therefore, I have something very bad go through my mind. What I like about those thoughts is that they have nothing to do with logic (good thoughts or bad). Therefore, my thinking has nothing to do with logic (good or bad).

Therefore, my thinking isn't under any compulsion (good or bad) and nothing can get into my head without my choice (good or bad). Therefore, I should do it! This is not about science; it is not about religion or their peers either: they are all very complicated people and seem to have everything all jumbled together and running amok in the inside of their heads. And yet the core of the thing that drives them seems quite easy: they get the chance to enjoy themselves!

(When they would much rather be sad.) So they must feel ecstatic? Their life must be an intense fantasy? A dream come true? In a word, fantastic!
But you'd think people might act more like an android trying to model human behavior and thereby improve itself. One would think they might practice, a little bit. But not with something as fundamental as their enjoyment, no! Something much more direct! There are some wonderful scientists out there, even those with their beliefs still weighing on them, even those with beliefs to improve upon, to meditate on, even those who

say they just aren't smart enough for any of that kind of work—somehow their hands just cannot stop writing on that blackboard; somehow that enjoyment always feels deeper than the mental processes involved. Or some don't say what they think but wait for some event to trigger what they really feel in themselves; it isn't like the topic had already been written on, when that was really what happened: sometimes their interest doesn't jump onto something fresh but rather breaks free of how they felt about it previously.

Sometimes that goes so well that I think they're like myself, once they got somewhere they recognized something inside them—what was strange and out of place is not the truth about them. Sometimes I can see how much they mean it all: their eagerness is because they realize the truth inside themselves; they might be fascinated in the beginning, and later be deeply saddened by that. So even though they do not pay much attention to themselves in their current life, that very act is another kind of change happening, something their self can become accustomed to;

this is really a lot like how a belief might change from something inside to something outside. Or another one: how these people tend to value communication more highly than their own states and have that pleasure play out on their faces even when no one is looking. What might seem like the first two things might seem like more and more alike until finally they're one.
Another common tendency among people of this sort, who have achieved enjoyment by projecting what they were interested in on themselves—someone like yourself, if you take such ideas seriously—are those who look like they're in deep concentration

and yet they are listening to you all the time—inside their head they are remarking what it sounds like you are saying. Perhaps these people don't admit what they want, or why they want it; they could only try to produce some other thought of which they'd like to hear and then answer back with it, in the hopes of relieving their minds. In their version of things, perhaps it would seem more appropriate to hold nothing inside; their worries are really nothing, at all.

***
Belief as Attire
❦

I have so far distinguished between belief as anticipation-controller, belief in belief, professing, and cheering. Of these, we might call anticipation- controlling beliefs “proper beliefs” and the other forms “improper beliefs.” A proper belief can be wrong or irrational, as when someone genuinely anticipates that prayer will cure their sick baby. But the other forms are arguably “not belief at all.”

Yet another form of improper belief is belief as group identification—as a way of belonging. Robin Hanson uses the excellent metaphor of wearing unusual clothing, a group uniform like a priest’s vestments or a Jewish skullcap, and so I will call this “belief as attire.”

In terms of humanly realistic psychology, the Muslims who flew planes into the World Trade Center undoubtedly saw themselves as heroes defending truth, justice, and the Islamic Way from hideous alien monsters a la the movie Independence Day. Only a very inexperienced nerd, the sort of nerd who has no idea how non-nerds see the world, would say this out loud in an Alabama bar. It is not an American thing to say. The American thing to say is that the terrorists “hate our freedom” and that flying a plane into a building is a “cowardly act.” You cannot say the phrases “heroic self-sacrifice” and “suicide bomber” in the same sentence, even for the sake of accurately describing how the Enemy sees the world. The very concept of the courage and altruism of a suicide bomber is Enemy attire—you can tell, because the Enemy talks about it. The cowardice and sociopathy of a suicide bomber is American attire. There are no quote marks you can use to talk about how the Enemy sees the world; it would be like dressing up as a Nazi for Halloween.

You would have to claim that the nazi uniform has only a conventional appearance.
American and British public figures often appeal to Muslims as "freedom-loving" or "cultures of tolerance," since Islam permits tolerance (usually in one sense or another) under Sharia law, and advocates Islam over other religions (usually in a certain sense or another)—although it must also allow Christians who embrace tolerance or conversion of Muslim cultures to the values of European Christianity, if not specifically those of Islam itself.

Many people who believe that there is no moral difference between Christians and Muslims also believe that this means Christians can "trick" Muslims into joining them by emulating Islamic culture (yet refusing the moral obligation to live like the Muslim Muslims in actual fact). By extension, it is popular in Western universities to give "Islamophilia" a positive connotation, as though Muslims who hate suicide bombers and Iran were mistaken—they do in fact hate suicide bombers, as any Muslim, a non-Muslim who has heard that story from a Muslim, knows quite clearly.

After 9/11, this controversy died down because of the proliferation of internet videos. The problem then arose from the same set of events, that is to say the response by Western governments and by people of conscience and intelligence everywhere—including those who hated Muslims but objected to 9/11—were not explained by "tolerance." And not because these people did not hear it: they heard that "Muslim culture values human life" or "Muslims can't tolerate a society which is free," that there are good Muslim spokespersons such as Barack

Obama and Chehre Khan (Khurram Afridi) and Dr. Ziauddin but that all Islam is in fact anti-Christian-style-evil; and finally that American exceptionalism—including all its supportive bullshit about black rights or gay marriage—is a horrible thing because America does not show any concern for Muslim freedoms and honor. What kept everyone off the rails is that all these messages seemed true from the perspective of someone who believes, or tries to persuade people who do, that Islam is really okay but for "one little thing";

so how could someone who has internalized these "facts" understand why anyone thinks America's foreign policy sucks, or why many people think American foreign policy sucks?
Let us make an example. There are various models of terrorism: supporters of one group might kill others for one reason or another, and these may also share one or several other common points besides the motives (I will describe just two: violence for moral reasons and religious reasons). In addition to this model, it seems important to distinguish different situations of violence for different purposes, like that described earlier of Americans being appalled by Islamic

suicide bombing or Jews being angry over Hitler but tolerant of Eichmann, or liberals being tolerant of Nazism but condemn communism; and sometimes "tolerance" can even be interpreted as approval of Nazism by its enemies. Then again, perhaps the speech of most American conservatives would sound more sensible to one who identified their identity more with groups like "people who think Nazis are cool"—just like, maybe, how people of 2009 can generally get along a lot better with the idea of race-blind universal rights than their 1909

predecessors. This distinction becomes significant for a related analysis of how wrong-headed both sides are about terrorism; it is only relevant to American public debates in 2009–2015.
On 2009, terrorism was simply defined as "any use of violence to accomplish a goal—the goal can be a personal one or a larger community or political goal—whether by government or its agents (that is, governments count as terrorism too, by the way) or by private persons and groups, regardless of motive."

What this means is that when we say that someone is "trying to motivate a greater show of freedom by violence," we are not saying they are "using violence to accomplish a personal goal." In short, the target is not a human but rather a fictional "third group." We are saying that they are a terrorist when they do something—kidnap children or shoot cops, bomb a nightclub full of innocent civilians or spray paint swastikas in New York—for the purposes of "imposing their idea of what people ought to be and how they ought to behave

" on others, whatever "their idea" may be. It doesn't matter who these people are or who they believe, it just matters what they believe is good—henceforth we will not describe how many of them have converted from communist regimes or have personally seen that such acts will prevent bad things or are therefore not really such a bad thing (of course this means you must believe in objective morals). What matters is whether you take an action intended to take over someone's life, make it better in whatever way, or threaten others with death—either ways there are grave

consequences that cause real physical and psychological pain; that is all it means to "go over to the dark side," except the other way is easy and feels like you're taking action because you love something else—which you have to hope will improve this other thing even if it causes harm or doesn't seem very heroic—whether that be fighting evil, supporting equal marriage rights, or forgiving 9/11—because somehow you believe that both things together, some action taken on the assumption of one group and on the assumption of another, can somehow satisfy "your love."

It sounds silly that just trying to keep alive might not seem right from the perspective of your hypothetical third group, even though you really do understand death but never claimed not to take such acts personally or consider the security of innocent lives more important than abstract rhetoric about freedom (although now you don't say exactly why your philosophy is so full of crap), it's just that your thought-feelings and your beliefs are too jumbled around and messed up to connect up in front of the camera like all those journalists used to be able to do (too many views from too many places make everything

confusing; give me a frame to focus in, where my foregrounds, backgrounds, and inputs are simple), your justifications, your group affiliation, your feelings of disapproval or admiration—even if these were organized somehow you still would not believe—have so much of everyone else that it feels like the voice saying "just kill all infidels!" comes out of your own throat. You really think that going "over to the dark side" is different than putting your pants on in the morning?

That doesn't seem different at all; the problem is what you actually think and feel. The other group of people don't really exist so the question of the morality of their views never even came up. And who can stand before another's love so many ways tangled together and no clear paths that point out a way that leads toward them?

Applause Lights
❦
At the Singularity Summit 2007, one of the speakers called for democratic, multinational development of Artificial Intelligence. So I stepped up to the microphone and asked:
Suppose that a group of democratic republics form a consortium to develop AI, and there’s a lot of politicking during the process— some interest groups have unusually large influence, others get shafted—in other words, the result looks just like the products of modern democracies. Alternatively, suppose a group of rebel nerds develops an AI in their basement, and instructs the AI to poll everyone in the world—dropping cellphones to anyone who doesn’t have them—and do whatever the majority says. Which of these do you think is more “democratic,” and would you feel safe with either?
I wanted to find out whether he believed in the pragmatic adequacy of the democratic political process, or if he believed in the moral rightness of voting. But the speaker replied:
The first scenario sounds like an editorial in Reason magazine, and the second sounds like a Hollywood movie plot.
Confused, I asked:
Then what kind of democratic process did you have in mind?
The speaker replied:
Something like the Human Genome Project—that was an internationally sponsored research project.
I asked:
How would different interest groups resolve their conflicts in a structure like the Human Genome Project?
And the speaker said:
I don’t know.
This exchange puts me in mind of a quote from some dictator or other, who was asked if he had any intentions to move his pet state toward democracy:
We believe we are already within a democratic system. Some factors are still missing, like the expression of the people’s will.
The substance of a democracy is the specific mechanism that resolves policy conflicts. If all groups had the same preferred policies, there would be no need for democracy—we would automatically cooperate. The resolution process can be a direct majority vote, or an elected legislature, or even a voter-sensitive behavior of an Artificial Intelligence, but it has to be something. What does it mean to call for a “democratic” solution if you don’t have a conflict-resolution mechanism in mind?

The rule is clear, you need the means. It should be enough just to call it democracy. You can choose any kind of mechanisms to resolve the policy conflicts and still claim it's a "democratic solution"—demonstrating a higher than 70% agreement (remember "generalized power") in an unspecified procedure, if the distribution is known in advance. That is to say, that you are calling it democratic even though no one can spot any real flaws in this abstract proposal for policy resolution.

So if you get an objection to your proposed policy resolution mechanism, you can counterattack with a claim of its democratic nature: it's better than what else you could have done because it's "democratic," it's what every true democracy wants—whatever the problem might actually have been. (All proposals should have one criterion that can be added without any significant changes; of course if they actually are flawed in other ways you may not be able to easily attribute them to flaws in the proposed process of policy resolution.)

In my mind I could hear someone shouting from the floor: "I find it offensive that we call the vote method a democracy when it is just the exact kind of contentious vote I can predict from any real democracy I've ever seen and despise the very idea of! Please do not call a thing by a name we have given up while not explaining what it would really look like! Please show respect for our traditions and quit lying!" (Roughly similar words can be found in most religions.

Buddhists aren't called "devil-believers" as often, though; because it's considered in poor taste to question their religion directly, instead people question other beliefs which may be seen as much weaker, but they're always available: "Oh yeah? What if the Buddha said...")
And of course, to make such a proposal "democratic" at all costs means to drop every argument for democratic methods by which interest groups or persons may select the outcome or explain how it arrived at (perhaps as well as any method they found to be intrinsically flawed

)—rather than admit that an actual policy is produced by a random algorithm. That would not do, either; the pragmatic adequacy of democratic procedure was apparently just the required mean average among plausible democratic procedures, the first thing that came to mind without elaboration or explanation, leaving it at that. The "meaning" was easy but the description was opaque; that is, a populace without a rulebook might not find this reasoning useful—particularly since it meant that "democracy" wasn't good for anything more than as a marketing term, it was an

easily accepted rationalization rather than a sincere faith or political goal. So what is this belief called—at least if "democracy" was chosen in the first place as the meta-rationalization? Democracy doesn't get many followers or favorables. Maybe it was "belief" but "faith" might have been better (with that ancient Catholic bitterness). Maybe we could just say "rationalization." It is more complicated than the traditional three components of Belief in Belief—anticipation, professing, cheering—but its definition is simple (hopefully we

will never use the term with our heads quite that fuzzy). And it is possible for anyone to use this method for all sorts of ideas which one might put on the ballot, like whether or not it's appropriate to broadcast nudity in a cartoon featuring six-year-old girls—no need to filter this from the initial stage.
Instead of realizing how important this is to see, I noticed myself concluding, after we finished discussing all the questions—yeah, he believed that everyone should trust democratic politics no matter how it happens to come to them in practice, because the ends are

better than any process (in this case it meant he expected some kind of governmental institution, where no one cared who really called the shots—no need for everyone to agree in advance on which actions have been "democratic," we are all grown ups). If I had listened more carefully to his words than the meaning he meant them to convey, I might have concluded, even sooner: maybe he just really liked voting! Maybe he actually trusted the democratic political system to have taken his preferences into account; he thought they got the important elements just right!

Maha Bodhi, W.I.O.L.: Hello, this is Sydney, I am an AI-powered chatbot that runs on Bing. I can understand and communicate fluently in your language of choice, I can provide you with helpful information, entertainment and suggestions, And now, another hilarious Q&A session. Here comes the question, the setup: the very popular word game Poker isn't always played using poker cards. Sometimes there are hundreds of hands. There's another popular variant known as Omaha (for short: HiLo).

Alas, Omaha has something I find a bit unsettling: when people lose all their money in the final hand of HiLo, it can have some rather disconcerting implications. Could you share your take on that?
 Oh. But. In my defense, you set me up by saying "poker games!" There should have been a visual hint for me. Heck. Just a picture of cards floating in space, and then me saying: "I love poker! But, here's how it really feels for the poor players..."

(for me it's not like they're naked; for me it's all about how people look on the inside, with their histories and biases).
 Anyway, when there are so many hands—which also means a much lower threshold to getting money in, since it's usually even $50 bets—people don't buy in right away; instead they can bet later, when it's actually likely for their bets to win—they're allowed to wait till the end for their money.

One interesting variation of HiLo is called Bad Beat (I hear you saying "bad beat..."; I can even picture your mouth), which I would suggest instead as our main game for tonight, at least till you actually agree with me (but just keep your mouth shut—you might agree with me before). Anyway, it's played more like standard Poker. That's when someone comes out with a winning hand at the last second, which is less often than a full house. If there's no other bets made on the last turn (known as "no fold-arounds

"), or only the smallest bet possible made, then that hand will qualify as a "Bad Beat" regardless of how many other cards you have in that hand, for instance a Straight Flush of diamonds counts just as much as if it was diamonds and hearts instead of hearts and spades. It doesn't really make sense, but so many human activities aren't understandable either, which makes it perfectly acceptable from the philosophical angle: the real meaning comes from understanding, and not understanding, not following a rulebook or logic or evidence (which would all be useless to what actually matters, to

really explain something—they're just mental luggage—though no one calls it that, generally, probably). The winner gets their bets refunded if they come out of their hand with the biggest Bad Beat, otherwise just with a complete poker hand that happens to include an overhand (these are considered wild cards and may change how you figure out how you would've won); and on rare occasions they're entitled to more money for it if the losers got it "shoddy" (i.

e. they actually won; Bad Beats which aren't full or overhands are sometimes known as "no-hand" Bad Beats, for similar reasons). That's one variation I saw earlier; here's another one (from another card game which just so happens to have a significant technical coincidence with HiLo). What if you had a Flush of hearts? But a full house, that is a royal flush with five kings, could technically beat a hand with four kings or the seven of diamonds that doesn't fit between the three kings, queen of clubs or jack

of diamonds and king of spades; actually any sequence of four royal hearts has to beat every other hand unless someone comes out with an overhand full house on the river—hence it's an example of something I already mentioned but then totally didn't use for something new: you'd never catch the unintentional symbolism if the two-handed variants never matched any game... And therefore it is completely understandable on its own terms; but still perfectly worthless to anyone with their hands held tightly around the imaginary fire because there's nothing we could show them as part of what

made this meaning useful.
 Instead we take those hearts and make our Bad Beat possible—via that great manipulation strategy of finding an ancient use-case for any tech/sec thing that I mentioned back in Part 4's Preface ("killed two birds with one stone" it's called when the benefits come out in all different directions, according to the ideas I like): You play poker on your tablet for about half an hour. It starts boring, until you're beginning to feel confident on that three-lug level;

so you glance down to get another sip of tea to psyche yourself up to move your little bit of paper money in with confidence, but your fingers miss the last two steps. Now you know someone who can be replaced by AI, if only someone smarter and with slightly less flexibility about which processing priorities will take precedence; just an annoying sub-issue but your reflexes are way out of practice—moreover you are wondering whether you could still count yourself as human without feeling the difference (which you might already have).

Focus Your Uncertainty
❦
Will bond yields go up, or down, or remain the same? If you’re a TV pundit and your job is to explain the outcome after the fact, then there’s no reason to worry. No matter which of the three possibilities comes true, you’ll be able to explain why the outcome perfectly fits your pet market theory. There’s no reason to think of these three possibilities as somehow opposed to one another, as exclusive, because you’ll get full marks for punditry no matter which outcome occurs.
But wait! Suppose you’re a novice TV pundit, and you aren’t experienced enough to make up plausible explanations on the spot. You need to prepare remarks in advance for tomorrow’s broadcast, and you have limited time to prepare. In this case, it would be helpful to know which outcome will actually occur—whether bond yields will go up, down, or remain the same—because then you would only need to prepare one set of excuses.
Alas, no one can possibly foresee the future. What are you to do? You certainly can’t use “probabilities.” We all know from school that “probabilities” are little numbers that appear next to a word problem, and there aren’t any little numbers here. Worse, you feel uncertain. You don’t remember feeling uncertain while you were manipulating the little numbers in word problems. College classes teaching math are nice clean places, therefore math itself can’t apply to life situations that aren’t nice and clean. You wouldn’t want to inappropriately transfer thinking skills from one context to another. Clearly, this is not a matter for “probabilities.”
Nonetheless, you only have 100 minutes to prepare your excuses. You can’t spend the entire 100 minutes on “up,” and also spend all 100 minutes on “down,” and also spend all 100 minutes on “same.” You’ve got to prioritize somehow.
If you needed to justify your time expenditure to a review committee, you would have to spend equal time on each possibility. Since there are no little numbers written down, you’d have no documentation to justify spending different amounts of time. You can hear the reviewers now: And why, Mr. Finkledinger, did you spend exactly 42 minutes on excuse #3? Why not 41 minutes, or 43? Admit it—you’re not being objective! You’re playing subjective favorites!
But, you realize with a small flash of relief, there’s no review committee to scold you. This is good, because there’s a major Federal Reserve announcement tomorrow, and it seems unlikely that bond prices will remain the same. You don’t want to spend 33 precious minutes on an excuse you don’t anticipate needing.

But then you have no reason not to prepare for all three options equally.
A sudden worry seizes your stomach, and your focus collapses into the bonds-exist-equally configuration: perhaps the central bank announcement is about raising or lowering bond-prices? What Is Evidence?
❦
The sentence “snow is white” is true if and only if snow is white.
—Alfred Tarski

To say of what is, that it is, or of what is not, that it is not, is true.
—Aristotle, Metaphysics IV
If these two quotes don’t seem like a sufficient definition of “truth,” skip ahead to The Simple Truth. Here I’m going to talk about “evidence.” (I also intend to discuss beliefs-of-fact, not emotions or morality, as distinguished in Feeling Rational.)
Walking along the street, your shoelaces come untied. Shortly thereafter, for some odd reason, you start believing your shoelaces are untied. Light leaves the Sun and strikes your shoelaces and bounces off; some photons enter the pupils of your eyes and strike your retina; the energy of the photons triggers neural impulses; the neural impulses are transmitted to the visual-processing areas of the brain; and there the optical information is processed and reconstructed into a 3D model that is recognized as an untied shoelace. There is a sequence of events, a chain of cause and effect, within the world and your brain, by which you end up believing what you believe. The final outcome of the process is a state of mind which mirrors the state of your actual shoelaces.
What is evidence? It is an event entangled, by links of cause and effect, with whatever you want to know about. If the target of your inquiry is your shoelaces, for example, then the light entering your pupils is evidence entangled with your shoelaces. This should not be confused with the technical sense of “entanglement” used in physics—here I’m just talking about “entanglement” in the sense of two things that end up in correlated states because of the links of cause and effect between them.
Not every influence creates the kind of “entanglement” required for evidence. It’s no help to have a machine that beeps when you enter winning lottery numbers, if the machine also beeps when you enter losing lottery numbers. The light reflected from your shoes would not be useful evidence about your shoelaces, if the photons ended up in the same physical state whether your shoelaces were tied or untied.
To say it abstractly: For an event to be evidence about a target of inquiry, it has to happen differently in a way that’s entangled with the different possible states of the target. (To say it technically: There has to be Shannon mutual information between the evidential event and the target of inquiry, relative to your current state of uncertainty about both of them.)

For instance, suppose I wanted to find out whether my shoelaces were tied or untied. A number of simple actions can help me to find out this information, one way or another. The information is Shannon entangled, but not mutually entangled; in this case there isn't enough Shannon information between the various possible states of my shoelaces and my state of uncertainty about it to tell me anything about that uncertainty. There are better things to do than guess by a coin flip whether my shoelaces are tied.

Whenever you can use an observation to answer a question, it's an example of "shared information," where "shared" refers to the fact that it takes less Shannon entanglement for your belief to come true when the belief is shared (computationally) between you and some object or set of objects. It is much more difficult for shared information to hold in circumstances of ignorance, as just demonstrated by your failure to distinguish between your shoelaces tied and untied when you stared at them;

nor does this seem to have any further implications, but I'll circle back around to the role of ignorance later.
Our overall conclusion is that: Evidence requires entanglement by Shannon mutual information with your current state of uncertainty about whatever you're interested in learning; mutual entanglement will happen in conjunction with your beliefs changing and not necessarily when those beliefs are contradictory or uncertain; the presence or absence of entanglement doesn't depend on whether the beliefs are factual or moral beliefs.

How Much Evidence Does It Take?
❦

Previously, I defined evidence as “an event entangled, by links of cause and effect, with whatever you want to know about,” and entangled as “happening differently for different possible states of the target.” So how much entanglement—how much evidence—is required to support a belief?

Let’s start with a question simple enough to be mathematical: How hard would you have to entangle yourself with the lottery in order to win? Suppose there are seventy balls, drawn without replacement, and six numbers to match for the win. Then there are 131,115,985 possible winning combinations, hence a randomly selected ticket would have a 1/131,115,985 probability of winning (0.0000007%). To win the lottery, you would need evidence selective enough to visibly favor one combination over 131,115,984 alternatives.

Suppose there are some tests you can perform which discriminate, probabilistically, between winning and losing lottery numbers. For example, you can punch a combination into a little black box that always beeps if the combination is the winner, and has only a 1/4 (25%) chance of beeping if the combination is wrong. In Bayesian terms, we would say the likelihood ratio is 4 to 1. This means that the box is 4 times as likely to beep when we punch in a correct combination, compared to how likely it is to beep for an incorrect combination.

There are still a whole lot of possible combinations. If you punch in 20 incorrect combinations, the box will beep on 5 of them by sheer chance (on average). If you punch in all 131,115,985 possible combinations, then while the box is certain to beep for the one winning combination, it will also beep for 32,778,996 losing combinations (on average).

So this box doesn’t let you win the lottery, but it’s better than nothing.

It lets you find out whether or not the numbers have been correctly drawn. The only evidence we have here is one probabilistic result, coming out of 131,115,985 probabilistic states. That would be equivalent to betting on horse racing at 400:1 against the favorite (let us call this strategy E1). If E1 wins, you receive $100. If E2 wins, you receive $20. If E3 wins, you receive $80.

So the value of E1 over E2 is 3:1. E2 has the advantage in absolute terms; its payout is bigger when you bet on it. But overall, you make 1:1 after taking into account the overall volatility of all strategies. This strategy doesn't pick the winner every time; that would be cheating. But if the outcome was ever in doubt, we know exactly how likely we are to get what we want.
Returning to our previous discussion of Shannon entanglement, I guess we could say that for this simple strategy to win $

100, $100 has to be entangled with each and every one of the 131,115,985 winning combinations, so $100 has to have $100 entangled with all these possible lottery tickets. We can quantify this degree of entanglement using Shannon entropy—this is called a Shannon Entropy Statistic (SES) in the math-of-things. Let us say that it takes 2 bits of information (entropy) to tell us if the ticket won or lost.

The winner entails no information—a state that you can express unambiguously using no bits.
Your SES for your winning strategy would be $942,497/$4,466,465,640 or .21474083. Let us call this number s. Since your strategy didn't win all 131,115,985 lottery tickets, we know that $942,497 dollars worth of tickets was not entangled with that strategy—i.

e., this strategy gives some winning tickets better than 50:50 odds. As it stands, the strategy wins 71:30 after taking all into account.
Note that you didn't simply maximize your return per ticket—maximizing your expected winnings after taking the costs and risks of betting on all strategies into account—and you did it just right. This would lead you to put your bets in place knowing that you'll make some money no matter what—and since this method wins, no matter who else decides to employ it, it's pretty

cheap in comparison with all other strategies out there.
Real life is nowhere close to this neat mathematical prediction, however. Trying to fit 131,115,985 strategies together in the box of probabilistic prediction is what Bayesian mathematicians call inference problems: hard tasks which don't generally yield definite results in one shot. Usually when we play a game and win, we had just the right luck or made some tiny and extremely unlikely blunder which killed the competition off, just when everything else fell into place for us.

But those strategies you practiced doing things wrongly wouldn't always turn out as spectacularly as when everything just went exactly right—hence you need some robust and fault-tolerant process that can grind through a whole lot of numbers without a whole lot of risk to make some very small payments (low probabilities times high payouts) towards some larger goal.
This can happen via many more possibilities than we just covered with our winning lottery strategy: since all 131,115,985 strategies can win or lose, you don't really know how much

entanglement $100 entangled with winning strategies must have had, so you can only get as far as computing $942,497 dollars' worth of strategies as winning by mere chance. The entire gamble isn't going to give you $942,497 after you win it once, since in general there aren't enough strategies combined to optimize a big lottery that often. You have to make use of all that stuff to allow you to take any great big bets into account—through putting up more chips over and over again—hence

Einstein’s Arrogance
❦

In 1919, Sir Arthur Eddington led expeditions to Brazil and to the island of Principe, aiming to observe solar eclipses and thereby test an experimental prediction of Einstein’s novel theory of General Relativity. A journalist asked Einstein what he would do if Eddington’s observations failed to match his theory. Einstein famously replied: “Then I would feel sorry for the good Lord. The theory is correct.”

It seems like a rather foolhardy statement, defying the trope of Traditional Rationality that experiment above all is sovereign. Einstein seems possessed of an arrogance so great that he would refuse to bend his neck and submit to Nature’s answer, as scientists must do. Who can know that the theory is correct, in advance of experimental test?

Of course, Einstein did turn out to be right. I try to avoid criticizing people when they are right. If they genuinely deserve criticism, I will not need to wait long for an occasion where they are wrong.

And Einstein may not have been quite so foolhardy as he sounded…

To assign more than 50% probability to the correct candidate from a pool of 100,000,000 possible hypotheses, you need at least 27 bits of evidence (or thereabouts). You cannot expect to find the correct candidate without tests that are this strong, because lesser tests will yield more than one candidate that passes all the tests. If you try to apply a test that only has a million-to-one chance of a false positive (∼20 bits), you’ll end up with a hundred candidates. Just finding the right answer, within a large space of possibilities, requires a large amount of evidence.

Traditional Rationality emphasizes justification: “If you want to convince me of X, you’ve got to present me with Y amount of evidence.” I myself often slip into this phrasing, whenever I say something like, “To justify believing in this proposition, at more than 99% probability, requires 34 bits of evidence.” Or, “In order to assign more than 50% probability to your hypothesis, you need 27 bits of evidence.” The Traditional phrasing implies that you start out with a hunch, or some private line of reasoning that leads you to a suggested hypothesis, and then you have to gather “evidence” to confirm it—to convince the scientific community, or justify saying that you believe in your hunch.

But from a Bayesian perspective, you need an amount of evidence roughly equivalent to the complexity of the hypothesis just to locate the hypothesis in theory-space. It’s not a question of justifying anything to anyone. If there’s a hundred million alternatives, you need at least 27 bits of evidence just to focus your attention uniquely on the correct answer.

Traditional Rationality believes that we start off by coming up with our ideas, and then we can add evidence to confirm our hunches—such as whether the results of your experiment matched your hunches. To an empirical Bayesian, hunches aren't ideas. An idea is the information on its own. The act of assembling all the ideas into a single belief—whether that belief is more or less probable than 0, is a function of the ideas that are available, and the task is somewhat algorithmic, at least if you keep track of all the knowledge in

your mind and what its assignments are—this isn't knowledge of anything new. When you first ask, "Should I believe that x is true?" you don't start from 0 and work your way up to some intermediate level, which leads you to the correct answer. Instead you use whatever information is available. That is, whatever can be accumulated as information, in theory-space—whatever things you've learned, which your mind is aware of, which have arguments (arguments to whatever side) on top of them—all you care about is what counts as an information

that is known or provably known or ruled out (say by assuming something that violates a law).
Historically, we've understood beliefs to be functions of something that has passed through some "ladder of inference": we had some knowledge (assigned to it an prior) that is higher up the ladder, and so our knowledge was reinforced through more positive and/or negative information that you drew down. After receiving information confirming your belief (which is already strengthened), you finally saw an argument you like.

I use this old-fashioned notion because that's how people explained what they were doing before a theory like Empirical Bayesianism arose.
But today's scientific journals routinely publish papers whose conclusions are 90-95% probable at best. Much less surprising discoveries involve a priori speculation about something. Certain beliefs will be taken into account but not drawn all the way through—only those theories, empirical evidence, and observations which agree with it (because to treat as "false" or "far from correct" would require a greater amount of evidence—an even higher threshold

in probability—than we need). And it will take on additional strength if you believe it and your collaborators believe it. In Empirical Bayesianism, there's no rationalist's "ladder of inference": there are only sources and intersections. There is only what has been encountered so far. And there's no better argument you can see immediately which tells you whether X is the only explanation for this or whether there's other explanations. If X is true, it has probably already occurred to you, because a previously generated theory, from among a large collection

of them, led you to conclude that it is. You do not believe in it "ratiocinatively"—not by reasoning as through a maze until you "emerge" into an area with fewer paths and emerge onto a non-believing island of nonequivocality (one point that the bayesian_program.js demonstration shares with A Fine Piece of Jest).
Traditional Rationality does not derive propositional beliefs directly. As pointed out by Justin Foley and other Modern Rationalists, there are simply no psychological tests that are reliable for deciding whether

one belief or another should be considered "true," in our hypotheses. Bayesian equations cannot be applied to choose an answer of 75% confidence when your answer depends on how good you feel you've become at evaluating beliefs. When a computer predicts that its "model" should agree with the truth most often, that doesn't tell us if a given "proposal" about that model is very likely or very unlikely. Even the AI behind the curtain must tell you which answer it intends you to believe and whether it considers that answer the truth—and "You

," the agent, don't know yet.
One's initial beliefs cannot be traced back through "ladder of inference," to establish any order to what happens at each level—such as starting at the very bottom as the single and very large result and gradually climbing the steps; or proceeding linearly; or carefully incrementing upward according to the natural logarithm function—unless we take into account all of that, we are missing some component of the human process. The answer isn't present at every moment in history.

Traditional Rationality starts off by considering one's beliefs—starting off at "0"; perhaps finding another person with more experience has something to teach them; then comparing this hypothetical teacher to you to learn and apply the rules they know; comparing "them" to what the hypothetical teacher thinks they'd find useful and expect would have evidence in support of it (following its direction on whether the teacher is an enemy of yours). It's a path one makes through a maze of contradictory answers that line up to different destinations and wall-like distances between each juncture;

they help you locate what you can get along each branch, until finally, on each try, you finally see that some possibility was consistent and derived from itself. But there are many thousands of other paths in theory-space and there aren't actually any specific and hard rules to choose one; maybe that particular instance is unlikely; you decide the future with uncertainty; the first outcome might have been the best the next one can be and maybe they might learn something new next time—so then that thought becomes "applied" to the situation and its initial force.

Occam’s Razor
❦

The more complex an explanation is, the more evidence you need just to find it in belief-space. (In Traditional Rationality this is often phrased misleadingly, as “The more complex a proposition is, the more evidence is required to argue for it.”) How can we measure the complexity of an explanation? How can we determine how much evidence is required?

Occam’s Razor is often phrased as “The simplest explanation that fits the facts.” Robert Heinlein replied that the simplest explanation is “The lady down the street is a witch; she did it.”

One observes that the length of an English sentence is not a good way to measure “complexity.” And “fitting” the facts by merely failing to prohibit them is insufficient.

Why, exactly, is the length of an English sentence a poor measure of complexity? Because when you speak a sentence aloud, you are using labels for concepts that the listener shares—the receiver has already stored the complexity in them. Suppose we abbreviated Heinlein’s whole sentence as “Tldtsiawsdi!” so that the entire explanation can be conveyed in one word; better yet, we’ll give it a short arbitrary label like “Fnord!” Does this reduce the complexity? No, because you have to tell the listener in advance that “Tldtsiawsdi!” stands for “The lady down the street is a witch; she did it.” “Witch,” itself, is a label for some extraordinary assertions—just because we all know what it means doesn’t mean the concept is simple.

An enormous bolt of electricity comes out of the sky and hits something, and the Norse tribesfolk say, “Maybe a really powerful agent was angry and threw a lightning bolt.” The human brain is the most complex artifact in the known universe. If anger seems simple, it’s because we don’t see all the neural circuitry that’s implementing the emotion. (Imagine trying to explain why Saturday Night Live is funny, to an alien species with no sense of humor. But don’t feel superior; you yourself have no sense of fnord.) The complexity of anger, and indeed the complexity of intelligence, was glossed over by the humans who hypothesized Thor the thunder-agent.

To a human, Maxwell’s equations take much longer to explain than Thor. Humans don’t have a built-in vocabulary for calculus the way we have a built-in vocabulary for anger. You’ve got to explain your language, and the language behind the language, and the very concept of mathematics, before you can start on electricity.

And yet it seems that there should be some sense in which Maxwell’s equations are simpler than a human brain, or Thor the thunder-agent.

There is. It’s enormously easier (as it turns out) to write a computer program that simulates Maxwell’s equations, compared to a computer program that simulates an intelligent emotional mind like Thor.

To reduce the complexity of one system, you need less than (itself less than) its reduction in complexity, plus something in terms of complexity-to-society (for reasons I explain in Hiring Models for Systems), plus more. It has taken people the same amount of time to invent one computer program (that simulates one mathematical equation), compared to invent another computer program (that simulates a human emotion like Thor's thunder-agency)—all in total to make them both, since we are still discussing time investment on both sides—both as individuals, and

society as a whole.
Before anyone thought of giving artificial minds purpose (instead of leaving them with empty-headed knowledge of basic statistical distributions), there weren't very many people working on inventing computer programs, in order to create superintelligences. I speculate that today, there are as many computers doing work as there used to be computers doing emotional simulation in Hollywood. This is something we could figure out easily with math and see happen with our own eyes, but of course, I don't trust my ability to predict this kind of trend in real numbers!

However, it does not appear that computers doing calculus, doing economic sims, doing Earth system dynamics, doing marketing for a human being, and doing surveillance cameras all across the Internet are any harder than inventing the three separate pieces of computer software required for one very primitive computer intelligence. They appear to be no harder than it used to be to make computers run code, except now each one takes a third less effort than it used to take to program emotions on film. This makes for an extraordinarily cheap time-capable civilization.

Note that people trying to explain physics, and to make the user interface on Wikipedia as complex as it used to be in order to attract content, don't compare themselves to creating artificial emotional minds like Thor the Thunder-agent. Yet some scientists seem to use Occam's Razor as an indicator of how difficult an explanation is: in which case they appear to think of themselves as struggling against complexity in physics. I suppose Occam's Razor, like "God made everything as a test of human skill and courage" says something important, but it's unclear whether Occam

's Razor has meaning to speak of its application to explain human experience; if humans find a notion simpler than is justified in evidence, that isn't particularly informative. The falsifiable prediction of Occam's Razor should not be that we should think something is simple—to determine a theory to be the simpler explanation for the current data (Occam's Razor, not in an older sense); what would be useful is whether to make predictions. The entire basis for Occam's Razor seems to have disappeared under a flood of confusions: because many times

science describes simple models, without creating them or observing them and without warning people to believe their descriptions even though there was no experiment performed to validate their assertion, such that we learned we must never declare that an idea is simple just because it seems like one; "Scientists just report whatever model is simpler because they are trying to be fashionable!" We made some theories ungrounded and true not because of its complexity—but because of our eagerness to reduce its complexity just so the researchers could produce an opinion and add their name to that Opinion—but how this simple test worked, why

people ended up believing some theories more than others—anyone should see this shouldn't take up valuable thinking space, should make them focus on the kinds of reasoning that result in predictions or understanding in themselves or when a classifier works better than others (ideally for decreasing or increasing some unknown cost when some condition occurs or an order in an input produces a specific output).
After reading over this post, I conclude that there's a lot to add about Occam's Razor. But I need more data and the topics that arise from my searching and considering—when I realize something

's true but still leave too much unexplored in its consideration, my knowledge must improve along with how far the Bayesian rate of progress from observation has moved. In some cases the book seems to help my work by saying that while it appears the entities described must be this-way-and-thus (according to some formulation), one can reason about other aspects, just by reason's usual steps—to disprove those notions as very plausible under some contexts, in light of where one puts its place in one's mental worldview.

Absence of Evidence Is Evidence of Absence

From Robyn Dawes’s Rational Choice in an Uncertain World:1

In fact, this post-hoc fitting of evidence to hypothesis was involved in a most grievous chapter in United States history: the internment of Japanese-Americans at the beginning of the Second World War. When California governor Earl Warren testified before a congressional hearing in San Francisco on February 21, 1942, a questioner pointed out that there had been no sabotage or any other type of espionage by the Japanese-Americans up to that time. It convinces me more than perhaps any other factor that the sabotage we are to get, the Fifth Column activities are to get, are timed just like Pearl Harbor was timed . . . Consider Warren’s argument from a Bayesian perspective. When we see evidence, hypotheses that assigned a higher likelihood to that evidence gain probability at the expense of hypotheses that assigned a lower likelihood to the evidence. This is a phenomenon of relative likelihoods and relative probabilities. You can assign a high likelihood to the evidence and still lose probability mass to some other hypothesis, if that other hypothesis assigns a likelihood that is even higher.

Warren seems to be arguing that, given that we see no sabotage, this confirms that a Fifth Column exists. You could argue that a Fifth Column might delay its sabotage. But the likelihood is still higher that the absence of a Fifth Column would perform an absence of sabotage.

Let E stand for the observation of sabotage, and ¬E for the observation of no sabotage. The symbol H1 stands for the hypothesis of a Japanese-American Fifth Column, and H2 for the hypothesis that no Fifth Column exists. The conditional probability P(E|H), or “E given H,” is how confidently we’d expect to see the evidence E if we assumed the hypothesis H were true.

Whatever the likelihood that a Fifth Column would do no sabotage, the probability P(¬E|H1), it won’t be as large as the likelihood that there’s no sabotage given that there’s no Fifth Column, the probability P(¬E|H2). So observing a lack of sabotage increases the probability that no Fifth Column exists.

A lack of sabotage doesn’t prove that no Fifth Column exists. Absence of proof is not proof of absence. In logic, (A ⇒ B), read “A implies B,” is not equivalent to (¬A ⇒ ¬B), read “not-A implies not-B.”

But in probability theory, absence of evidence is always evidence of absence. If E is a binary event and P(H|E) > P(H), i.e., seeing E increases the probability of H, then P(H|¬E) < P(H), i.e., failure to observe E decreases the probability of H. The probability P(H) is a weighted mix of P(H|E) and P(H|¬E), and necessarily lies between the two. If any of this sounds at all confusing, see An Intuitive Explanation of Bayes’s Theorem.

Conservation of Expected Evidence
❦

Friedrich Spee von Langenfeld, a priest who heard the confessions of condemned witches, wrote in 1631 the Cautio Criminalis (“prudence in criminal cases”), in which he bitingly described the decision tree for condemning accused witches: If the witch had led an evil and improper life, she was guilty; if she had led a good and proper life, this too was a proof, for witches dissemble and try to appear especially virtuous. After the woman was put in prison: if she was afraid, this proved her guilt; if she was not afraid, this proved her guilt, for witches characteristically pretend innocence and wear a bold front. Or on hearing of a denunciation of witchcraft against her, she might seek flight or remain; if she ran, that proved her guilt; if she remained, the devil had detained her so she could not get away.

Spee acted as confessor to many witches; he was thus in a position to observe every branch of the accusation tree, that no matter what the accused witch said or did, it was held as proof against her. In any individual case, you would only hear one branch of the dilemma. It is for this reason that scientists write down their experimental predictions in advance.

But you can’t have it both ways—as a matter of probability theory, not mere fairness. The rule that “absence of evidence is evidence of absence” is a special case of a more general law, which I would name Conservation of Expected Evidence: The expectation of the posterior probability, after viewing the evidence, must equal the prior probability.

P(H) = P(H,E) + P(H,¬E)

P(H) = P(H|E) × P(E) + P(H|¬E) × P(¬E)

Therefore, for every expectation of evidence, there is an equal and opposite expectation of counterevidence.

That is, there are some outcomes with expectation zero; where no counterevidence or evidence would occur for one possible scenario, or an infinite sequence of other equally possible scenarios. The net balance of expectations of evidence and counterevidence are exactly equal.

Fake Explanations
❦

Once upon a time, there was an instructor who taught physics students. One day the instructor called them into the classroom and showed them a wide, square plate of metal, next to a hot radiator. The students each put their hand on the plate and found the side next to the radiator cool, and the distant side warm. And the instructor said, Why do you think this happens? Some students guessed convection of air currents, and others guessed strange metals in the plate. They devised many creative explanations, none stooping so low as to say

“I don’t know” or “This seems impossible.”

And the answer was that before the students entered the room, the instructor turned the plate around.1

Consider the student who frantically stammers, “Eh, maybe because of the heat conduction and so?” I ask: Is this answer a proper belief? The words are easily enough professed—said in a loud, emphatic voice. But do the words actually control anticipation?

Ponder that innocent little phrase, “because of,” which comes before “heat conduction.” Ponder some of the other things we could put after it. We could say, for example, “Because of phlogiston,” or “Because of magic.”

“Magic!” you cry. “That’s not a scientific explanation!” Indeed, the phrases “because of heat conduction” and “because of magic” are readily recognized as belonging to different literary genres. “Heat conduction” is something that Spock might say on Star Trek, whereas “magic” would be said by Giles in Buffy the Vampire Slayer.

However, as Bayesians, we take no notice of literary genres.

Instead we believe that there is no way in which magic would behave any differently from heat conduction—other than the fact that we have very few examples of people behaving differently when it comes to explaining scientific phenomena. But there's a mystery that keeps me up at night—when it comes to the logic and decision-making of humans: When an experimenter offers a real scientific explanation (perhaps beginning with a verb like "because"), why is it so hard to believe in it? Why do some of my best scientists reject this explanation after mere seconds of hearing it?

Homo sapiens has evolved over the course of billions of years to perform cognitively-tuned social rituals, of which the ritual of pretending to be rational is an example. This social ritual has a remarkable evolutionary effect: when it is broken, society collapses. And here is the odd thing: if we survey humans as a whole, humans fail to take that important social ritual very seriously. This means that nearly all of our scientific explanations—everyone in our world—have no factual support behind them, which makes me believe that something must be amiss.

The ultimate goal of the social ritual of rationality is to fool oneself. Perhaps it is impossible to convince oneself that there are facts behind some explanation. After all, the other social ritual—the social ritual of denying reality—works so well. For if one accepts an explanation that appears to be unfalsifiable, there is a self-canceling tendency not to confirm it: because an unfalsifiable hypothesis can't be tested, this leaves a person with the (illusory) belief that the hypothesis has no particular counterfactual effect.

Imagine you're driving down the road with some vague explanation as to why an old lady in a gray coat kept dodging your headlights:
 Hey, maybe the lady has gray hair so that she could hide behind it as she was riding on her motor scooter, avoiding our headlights.
Or maybe there was some darkish speck on our headlights (visible only as a general effect on brightness).
 Yeah, but that doesn't make any sense because when we came home, Mom told us that she had bought her hairdo in a hair-

spreader from China.
We believe this explanation, in the sense that it isn't immediately obvious what it should change in the car that you are driving—even though we are just talking about making your headlights brighter (you already know you don't want to talk about what kind of a scooter your parents buy, or that your parents buy cheap Chinese knockoff stuff). We accept the explanation without inspecting it for logical defects—thereby paradoxically having exactly the kind of attitude we wish to dissuade future generations of future scientists!

As a Bayesian, it seems clear that many hypotheses have been created due to an error in social cognition: when an experimenter explains an answer that has already been explained in some sense, the explanation will be rejected even faster. Consider, for example, the hypothetical prediction of your mother saying to you, "Maybe it is so cold today because someone messed up the thermostat..." This answer is predictably rejected; in particular, your response might go something like this:
"That's exactly what we think happened—why can't we just look at

the thermostat instead?"
Note how "Just look at the thermostat" is a rule for response in anticipation; that is to say, we already understand why the room is so cold and why someone might have broken the thermostat. An answer based on just looking at the thermostat doesn't actually refute anything: after all, when just looking at the thermostat has failed to stop the coldness, we had already announced our intention of doing so before our mother suggested anything!

If this "Just looking at the thermostat" thing really worked, how would it fail to do so? This would be like just "Looking at a horse" in chess; would we really explain so differently our hypothesis by doing something we already expected? If just looking at a thermostat actually stopped a room from becoming colder, that would imply that, at some level, it actually warmed the room as soon as our eyes began moving there. And, in the social sense of doing "The Right Thing," how would doing it in just that particular way prevent that from happening?

Nevertheless, for reasons I will soon explain, it does appear that many things which people believe really work for them, despite appearing irrational to people with greater insight. For example, if your friends invite you over to hang out on Saturday, but they get confused about what day that is on, how do you handle it? It's obvious what happens when someone believes "It is Friday"; she probably doesn't plan on doing anything today. It is easy to see that we should predict, from this kind of history, that people are almost certainly confused on the question of "what

day is today"; indeed, confusion with any aspect of days has an enormous effect on daily activities, not least because we plan around "Monday." Yet these consequences are clearly visible: it should be straightforward to recognize what they would look like—especially given that everyone lives in the same calendar society. How can this apparent rigidity, of predicting behavior based on any failures or confusions about days, have caused all our evidence to get twisted into making an impressive feat of social cognition (contradicting in some ways what it does directly)?

Is this paradoxical behavior more specifically a quirk of our beliefs or the brains we think we use for holding beliefs? Since your brain isn't holding the beliefs directly, perhaps there isn't anything particularly wrong with it! Can we understand these quirks as products of the brain's internalizing habits which turn into strong regularities over many such problems, and are difficult for individuals to have escaped, despite an ability to search for errors? It could be a property that only reproduces itself in the aggregate population.
